prompt:
Section A - Short Answer Questions. Answer ten of the items (a), (b), (c)... in Question 1.

(b) (i) Is the election process to Seanad Éireann a democratic process? Give a reason for your answer.
(ii) What is the purpose of the Seanad?
(4 marks)
model_answer:
(i) No, it is not fully democratic. It breaks the principle of 'one person, one vote'. Of the 60 senators, 11 are nominated by the Taoiseach, 6 are elected only by university graduates and 43 are chosen in panel elections by TDs, outgoing senators and councillors, so most citizens have no vote.
(ii) Its main purpose is to debate and consider Bills passed by the Dáil. It can propose amendments or delay a Bill, acting as a check and balance, although the Dáil can override it.
marking_scheme: Section A: each item is marked out of 4 (ten items answered; 2 extra marks are added to each of the five items with the highest marks, so Question 1 totals 50). (i) One valid explanation, 2 marks (good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0). E.g. the Seanad goes against the most basic principle of a modern democratic electoral system - equality between citizens, 'one person one vote'; the Seanad has 60 members: the Taoiseach nominates 11, 6 are elected by university graduates and 43 in Seanad panel elections. (ii) One fact, 2 marks (good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0). E.g. the vast majority of Bills come from the Government and are passed by the Dáil first, then sent to the Seanad for debate and consideration; within 90 days the Seanad may propose amendments, reject or pass a Bill; the Dáil has the power to override the Seanad's rejection of a Bill.

prompt:
Section A - Short Answer Questions. Answer ten of the items (a), (b), (c)... in Question 1.

(c) Explain what it means to say that human rights are - universal, inalienable and indivisible.
Universal ...
Inalienable ...
Indivisible ...
(4 marks)
model_answer:
Universal: human rights belong to every person everywhere in the world, equally, simply because they are human. Article 1 of the UDHR says 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
Inalienable: rights cannot be taken away or given away, except in specific situations by due process - e.g. a person convicted by a court can lose their liberty.
Indivisible: all rights have equal status and depend on each other; you cannot rank them, and denying one blocks the enjoyment of others.
marking_scheme: Section A: each item is marked out of 4 (ten items answered; 2 extra marks are added to each of the five items with the highest marks, so Question 1 totals 50). First explanation 2 marks (good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0); the other two 1 mark each. If the first part gets 1 mark or less, the second/third is marked out of 2. Universal: everyone is born with the same rights; they belong to all humans in every society and should apply to all persons in the world equally. Inalienable: 'inability of something to be taken from or given away by the possessor' - human rights should not be taken away, except in exceptional situations and according to due process (e.g. the right to liberty may be restricted if a court finds a person guilty of a crime). Indivisible: all human rights have equal status and cannot be placed in a hierarchical order.

(d) Is it possible to talk about a shared Irish identity in Ireland today? Justify your answer.
(4 marks)
model_answer: Only partly. There is still a shared identity built on common history and traditions: the GAA calls its games 'a means of consolidating our Irish identity', Irish people worldwide celebrate St Patrick's Day, and most children learn the same curriculum - Anderson's 'imagined community'. But Ireland is now multicultural: 17% of residents were born abroad and 182 languages are spoken (CSO 2016), and religion and language are no longer shared by all. So today there are many Irish identities rather than one.
marking_scheme: Section A: each item is marked out of 4 (ten items answered; 2 extra marks are added to each of the five items with the highest marks, so Question 1 totals 50). One valid reason: very good 3-4, good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0. Irish national identity arises from the shared history and traditions of Irish people (these traditions are in flux; older ones are still vibrant in many areas, new ones are emerging). Arguments in favour: the GAA's Official Guide says its games are 'a means of consolidating our Irish identity'; a shared sense of identity among Irish people around the world, e.g. St Patrick's Day, growth of GAA clubs worldwide, interest in Irish language and culture; most children attend schools with a common curriculum and stories of what it means to be Irish; imagined communities. Arguments against: many things that defined being Irish are no longer shared by all - language, history, religious beliefs; Ireland is more multicultural - 17% of residents were born in other countries and 182 languages are spoken (CSO 2016), so there are many Irish identities, not one; travel and cultural globalisation mean young people may share more with young people across the Western world than with people in their own town.

prompt:
Section A - Short Answer Questions. Answer ten of the items (a), (b), (c)... in Question 1.

(f) Give three pieces of information to explain the function of the European Court of Human Rights.
(4 marks)
model_answer:
1. The Court, based in Strasbourg, applies the European Convention on Human Rights and makes sure member States respect its rights.
2. It examines complaints (applications) from individuals, or sometimes States, after they have gone through their own national courts.
3. If it finds a State has breached a right, it gives a judgment finding a violation, which is binding - e.g. Norris v Ireland (1988) led Ireland to decriminalise homosexuality in 1993.
marking_scheme: Section A: each item is marked out of 4 (ten items answered; 2 extra marks are added to each of the five items with the highest marks, so Question 1 totals 50). Three relevant pieces of information: 2 marks + 1 mark + 1 mark (good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0; if the first is awarded 1 mark or less, the second/third is marked out of 2). E.g. the Court applies the European Convention on Human Rights; its task is to ensure that States respect the rights and guarantees set out in the Convention; it does this by examining complaints ('applications') lodged by individuals or sometimes by States; where it concludes that a member State has breached one or more of these rights, the Court delivers a judgment finding a violation.

(g) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of Proportional Representation (PR) by single transferable vote (STV).
Advantage ...
Disadvantage ...
(4 marks)
model_answer:
Advantage: seats closely match each party's share of the vote, and transfers mean a vote is not wasted if your first choice is eliminated, so small parties and Independents get represented.
Disadvantage: TDs compete with candidates from their own party and focus on local issues to win votes (parish pump politics), and it often produces weak coalition governments.
marking_scheme: Section A: each item is marked out of 4 (ten items answered; 2 extra marks are added to each of the five items with the highest marks, so Question 1 totals 50). One advantage 2 marks, one disadvantage 2 marks (good 2, fair 1, irrelevant 0). Advantages, e.g.: the distribution of seats corresponds closely with the proportion of total votes cast for each party; if a voter's first preference is eliminated early, their vote carries on and further preferences help elect later candidates; gives representation to small parties and Independents. Disadvantages, e.g.: possibly too candidate-focused, leading to localism (TDs focus on local issues rather than a national vision); produces unstable and internally divided coalition governments; intra-party electoral competition; personality politics / parish pump politics.

(h) Name two consequences of income inequalities in Ireland on an individual's life chances.
(4 marks)
model_answer:
1. Education: children from lower-income families may lack the cultural capital (Bourdieu), grinds, Irish college and home supports that richer families buy, so they get poorer results and fewer college places.
2. Health and housing: lower income can mean relying on public healthcare waiting lists, a poorer diet, and insecure rented housing or debt, trapping people in a poverty cycle.

prompt:
Section B - Data-Based Questions. Read the documents below and answer the question.

Document A
Below is an extract from the Executive Summary of a report published by the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) Research Programme. The programme is financed by the Irish Government.

[EPA Research Report No. 223 - Climate, Water, Sustainability. 'A Summary of the State of Knowledge on Climate Change Impacts for Ireland'. Authors: Margaret Desmond, Phillip O'Brien and Frank McGovern. Cover slogan: 'We need to talk about climate change'. www.epa.ie]

The purpose of this report is to provide an accessible summary of the available information on ongoing climate change and projected impacts for Ireland in a format that will be of use to policymakers, sectoral and local decision-makers and other stakeholders interested in or working on adaptation to climate change in Ireland.

The national information is largely based on Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) funded research and linked research funded by other national bodies, including Met Éireann, the Office of Public Works (OPW), the Marine Institute and research carried out by third-level institutes.

Warming of the global climate system is undeniable and it is extremely likely that human influence has been the dominant cause of the observed warming since the mid-20th century.

Actions are being taken to mitigate or limit climate change, most notably the 2015 Paris Agreement. However, many changes and their associated impacts are "locked-in" to the Earth's climate systems and the actions of the past will drive changes to the climate for decades to come.

The impacts of climate changes are evident on natural and human systems on all continents and across the oceans. Observations show that Ireland's climate is also changing. These changes are projected to continue and increase over the coming decades. Climate change means not only changes in the average climate such as temperature, rainfall and increasing sea levels, but also changes in the frequency and intensity of extreme weather and climate events. It is recognised that extreme events, such as severe flooding, droughts and heat/cold waves, can have important socio-economic consequences. Changes in their frequency and intensity are therefore of particular interest to policymakers and stakeholders.

In Ireland, climate change will have diverse and wide-ranging impacts on the environment, society, economic sectors and natural resources, including managed and natural ecosystems, water resources, agriculture and food security, human health, and coastal infrastructures and zones. Extreme weather events cause immediate and severe infrastructural, economic and societal disruption.

(a) In Document A, what is the significance of the term 'locked-in' in relation to climate change?
(15 marks)
model_answer:
'Locked-in' means that some climate change can no longer be prevented. Document A says many changes and their impacts are 'locked-in' to the Earth's climate systems and 'the actions of the past will drive changes to the climate for decades to come'.

Firstly, this means that even with actions to limit climate change, such as the 2015 Paris Agreement, some effects cannot now be avoided through policy. Secondly, a certain amount of warming is now inevitable because of human actions in the past - the report says human influence has been 'the dominant cause' of warming since the mid-20th century.

The significance is that cutting emissions is not enough on its own. Ireland must also adapt to changes that are already coming, such as higher sea levels and more severe flooding, droughts and heat waves.
marking_scheme: Section B (150 marks): 15 + 15 + 30 + 25 + 25 + 40. 15 marks = two pieces of information 2 x 5 marks (very good 4-5, good 2-3, fair 0-1) + cohesion 5 marks (very good 4-5, good 2-3, fair 0-1). Answers must refer to: how some of the effects of climate change cannot now be averted through policy or action; a certain amount of climate change is now inevitable due to human actions in the past.

prompt:
Section B - Data-Based Questions. Read the documents below and answer the question.

Document B
In September 2017, Trócaire published a report 'Still Feeling the Heat' which outlined how climate change is impacting on five countries - the Philippines, Honduras, Kenya, Malawi and Ethiopia. The report was produced by Trócaire's Policy, Research and Advocacy unit, with support from Maynooth University and the University of Malawi.

It draws on more than 170 publications from recent research and international scientific journals and claims to 'provide a solid scientific evidence base for understanding the impacts and uncertainties of climate change in each of the aforementioned countries.'

Ethiopia
In brief: Massively reliant on rain-fed and low-tech agriculture, highly vulnerable to climate change.
Right now: Growing season has already reduced by 15 per cent in the region. Cyclical droughts that used to happen about once a decade have now affected the country in 2011, 2012, 2015, 2016, and 2017.
Future climate change risks: Worsening difficulties with access to water, increased occurrence of drought, large decreases in staple cereal crops, and increased vulnerability to disease.
Annual emissions of CO2 per capita: 0.1 metric tons - nearly seventy-four times less than Ireland.

Introduction
Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable to global climate change, because of its reliance on agriculture.

80% of Ethiopians live in rural areas and most rely on subsistence farming for survival. Nearly 95% of the country's agricultural production is cultivated on family holdings, most less than 1 hectare. Agriculture accounts for 37% of GDP and as much as 90% of exports and employment.

Farmers and pastoralists in Ethiopia rely on two annual rainy seasons. Rainfall is already highly variable. As most farmers have no access to irrigation, when the rains do not come, it can equal catastrophe.

Over the period 1980-2010 ten major drought disasters were reported in Ethiopia. Consecutive but separate droughts in 2015/16 and 2017 each affected over 15 million people.

Each successive drought makes it more difficult to recover, making the people of Ethiopia all the more vulnerable to climate change.

Already in Ethiopia, temperatures have been rising, and the length of the main growing season across eastern Africa has reduced by 15%. Even if drastic reductions in emissions are achieved, future climate changes are expected to significantly reduce Ethiopia's main cereal crops.

Climate change is also likely to make 39-59% of current coffee growing areas of Ethiopia unsuitable to coffee production, a crop that supports 15 million farmers and accounts for a quarter of Ethiopia's export earnings.

If emissions continue unabated, average temperature increases of approximately 4°C could be devastating. And yet, Ethiopia has relatively little control over which scenario plays out - since its carbon dioxide emissions, at 0.1 metric tons per capita, are already among the lowest in the world, it must rely on other countries reducing their carbon emissions to ensure its future.

(b) What would you conclude about the future of Ethiopia from Document B?
(15 marks)
model_answer:
Ethiopia faces a very difficult future. Firstly, it is highly vulnerable because it relies so heavily on rain-fed agriculture: 80% of people live in rural areas, most depend on subsistence farming, and agriculture provides up to 90% of exports and employment. Droughts that used to come once a decade struck in 2011, 2012, 2015, 2016 and 2017, and the growing season has already fallen by 15%. Future risks include worse access to water, more drought, large falls in cereal crops, more disease, and the loss of 39-59% of coffee-growing land.

Secondly, its future is largely out of its own hands. Its emissions are only 0.1 metric tons of CO2 per person, about 74 times less than Ireland, so it must rely on other countries cutting their emissions to ensure its future.
marking_scheme: Section B (150 marks): 15 + 15 + 30 + 25 + 25 + 40. 15 marks = two pieces of information 2 x 5 marks (very good 4-5, good 2-3, fair 0-1) + cohesion 5 marks. Answers must refer to: Ethiopia faces a challenging future in which its reliance on agriculture will make it very vulnerable to climate change; it will face worsening difficulties with access to water, increased drought, large decreases/reductions in staple cereal crops and increased vulnerability to disease; it will rely heavily on other countries to mitigate these risks - it needs other countries to reduce their carbon emissions to ensure it has a future.

In Ireland, climate change will have diverse and wide-ranging impacts on the environment, society, economic sectors and natural resources, including managed and natural ecosystems, water resources, agriculture and food security, human health, and coastal infrastructures and zones. Extreme weather events cause immediate and severe infrastructural, economic and societal disruption.

(d) Are the claims made in Document A reliable? Justify your answer by referring to the authorship and potential bias of the report and its relevance to policy and decision makers.
(25 marks)
model_answer:
Overall the claims are reliable, but the report has limits.

Authorship: The report comes from the Environmental Protection Agency's research programme, a credible scientific body, and is written by named authors (Desmond, O'Brien and McGovern) who appear to be scientists or academics. This may explain its calm, less urgent tone that avoids alarming people. prompt:
Section B - Data-Based Questions. Read the documents below and answer the question.

Document B
In September 2017, Trócaire published a report 'Still Feeling the Heat' which outlined how climate change is impacting on five countries - the Philippines, Honduras, Kenya, Malawi and Ethiopia. The report was produced by Trócaire's Policy, Research and Advocacy unit, with support from Maynooth University and the University of Malawi.

It draws on more than 170 publications from recent research and international scientific journals and claims to 'provide a solid scientific evidence base for understanding the impacts and uncertainties of climate change in each of the aforementioned countries.'

Ethiopia
In brief: Massively reliant on rain-fed and low-tech agriculture, highly vulnerable to climate change.
Right now: Growing season has already reduced by 15 per cent in the region. Cyclical droughts that used to happen about once a decade have now affected the country in 2011, 2012, 2015, 2016, and 2017.
Future climate change risks: Worsening difficulties with access to water, increased occurrence of drought, large decreases in staple cereal crops, and increased vulnerability to disease.
Annual emissions of CO2 per capita: 0.1 metric tons - nearly seventy-four times less than Ireland.

Introduction
Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable to global climate change, because of its reliance on agriculture.

80% of Ethiopians live in rural areas and most rely on subsistence farming for survival. Nearly 95% of the country's agricultural production is cultivated on family holdings, most less than 1 hectare. Agriculture accounts for 37% of GDP and as much as 90% of exports and employment.

Farmers and pastoralists in Ethiopia rely on two annual rainy seasons. Rainfall is already highly variable. As most farmers have no access to irrigation, when the rains do not come, it can equal catastrophe.

Over the period 1980-2010 ten major drought disasters were reported in Ethiopia. Consecutive but separate droughts in 2015/16 and 2017 each affected over 15 million people.

Each successive drought makes it more difficult to recover, making the people of Ethiopia all the more vulnerable to climate change.

Already in Ethiopia, temperatures have been rising, and the length of the main growing season across eastern Africa has reduced by 15%. Even if drastic reductions in emissions are achieved, future climate changes are expected to significantly reduce Ethiopia's main cereal crops.

Climate change is also likely to make 39-59% of current coffee growing areas of Ethiopia unsuitable to coffee production, a crop that supports 15 million farmers and accounts for a quarter of Ethiopia's export earnings.

If emissions continue unabated, average temperature increases of approximately 4°C could be devastating. And yet, Ethiopia has relatively little control over which scenario plays out - since its carbon dioxide emissions, at 0.1 metric tons per capita, are already among the lowest in the world, it must rely on other countries reducing their carbon emissions to ensure its future.

(e) Is the integration of commentary with statistics effective in communicating research findings? Justify your answer with reference to Document B.
(25 marks)
model_answer:
Yes, Document B integrates commentary and statistics very effectively.

Statistics used: The 'In brief' box gives key figures at a glance, e.g. the growing season has fallen by 15% and CO2 emissions are 0.1 metric tons per person, 'nearly seventy-four times less than Ireland'. The introduction adds more: 80% of Ethiopians live in rural areas, agriculture is 37% of GDP and up to 90% of exports and employment, and droughts in 2015/16 and 2017 each affected over 15 million people.

Evaluation: Firstly, the commentary explains what the numbers mean. For example, it explains that because most farmers have no irrigation, 'when the rains do not come, it can equal catastrophe'. This helps non-experts make sense of the data. Secondly, it focuses the reader on the human impact: the coffee statistic (39-59% of land lost) is linked to 15 million farmers' livelihoods, and the emissions figure is used to show the injustice that Ethiopia must rely on other countries. This matters for an NGO like Trócaire, which wants to raise awareness and remind developed countries of their responsibilities.

So the mix of brief figures and clear explanation makes the research findings accessible and persuasive, while still resting on evidence from over 170 publications.

(f) Drawing on both Document A and Document B and your wider learning in Politics and Society, do you agree with the following statement from Mary Robinson? Justify your answer.
"Climate change is the greatest threat to human rights in the 21st century."

model_answer:
I largely agree with Mary Robinson.

Firstly, climate change threatens the most basic rights. Article 3 of the UDHR protects the right to life and Article 25 the right to an adequate standard of living, including food. Document B shows these are already at risk in Ethiopia: most people depend on subsistence farming, the growing season has fallen by 15%, and droughts in 2015/16 and 2017 each affected over 15 million people. Future risks include water shortages, crop failures and disease, which also threaten the rights to water, health and development. Because rights are indivisible, losing food and water undermines education and other rights too.

Secondly, it is a question of justice. Ethiopia emits only 0.1 metric tons of CO2 per person, 74 times less than Ireland, yet it suffers far more. prompt:
Section C - Discursive Essays. Answer any two of Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Question 3
During his campaign for leadership of Fine Gael, May 2017, Leo Varadkar sent this tweet: "I am proposing a new social contract for Ireland. #fgle17"

In the context of the serious social issues facing Irish society today, evaluate whether a new social contract is needed in this country.

[Your answer should be supported by examples and evidence and make reference to at least two named theorists you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
A social contract is an agreement in which citizens give up some freedom in return for protection and services from the state. Thomas Hobbes argued we accept a strong ruler to escape a 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short' state of nature. John Locke argued government rests on trust and the consent of the people, and must protect life, liberty and property. When Leo Varadkar proposed 'a new social contract', he was suggesting the current deal between citizens and the State is not working for everyone. I will argue that serious problems in housing, inequality and access to services show that Ireland needs a renewed social contract, although some parts of the existing one work well.

Housing and homelessness
The clearest sign the contract is failing is homelessness. Focus Ireland reported over 11,000 people homeless in January 2023, and the Children's Rights Alliance recorded 3,442 homeless children in December 2022, up from 2,327 in 2020. Homelessness has risen by 178%. The Ombudsman for Children's 2019 report 'No Place Like Home' recommended considering a right to housing in the Constitution. An all-party committee criticised the Government's reliance on the private sector for social housing and the way official figures leave out rough sleepers and hidden homelessness. In Locke's terms, a government that cannot protect its citizens' basic security is losing the trust it depends on. Plans such as Housing for All, the First Home Scheme and cost rental homes show some effort, but critics say they do not tackle root causes.

Inequality and the welfare state
The ESRI found that before taxes and benefits Ireland has the most unequal income distribution in the EU. However, the same research found no tax system in Europe does more to reduce inequality, and the CSO (2022) says almost four in ten people would be in poverty without social welfare. So the existing contract does protect many people. John Rawls would support strengthening it: his 'social lottery' means people do not choose the family or class they are born into, so inequalities are only fair if they benefit the least well off. A new contract based on Rawls would focus on housing, education and health for those at the bottom.

Education and other groups left behind
Article 42 promises free primary education, yet in 2022 parents spent on average €1,195 per primary and €1,518 per secondary child, and 29% went into debt for back-to-school costs. Asylum seekers in Direct Provision, with families sharing single rooms for an average of 24 months, also show that some people are not fully protected by our current contract.

The counter-argument
Robert Nozick would reject a bigger state. For him only a minimal state - police, courts and defence - is justified, and taxing earnings to redistribute is a kind of 'forced labour'. From this view, a new contract should reduce taxes and let the free market and private builders solve housing. Some also argue the current system, with a progressive tax system and strong welfare, simply needs better delivery, not a new contract.

Conclusion
Weighing the evidence, I believe a new social contract is needed. The existing system reduces income inequality, but rising homelessness, the hidden cost of 'free' education and the treatment of asylum seekers show that the State is not meeting its side of the bargain for its most vulnerable citizens. Following Locke and Rawls rather than Nozick, a renewed contract should include clear rights such as a right to housing, so that the State earns back the trust of all its citizens.

Question 4(a)
In 1918, Irish women over 30 who owned property were allowed to vote and to stand for election for the first time. Prior to this women were largely excluded from and therefore not visible in public life due to the patriarchal nature of Irish society at the time.

This year as we celebrate the 100th anniversary of the parliamentary vote for women, is the invisible woman still a phenomenon in Irish society today? Discuss.

[Your answer should include examples and evidence to support your position. You should also refer to the views of two or more named theorists you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Patriarchy is a system in which men hold most power and resources, marginalising women. In 1918 women were largely invisible in Irish public life. A century later women can vote, stand for election and work in every profession. However, I will argue that the 'invisible woman' is still a phenomenon, especially in unpaid care work, in leadership and in the home, using the ideas of Sylvia Walby and Kathleen Lynch.

Invisible work in the home
Sylvia Walby describes 'private patriarchy', where women's unpaid domestic labour supports the economy and allows men to do paid work. In her first structure of patriarchy, the household, women's unpaid work is 'invisible and undervalued'. The evidence supports her: the 2016 census found 195,263 unpaid carers, over 60% of them women, doing work worth €10 billion a year to the State. Kathleen Lynch calls this affective inequality: care is seen as 'natural' for women rather than real work, so it goes unpaid. She notes that 'care commanders' who make decisions are usually men, while the 'footsoldiers' who do the caring are usually women. Article 41.2 of the Constitution still refers to a woman's 'life within the home'.

Under-representation in public life
Walby's 'public patriarchy' describes how the state and politics exclude women. After gender quotas were introduced in 2012, women TDs rose from 16% (2011) to 22% (2016), but only 22.5% in 2020, leaving Ireland 98th in the world for women in parliament. The National Women's Council argues that the women furthest from power - low-income, Traveller, disabled and LGBTQ+ women - are the most invisible of all.

Pay and violence
Women earned 14.4% less than men on average in 2020, and the gap is larger in higher-paid jobs. Many more women than men work part-time or take career breaks for childcare. Women's Aid (2021) found one in four women who have been in a relationship have experienced domestic violence, which Walby sees as a structure of patriarchy that the state perpetuates by not interfering.

Counter-argument: women are more visible than ever
There has been real progress. The 2018 referendum to repeal the 8th Amendment (66.4% Yes) showed women's issues at the centre of national debate. Gender quotas, EU rules forcing companies to disclose pay gaps, and seven weeks' paid parental leave for both parents (2022) all increase women's visibility. Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach supports such policies, as they give women real freedom to take part in work and politics. Some, such as Claudia Goldin, argue the pay gap reflects women choosing flexibility rather than discrimination.

Conclusion
Women are far more visible than in 1918, with legal equality and growing representation. However, the evidence on unpaid care, the low share of women in the Dáil, the pay gap and domestic violence shows that, as Walby and Lynch argue, much of women's contribution remains hidden and undervalued. The invisible woman is still a phenomenon, now in the home and in the halls of power rather than at the ballot box.

prompt:
Section C - Discursive Essays. Answer any two of Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Question 4(b)
Would the theorist Kathleen Lynch agree that inequality in Irish society is perpetuated by the education system?

[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the views of one other named theorist you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Kathleen Lynch of the UCD School of Education argues for 'equality of condition': real equality needs equal conditions of life, not just equal access. She writes that 'we need to have a significantly more equal distribution of wealth and income to have substantive equality of opportunity in education'. I will argue that Lynch would agree that the Irish education system perpetuates inequality, and I will contrast her view with Robert Nozick's.

The hidden cost of 'free' education
Article 42 of the Constitution promises free primary education, but the Irish League of Credit Unions (2022) found back-to-school costs averaged €1,195 per primary and €1,518 per secondary child. 29% of parents went into debt to cover them and 66% called them a financial burden. Voluntary contributions averaged €124 at primary and €146 at secondary, and the St Vincent de Paul 'Closing the Gap' report (2023) found 87% of parents had to cut back to pay them, with children facing shame if they did not. Lynch would say this shows equal access on paper but not equality of condition, because poorer families start behind.

Class, capital and results
Pierre Bourdieu's idea of cultural capital helps explain Lynch's point: middle-class parents pass on skills, knowledge and networks that help their children succeed, so education reproduces class inequality. Wealthier families can pay for grinds and Irish college, and school league tables reward schools that send students to Trinity, UCD or UCC. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (2022) noted 'persistent barriers for disadvantaged children', including Traveller, Roma, asylum-seeking and disabled children, and called for help with the hidden costs of education.

Unequal schools
Resources vary between schools, and those in disadvantaged areas struggle to provide supports. Patronage also limits choice: just under 95% of primary schools have a Catholic or Church of Ireland patron, so families who want a non-religious school may have to travel or pay. Lynch would argue that unless social class inequality outside school is tackled, 'there can be no meaningful equality of opportunity in education'.

The State's response
There are real efforts. Free secondary education, introduced by Donogh O'Malley in 1966, transformed access. Today the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance, the Free Primary Schoolbooks Scheme and the School Meals Programme (228,007 children in 2021/22) reduce pressure on families. These show progressive realisation of the right to education.

Robert Nozick's view
Nozick, a libertarian, would reject Lynch's call for redistribution. He would support a free-market system in which families pay for the education they choose, arguing that competition makes schools improve and that people value what they pay for. Low-income families could be helped by means-tested grants such as SUSI. For Nozick, unequal outcomes are not unjust if they result from free choices. However, his view ignores the structural barriers that the evidence above shows.

Conclusion
Lynch would clearly agree that the education system perpetuates inequality. Hidden costs, voluntary contributions and differences in cultural capital mean children's chances still depend on their parents' income. Government schemes help, but only equality of access is provided, not equality of outcome. I agree with Lynch that real change needs a more equal society, not just more school places.

prompt:
Section C - Discursive Essays. Answer any two of Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Question 5(a)
"As President of the United States, I will always put America first, just like you, as the leaders of your countries, will always - and should always - put your countries first."
President Trump gave this message to other world leaders at the United Nations Assembly, on September 19th 2017.

Does President Trump's 'America First' policy and the rise of nationalism in other countries show that the world is becoming increasingly divided into 'us and them'? Discuss.

[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the views of two named theorists you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Nationalism means identifying with your nation and supporting its interests, often to the exclusion of other nations. Trump's 'America First' message at the UN put national interest above international cooperation. I will argue that rising nationalism does show a world increasingly divided into 'us and them', using Samuel Huntington, Benedict Anderson and Thomas Hylland Eriksen, but that strong counter-movements, explained by Kwame Anthony Appiah and Edward Said, show the division is not complete.

Nations as imagined communities
Benedict Anderson describes a nation as 'an imagined political community both inherently limited and sovereign'. 'Limited' means every nation has boundaries beyond which lie 'others'. Nationalism is so powerful that people will kill and die for it. 'America First' appeals to this imagined community and draws a sharp line between Americans and outsiders.

Evidence of a divided world
In the US, divisive rhetoric deepened the split between conservatives and liberals, and pro-Trump supporters stormed the Capitol on 6 January 2021. In Europe, far-right parties in Hungary, Poland and Italy have fuelled anti-immigrant and nationalist feeling. In the 2016 Brexit referendum Leave won 51.9%; Lord Ashcroft's poll found 49% of Leave voters wanted UK decisions taken in the UK and a third wanted control over immigration and borders. Home Office data show racially and religiously motivated hate crime spiked after the referendum. Even in Ireland, 'Ireland is Full' protests in 2022-23 targeted refugees, and a 2023 poll found 56% believed Ireland had taken in too many.

Explaining the trend
Huntington argues that after the Cold War, conflict is between civilisations with different values, and that conflict happens along 'cultural fault lines'. He would see 'America First' and the rise of nationalism as proof of an 'us vs them' world. Eriksen offers a deeper explanation: globalisation makes the world change 'too fast, unequal and uneven', so people feel powerless and retreat to their 'own'. His seven principles of identity politics, such as competition for jobs and 'first comers versus invaders', fit Brexit well. He argued Brexit was not just small-minded nationalism but a reaction to people feeling disconnected from power.

The counter-argument
Edward Said criticised Huntington's view as 'reductive', a dangerous oversimplification that ignores the diversity within each culture. He said we should focus on 'the slow working together of cultures that overlap, borrow from each other and live together'. Appiah argues we can be 'citizens of the world' while loving our own home. There is evidence for this too: tens of thousands marched in 'Ireland for All' rallies in 2023, the multicultural town of Ballyhaunis integrates over 20 ethnic minorities, and the UN still brings nations together on climate change and poverty. John Hume showed in Northern Ireland that 'the answer to difference is to respect it'.

Conclusion
The evidence from the US, Brexit and Europe shows that nationalism and 'us and them' thinking are rising, as Huntington and Eriksen predict. However, as Said and Appiah argue, this is not inevitable. The world is becoming more divided, but cooperation and cosmopolitan values remain strong, so the outcome depends on the choices of leaders and citizens.

prompt:
Section C - Discursive Essays. Answer any two of Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Question 5(b)
"One of the good things about globalisation is it has created a single international music community, and I feel very much part of it." - The Edge, musician and U2 band member

Globalisation is breaking down national cultures and identities and creating a cosmopolitan culture and a cosmopolitan identity. Discuss.

[Your answer should include examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the views of two named theorists you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Globalisation is the growing interdependence of the world's economies, populations and cultures through technology, trade and the flow of people and information. Cosmopolitanism is the idea that all humans belong to one community and can be 'citizens of the world'. I will argue that globalisation is creating a cosmopolitan culture alongside national identities, rather than simply breaking them down, using the views of Kwame Anthony Appiah and Thomas Hylland Eriksen.

Evidence of a cosmopolitan culture
As The Edge suggests, travel, trade and the internet expose people to many cultures. Social media creates 'virtual communities' that share interests across borders. Appiah says globalisation makes cosmopolitanism more relevant than ever. He argues that cultures do not simply disappear; instead 'cultural hybridisation' blends elements of different cultures to create new forms. The town of Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo, shows this locally: over 20 ethnic minorities make up more than half the population, children of over a dozen nationalities play for the local GAA club, and cultural festivals and language exchanges build social cohesion. Here a cosmopolitan identity grows through a very Irish institution.

Is national culture being broken down?
There is evidence that dominant global cultures are replacing local ones - 'cultural homogenisation' or 'McDonaldisation'. Sean Moncrieff wrote in the Irish Times (2019) that change in Ireland 'wasn't transported here in the baggage of Nigerians or Poles... We're building Starbucks.' Global US-owned platforms such as Netflix and Google invest little in Irish content, so RTÉ and TG4 carry much of the burden of producing Irish culture. Most people do not speak Irish daily. This suggests globalisation is weakening some national traditions, but replacing them with Western consumer culture rather than a truly cosmopolitan one.

The counter-argument: localisation
Eriksen argues that the world is 'interconnected... but not a smoothly and seamlessly integrated one'. Fast, uneven change makes people feel powerless, so they hold on more strongly to local, national, religious or ethnic identity - 'localisation'. Brexit is an example: 52% voted Leave, many to regain control over borders and decisions. Anti-refugee 'Ireland is Full' protests and the rise of nationalist parties in Europe show that globalisation can strengthen national identity and 'us vs them' thinking. Meanwhile, national identity remains strong: GAA clubs exist around the world and St Patrick's Day is celebrated globally - Irishness is being spread by globalisation, not erased.

Conclusion
Globalisation is creating a cosmopolitan culture, especially among young people connected by music, media and migration, as Appiah and the Ballyhaunis example show. However, it is not simply breaking down national identities. As Eriksen argues, it often provokes a stronger local response. People increasingly hold multiple, hybrid identities - Irish and European and global at the same time.

prompt:
Section C - Discursive Essays. Answer any two of Questions 3, 4, 5 and 6.

Question 6
"Underdevelopment is caused by people in less developed countries not having the knowledge, technology and industry of people in developed countries." - NCCA Curriculum Specification, Politics and Society, p.38

Discuss whether you agree or disagree with this statement. Justify your position.

[Your answer should include current examples and evidence to support your position. You should also refer to two or more relevant international agreements / organisations and / or the views of two or more named theorists you have studied. Relevant international agreements or organisations include The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, Paris Climate Agreement, the World Bank, The World Economic Forum etc.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Underdevelopment means economic and social deprivation: poor infrastructure, limited education and healthcare and a low standard of living. The UN lists 46 Least Developed Countries, such as Sierra Leone and Afghanistan. The statement reflects modernisation theory, which blames a lack of knowledge, technology and industry. I will argue that this is only a small part of the explanation, and that Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory, unfair global institutions and local corruption explain underdevelopment better.

The case for the statement
Walt Rostow's modernisation theory says all countries pass through five stages, from traditional farming society, through 'take off', to high mass consumption. Advanced technology and industry have driven growth in the USA, Germany and Japan, and Singapore developed very fast by investing heavily in education. The World Bank's Skills and Training Enhancement Project in Bangladesh tries to transfer skills to reduce poverty. In Ethiopia, most farmers rely on low-tech, rain-fed agriculture with no irrigation, so drought 'can equal catastrophe'. This suggests technology and knowledge do matter.

Dependency theory
Andre Gunder Frank rejects this. He argues that underdevelopment was 'generated by the very same historical process which also generated economic development: the development of capitalism itself'. Wealthy 'core' states extract cheap labour and raw materials from 'periphery' states, first through colonialism and now through unfair trade. The evidence supports him: the DRC has some of the world's richest deposits of cobalt, used in smartphones, yet children work in mines for one to two dollars a day while corporations earn billions. The problem is not a lack of resources but who profits from them.

International organisations
The IMF and World Bank are meant to help but are dominated by rich countries - the US has 16.5% of IMF votes while all of Africa has 6%. After Ebola, Sierra Leone's 2017 IMF loan required cuts to health and education spending. Critics say such conditional aid creates dependency. Christian Aid estimated Sierra Leone lost about 131 million dollars in 2014-2016 through tax breaks for five mining companies. The WTO's rules can also favour developed countries with more negotiating power.

Corrupt local elites
Internal factors matter too. Human Rights Watch says Sierra Leone has one of the world's highest rates of bribery and corruption, especially in health and education, which stops growth reaching citizens. Frank himself notes that Western powers often act together with local leaders.

Climate injustice and global goals
Developing countries also suffer from problems caused by others. Ethiopia emits only 0.1 metric tons of CO2 per person, yet droughts are wrecking its harvests. The Paris Agreement (2015) and the Sustainable Development Goals, which apply to all countries, recognise that poverty, inequality and climate change are connected and need shared action, not just technology transfer.

Conclusion
I disagree with the statement. Knowledge and technology help, but underdevelopment is mainly caused by historical exploitation, unfair trade and lending rules, corruption and climate change. As Frank argues, rich and poor countries are linked, and a fairer global system - through reformed institutions and real commitment to the SDGs - is needed, not just modernisation.

prompt:
Question 1 (a)
Explain what is meant when human rights are described as absolute rights and qualified rights. Give an example of each.
Absolute: ... Example: ...
Qualified: ... Example: ...
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Absolute: an absolute right can never lawfully be interfered with or taken away, under any circumstances, not even in an emergency.
Example: the prohibition of torture (also freedom of thought).

Qualified: a qualified right can sometimes be interfered with by the government if this is in the interest of the wider community or to protect other people's rights. The interference must meet a real social need, such as protecting the common good.
Example: freedom of movement and assembly were restricted during the Covid-19 pandemic to protect public health. (Freedom of expression can also be limited by hate speech laws.)

Two relevant examples: 1 mark + 1 mark.

prompt:
Question 1 (c)
Explain the role of the Equal Status Acts 2000-2015 in protecting against discrimination.
(5 marks)
model_answer: The Equal Status Acts make it illegal to discriminate against people when providing goods and services, education and accommodation. This covers things like access to a place, transport, cultural activities, health services and schools. Discrimination is banned on the nine grounds: gender, marital status, family status, age, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation and membership of the Travelling Community. A tenth ground, receiving housing assistance (e.g. HAP), was added in 2015. The Acts outlaw both direct discrimination (treating someone less favourably) and indirect discrimination (a rule that seems neutral but has an unfair impact), so people have legal protection and can challenge unfair treatment.

model_answer: In my view, school uniforms are mainly socially divisive in Ireland today. (g) Drawing on both documents, your wider learning and contemporary evidence, discuss whether Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 5, which aims to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls, is attainable.

SDG 5 is one of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals adopted by world leaders in 2015, to be met by 2030. Unlike the Millennium Development Goals, the SDGs are universal: they apply to rich and poor countries alike. I will argue that real progress towards SDG 5 is possible, but full gender equality by 2030 is unlikely.

The documents show how far away the goal is. Document A reports that 87,000 women were killed in 2017, 50,000 by partners or family - 137 every day. Women are 82% of the victims of intimate partner homicide. Document B shows women killed on a single day in India, France and Kenya, so this is not only a problem for poorer countries. prompt:
Question 3 (a)
As we celebrate 100 years of Dáil Éireann, discuss whether the Irish electoral system is in need of reform.
[Your answer should include examples and evidence to support your position. You should also refer to the views of at least two theorists you have studied, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The First Dáil met in 1919, and a century later Ireland is a stable democracy. Our electoral system - proportional representation by single transferable vote (PR-STV) in multi-seat constituencies - is used to elect TDs and the President. The question is whether it truly represents the will of all Irish people. In this essay I will argue that PR-STV itself is broadly fair and should be kept, but that the wider electoral system needs targeted reform, because women, minorities and young people remain under-represented. I will use the ideas of John Locke and John Rawls, with Thomas Hobbes as a contrasting view.

Argument 1: PR-STV represents the will of the people better than the alternatives
PR-STV is proportional: seats broadly match votes. In the 2020 general election Sinn Féin won 24.53% of first preferences, Fianna Fáil 22.18% and Fine Gael 20.86%, and the 160 seats were shared out in a way that reflected this close result. Under the first-past-the-post system used for UK elections, the candidate with the most votes wins and a close second gets nothing, so many votes are wasted. PR-STV also gives smaller parties and independents a real chance of a seat, producing a more diverse Dáil. John Locke argued that government is legitimate only when it has the consent of the people. A system where almost every vote counts towards the result gives Irish governments strong legitimacy, so in this respect the system does not need reform.

Argument 2: PR-STV encourages parish-pump politics and weak coalitions
Critics argue that PR-STV makes TDs focus on local issues rather than national policy. Candidates from the same party compete against each other in the same constituency, so they try to win votes by delivering local services. The dominance of the Healy-Rae family in Kerry is often given as an example of 'parish-pump politics'. PR-STV also tends to produce coalition governments, which can be slow to agree laws. Thomas Hobbes would see this as a weakness: for him the purpose of government is peace and stability, provided by a strong sovereign, not a divided parliament. However, coalitions also force compromise and bring wider representation, so I believe this is a reason to reform how TDs work (for example, strengthening Oireachtas committees) rather than to scrap PR-STV.

Argument 3: Women are under-represented
After a century of the Dáil, women are still a minority. Women were only 16% of TDs in 2011. Since 2012 parties must run at least 30% women and 30% men candidates or face penalties, and women rose to 22% in 2016 - 35 women, more than ever before. But by 2020 the figure was only 22.5%, and Ireland ranked 98th in the world for women in national parliaments. The 2021 Citizens' Assembly on gender equality recommended raising the quota to 40% and extending it to European, Seanad and local elections. John Rawls argued that positions of power must be open to all under 'fair equality of opportunity'. The evidence shows this is not yet true for women in Irish politics, so reform is needed.

Argument 4: Minorities and young people lack a voice
Some groups have little or no voice in our system. Members of the Travelling Community, LGBTQ+ people and people living in Direct Provision are rarely elected or listened to. Irish citizens under 18 cannot vote, even on issues like climate change that will shape their future - which is why Fridays for Future Ireland campaigned to lower the voting age to 16. Irish citizens living abroad cannot vote, even in referenda such as Marriage Equality. Behind Rawls's 'veil of ignorance', not knowing which group we would belong to, we would choose a system that protects the least powerful. This supports reforms such as votes at 16 and votes for emigrants.

Counter-argument: the system already reforms itself
Some argue the system is already flexible. The Citizens' Assembly, randomly selected from the electoral register to reflect Irish society, has influenced major decisions and gives ordinary people a voice between elections. Gender quotas have already worked. However, critics ask whether the Assembly is just a 'talk tank', since the Government decides whether to act on it.

Conclusion
One hundred years on, the core of the Irish electoral system - PR-STV - remains fair and proportional, and it should be kept. But representation is about more than counting votes accurately. Locke reminds us that legitimacy depends on consent, and Rawls that power must be open to all. As long as women hold under a quarter of Dáil seats and young people, emigrants and minorities have little voice, the system needs reform: stronger gender quotas, votes at 16, votes for citizens abroad and reform of the Seanad would help the Dáil truly represent the will of all Irish people.

Knowledge (K) - 20 marks: excellent 18-20 (clear and critical understanding; extensive knowledge of the issue); very good 14-17 (logical essay based on comprehensive knowledge, no significant omissions or errors); good 10-13; fair 5-9; weak 0-4.

prompt:
Question 3 (b)
Where does the right to a peaceful protest begin and end in a democratic society?
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The right to peaceful protest comes from freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. It is protected in the Irish Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). In this essay I will argue that the right to protest begins wherever citizens want to express a view or challenge those in power peacefully, and that it ends only when a protest uses violence, intimidation or hatred that destroys the rights of others. I will use the ideas of John Locke, Thomas Hobbes and John Rawls.

Where the right begins: speaking truth to power
In a democracy, protest is a way to 'speak truth to power'. It has driven great social movements, from Martin Luther King and the US Civil Rights movement to Gandhi in India and Nelson Mandela in South Africa. Civil disobedience - refusing to obey laws considered unjust - can be a form of peaceful protest that forces debate and leads to progressive change. John Locke argued that government rests on the consent of the people and that citizens have a right to resist when power is abused. For Locke, 'wherever law ends, tyranny begins' - so citizens must be free to challenge laws they see as unjust. John Rawls's first principle of justice says each person should have an equal right to basic liberties, including freedom of speech and assembly. On these views, the right to protest begins with every citizen.

Protest gives a voice to the voiceless
Protest is especially important for people who cannot vote. On 15 March 2019, more than 1.4 million students took part in climate strikes in over 125 countries, inspired by Greta Thunberg's Fridays for Future - the biggest global climate action in history. In Dublin more than 10,000 students gathered at Merrion Square. Most of these young people are under 18 and have no vote, so protest is their main way to show government where to focus attention. FFF Ireland's demands included declaring a climate emergency, and the movement went on to campaign for votes at 16. This shows peaceful protest strengthening democracy, not threatening it.

Where the right ends: violence, intimidation and hatred
The right to protest is not unlimited. Sometimes the rights of the individual must be set aside to protect the rights of the majority. When protest turns into hatred or violence, it infringes the rights of others. In Ireland, growing anti-refugee protests in 2023 included threats to burn hotels housing refugees and attacks on migrant camps, often stirred by false rumours spread on social media. In November 2023 there were far-right riots on O'Connell Street in Dublin. President Michael D. Higgins said those 'sowing hate and building fear' must be opposed 'publicly, vocally and unequivocally'. Here, the protest no longer expresses a view - it intimidates vulnerable people and threatens their right to safety. Irish law on hate speech, now being updated by the Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Bill, reflects this limit. I believe this is where the right to protest ends.

Temporary limits for the common good
Freedom of assembly is a qualified right: the state can limit it to protect the wider community, as long as the limit meets a real social need. During the Covid-19 pandemic, public gatherings were restricted to protect public health. Most people accepted these limits because they were temporary and necessary.

The danger of going too far: Hobbes and authoritarian states
Thomas Hobbes would allow almost no right to protest. Once citizens sign the social contract, they give up the right to challenge the sovereign; protest threatens stability and could return society to the 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short' state of nature. Some states act in this spirit. The 2019 pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong were met with the erosion of democracy and free expression. This shows the danger of governments using 'order' as an excuse to silence people. Critics of Ireland's new hate offences law also warn that it may go too far and stifle free speech.

Conclusion
In a democracy, the right to peaceful protest begins with every citizen, especially those with no other voice, and Locke and Rawls show why it is essential to legitimate government. It ends when protest uses violence, intimidation or hatred against others, because then it destroys the rights it claims to use. Any limits must be set by law, be necessary and be proportionate - otherwise, as Hong Kong shows, the state becomes Hobbes's Leviathan and democracy itself is lost.

prompt:
Question 4
[Image text: Rain Forests are disappearing. Every minute forest the size of 20 football fields is cut down.]
Given the focus on environmental destruction in recent times, discuss whether a consumer's purchasing choices can address this problem.
[Your answer should include current examples and evidence to support your position. You should also refer to two or more relevant international agreements/organisations* and/or the views of two or more theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.
*Relevant international agreements or organisations include The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, Paris Climate Agreement, The World Bank, The World Economic Forum, etc.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Every minute, an area of rainforest the size of 20 football fields is cut down. Much of this destruction is driven by what we buy: palm oil, cheap clothes, food and electronics. Sustainable development, as defined in the Brundtland Report, means 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. In this essay I will argue that consumers' purchasing choices can help to address environmental destruction, but on their own they cannot solve it. Real change needs governments, corporations and international agreements as well. I will refer to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, the Paris Climate Agreement and the European Green Deal, and to the ideas of Vandana Shiva and Father Sean McDonagh.

Argument 1: Consumer choices can change corporate behaviour
Consumers have real power because companies depend on sales. Palm oil is found in margarine, lipstick, biscuits, chocolate and detergent. The WWF shows that palm oil plantations cause rainforest destruction and loss of habitat for orangutans, elephants, rhinos and tigers, and that the 2015 Indonesian fires released almost as much greenhouse gas as Indonesia emits in a whole year. In 2018 the retailer Iceland partnered with Greenpeace on the 'Rang-tan' video about orangutans losing their homes to palm oil used by Unilever, Mondelez and Nestle. Campaigns like this make consumers aware and put pressure on brands. Tools such as the Good On You app rate brands on their impact on people, planet and animals, and B Corp certification helps consumers tell 'good companies' from 'good marketing'. These choices support SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production.

Argument 2: Responsible consumption reduces harm directly
Individual choices add up. Fast fashion is the second largest polluter of clean water after agriculture, because of cheap toxic dyes, and it puts stress on land and biodiversity. Buying fewer, longer-lasting clothes, reducing meat, and choosing local produce all cut demand for destructive production. Localisation - buying from local farmers and businesses - means a smaller carbon footprint from less long-distance transport. Father Sean McDonagh argues that overconsumption and materialism are at the heart of 'biocide', the destruction of biodiversity through deforestation and pollution, and that caring for the earth is a moral duty. For McDonagh, changing how we consume is part of the answer.

Argument 3: The limits of consumer power
However, consumer choice has serious limits. Many companies 'greenwash', portraying themselves as environmentally friendly while continuing harmful practices, which misleads consumers. Not everyone can afford green choices: socioeconomic inequality means poorer families often must buy the cheapest option. The scale of the problem can also overwhelm an individual: Irish climate activists point out that just 100 corporations are responsible for 70% of global carbon emissions. Vandana Shiva argues that the real problem is the profit-driven model of large multinational corporations, which control seeds, patent life and push monocultures that destroy biodiversity. For Shiva, consumers cannot simply shop their way out of a system designed by corporations, supported by bodies like the WTO and IMF.

Argument 4: International agreements and governments are essential
Because the problem is global, it needs global solutions. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015, are universal and include SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 15 (Life on Land), which aims to protect forests. The Paris Climate Agreement commits countries to cut emissions to limit global warming. The European Green Deal (2019) aims to make the EU climate neutral by 2050, and the European Climate Law makes its 55% emissions reduction target legally binding. Laws can ban harmful products and force corporations to change in a way no single shopper can. However, governments also face problems: some still subsidise fossil fuels and choose short-term growth, and Yanis Varoufakis has criticised the Green Deal as 'greenwashing' limited by austerity. The voluntary UN Global Compact shows the weakness of relying on businesses to act without rules.

Conclusion
Consumers' purchasing choices do matter. They can reduce demand for destructive products, reward genuinely sustainable companies and, through campaigns like Rang-tan, push brands to change. But as Shiva shows, the deeper causes lie in a profit-driven global system, and not everyone has the means to choose green. I conclude that consumer choices are a necessary part of the solution, but they can only address environmental destruction when combined with strong government regulation and binding international agreements such as the Paris Agreement and the SDGs.

prompt:
Question 5
10 December 2018 marked the 70th Anniversary of the adoption by the UN General Assembly of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR).
70 years later are human rights declarations and conventions anything more than ideas on paper doing little to improve the lives of people who find themselves in a position of poverty and powerlessness?
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations in 1948, after the horrors of World War II and the Holocaust. It declares that 'all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights'. It was a catalyst for later conventions such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) and the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). In this essay I will argue that these declarations and conventions are more than ideas on paper where they are backed by enforcement and resources, but that for many of the world's poorest and most powerless people they remain largely unfulfilled promises. I will draw on Martha Nussbaum, Kathleen Lynch and John Locke.

Argument 1: Declarations have driven real progress
There is clear evidence that rights frameworks have improved lives. UNICEF reports that in 1990, 1 in 11 children died before the age of five; by 2021 this had fallen to 1 in 26. In Afghanistan between 2001 and 2021, with international support including UNESCO, school enrolment rose tenfold, girls in primary school rose from almost zero to 2.5 million, and female literacy almost doubled. These gains reflect the right to education in Article 26 of the UDHR and the UNCRC. John Locke argued that all humans are born with natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government exists to protect them. Declarations put Locke's idea into international law and give people a standard to hold governments to.

Argument 2: Where rights can be enforced, they change lives
The ECHR shows that conventions can have real power. Through the right of individual petition, a person can bring a case to the European Court of Human Rights. In Norris v Ireland (1988), David Norris challenged Irish laws criminalising homosexual acts. The Court found a breach of his right to private life under Article 8, and in 1993 the Oireachtas decriminalised sex between men - a step towards the 2015 Marriage Equality referendum. The Council of Europe has also made abolition of the death penalty a condition of membership, and there have been no executions in member states since 1997. In Ireland, the Children's Rights Alliance grades the Government each year on children's rights; its grade for child safety online rose from 'C-' to 'A' in 2023 after the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act. Monitoring by bodies like the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child pushes states to act.

Argument 3: For the poorest, rights remain on paper
Yet for many of the poorest and most powerless, signing a convention changes little. South Sudan ratified the UNCRC in 2015, but about 1 in 10 children die before their fifth birthday, 1.4 million children under five face malnutrition, and the country ranked 185th of 189 on the Human Development Index in 2021. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, more than 7 million children are out of school, 15% of children aged 5-17 are in child labour, and some cobalt miners earn as little as nine cents a day producing minerals for the smartphones of wealthy consumers. Under Taliban rule, about 80% of school-aged Afghan girls and young women are out of education (UNESCO 2023), despite the UN reminding them they are bound by international law. The DRC Children's Parliament put it well in 2023: 'passing laws is not enough'.

Argument 4: Even in Ireland, the powerless are least protected
Rights frameworks also fall short at home. Ireland has signed the UDHR and ratified almost all conventions that come from it, yet people in Direct Provision have lived for years with whole families in a single room, and homelessness rose to over 11,000 people by January 2023. Traveller and Roma education received a 'D' grade from the Children's Rights Alliance in 2022. Economic and social rights are subject to 'progressive realisation', which allows states to delay full delivery because of limited resources - so those in poverty are told to wait.

Theoretical perspective: rights do not go far enough
Martha Nussbaum argues that a rights-based approach does not go far enough. Her capabilities approach asks not what rights people have on paper, but what they are actually able to do and be. A girl in Afghanistan may have a 'right' to education, but without the capability to attend school, the right is empty. Nussbaum calls for a 'social minimum' guaranteed to all. Kathleen Lynch makes a similar point: rights often give equality of access and opportunity, but not equality of condition or outcome, so poverty and powerlessness continue. On the other side, Robert Nozick would warn that positive rights force some people to pay for others, which is why states resist them.

Conclusion
Seventy years after the UDHR, human rights declarations and conventions are clearly more than ideas on paper: they have cut child deaths, opened schools and, through the European Court of Human Rights, changed laws. But for people in deep poverty and powerlessness - in South Sudan, the DRC, Afghanistan, and in Direct Provision in Ireland - they too often remain promises. As Nussbaum argues, rights only become real when people have the actual capability to use them. Declarations need enforcement, resources and political will to fulfil their purpose.

prompt:
Question 6 (a)
In 2018, 200 residents in Wicklow opposed the transformation of the Grand Hotel into a Direct Provision centre which aimed to house 100 refugees.
Discuss the above incident with particular reference to the ideas of either Benedict Anderson or Thomas Hylland Eriksen. Your answer should also include examples and evidence to support your position.
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
In 2018, about 200 residents in Wicklow opposed plans to turn the Grand Hotel into a Direct Provision centre for 100 refugees. Direct Provision is Ireland's system for housing asylum seekers in communal centres, often former hotels, while their applications for international protection are decided. Incidents like this raise key questions about identity: who belongs to a community, and why do some people react to newcomers with fear? In this essay I will analyse the Wicklow incident mainly through Thomas Hylland Eriksen's ideas on identity politics. I will argue that the opposition is best understood not as simple racism, but as a reaction to rapid change and competition for resources, which Eriksen's seven principles explain well - although the Direct Provision system itself must also share the blame.

Eriksen and identity in a fast-changing world
Eriksen, a Norwegian anthropologist, argues in his book Overheating that the world is changing 'too fast, unequal and uneven'. Globalisation and rapid change create uncertainty and powerlessness at local level. When this happens, local communities assert their own identity more strongly and move towards their 'own' - the basis of identity politics. He says identity is created 'both from the inside and the outside, in the encounter between one's own presentation of self and the perceptions of others'. Ireland has changed enormously, with far more immigration than a generation ago. For some residents of a small town, the sudden arrival of 100 asylum seekers can feel like a symbol of change they did not choose.

Principle 1: Competition over resources
Eriksen's first principle is competition over natural, political or economic resources. Ireland faces a serious housing crisis, and many towns have pressure on schools, GP services and public transport. Residents may fear that newcomers will compete for these scarce resources. This fear was also seen in later years: an Irish Times poll in February 2023 found 56% of people felt Ireland had taken in too many refugees in the past year, at a time when the housing and cost-of-living crises were severe. Eriksen would argue that economic insecurity, not the refugees themselves, drives this reaction.

Principles 6 and 7: 'We were here first' and 'the other'
Eriksen's sixth principle is 'first comers compared to invaders' - the feeling that 'we were here first' and newcomers do not have the same claim to the place. His seventh principle is that social complexities are narrowed down to a simple contrast, so anyone outside the group becomes 'the other'. Asylum seekers in fact come from many countries and situations; many are fleeing persecution, war or repressive governments. Yet in protests they are often reduced to a single threatening image. Later anti-refugee protests in Ireland used narratives about 'unvetted' or 'military age' young men, and false rumours spread on social media. This is exactly the oversimplification Eriksen describes. Principle 5, symbolism and rhetoric, is also seen in slogans like 'Ireland is Full'.

Counter-argument: opposition to the system, not the people
It would be too simple to say all 200 residents were hostile to refugees. Some objected to the Direct Provision system itself. Direct Provision was meant to be a short-term emergency measure in 2000, yet the average stay was 24 months, and some residents stayed up to 12 years. Whole families often share a single room without cooking facilities, and children make up about 30% of residents. Centres are run by private contractors for profit, and in 2020 the State spent over €175 million on the system. Residents placed in a hotel in a small town, often with little consultation, have little chance to integrate. The Government itself accepted these failings in its 2021 White Paper, which planned to replace Direct Provision with own-door accommodation in the community. So some opposition may reflect concern for the asylum seekers as well as for the town.

An alternative perspective: cosmopolitanism
Kwame Anthony Appiah offers a contrasting view: cosmopolitanism, the idea that we are citizens of the world and that our moral concern should not stop at national borders. Many Irish communities have welcomed asylum seekers, and in February 2023 tens of thousands marched in Dublin with 'Ireland for All' in support of refugees. This shows that Eriksen's identity politics is not inevitable: where people meet newcomers and see shared humanity, the 'us vs them' divide can weaken. Eriksen himself says cultures can evolve through exchange if differences are respected - identity is 'universality plus difference', dynamic rather than fixed.

Conclusion
The Wicklow incident is a clear example of Eriksen's identity politics at work. Rapid change, competition for scarce resources such as housing, the feeling of 'we were here first' and the reduction of complex people to 'the other' all help to explain why residents opposed the centre. However, the poor design of the Direct Provision system, which placed people in isolated hotels for years, made integration harder and fuelled local fears. I conclude that the way to prevent such conflicts is not only to challenge prejudice, but to tackle the housing and service pressures that feed competition, consult communities, and end Direct Provision in favour of real integration.
