prompt:
Question 6 (b)
The tweet below is a quote from a speech by Simon Coveney, the Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, to the 2018 British Irish Association's annual conference.
[Tweet from the Irish Foreign Ministry, 8 September 2018: "The invisible border is the most tangible product of the Peace Process... It has transformed the landscape and allowed identity to breathe more freely."]
With particular reference to the border on the island of Ireland, discuss whether borders define identity.
[Your answer should include examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the views of two theorists you have studied, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Identity is the set of characteristics by which a person or group is recognised; it shapes our sense of self. Borders mark where one state ends and another begins. Simon Coveney's comment that the 'invisible border' has 'allowed identity to breathe more freely' suggests that borders can shape - and even restrict - identity. In this essay I will argue that borders strongly influence identity, as partition on the island of Ireland clearly shows, but that they do not fully define it: identity is fluid and is also shaped by history, religion, culture and globalisation. I will use the ideas of Benedict Anderson and Thomas Hylland Eriksen.

Argument 1: Partition shaped distinct identities
The border created in 1921 divided the island into two states with different social, political and religious frameworks. Over a century, distinct identities developed on each side. In the Republic, identity has stressed Irish nationalism and independence, celebrated through figures like de Valera and Collins and commemorations such as the 1916 centenary at the GPO in 2016. In Northern Ireland, identity is deeply divided between mainly Protestant unionists who identify as British and mainly Catholic nationalists who identify as Irish. Murals on both sides - the union flag and British regiments, or republican leaders and the 1916 Rising - show how communities use symbols to assert who they are. Here, the border clearly helped define identity.

Anderson: the nation is 'limited'
Benedict Anderson defined the nation as 'an imagined political community - both inherently limited and sovereign'. 'Limited' means every nation has fixed boundaries beyond which other nations lie. Borders are therefore central to how a national community imagines itself: they mark who is 'us' and who is 'them'. For unionists, the border protects their place in the United Kingdom; for nationalists, it divides the Irish nation. Yet Anderson also stresses that the nation is 'imagined': members feel connected to millions they will never meet. Many people in Northern Ireland imagine themselves as part of an Irish community that crosses the border. The GAA, organised on an all-island basis, creates a shared Irish identity on both sides. So the imagined community does not always follow the lines on the map.

Eriksen: identity politics and the border
Thomas Hylland Eriksen argues that identity is created 'both from the inside and the outside'. His seven principles of identity politics help explain the conflict around the border. Competition: after Northern Ireland was set up, unionists had a near monopoly on housing, jobs and government, and many Protestants first saw power-sharing as a sell-out. Suffering and injustices: Catholics remember plantation and discrimination, while for Protestants the Siege of Derry (1689) is central to their marching tradition. Symbolism and rhetoric: commemorations and marches such as the 12 July Orange Order parades keep identities alive. During the Troubles, social complexities were narrowed to 'us vs them'. A hard, militarised border helped sustain these divisions.

Argument 2: The invisible border let identity 'breathe'
Coveney's point is that when the border became invisible after the Peace Process, people could hold more than one identity without crossing checkpoints. The 2021 Northern Ireland census shows this: 31.9% identified as British, 29.1% as Irish and 19.8% as Northern Irish. A growing regional identity, neither simply British nor Irish, suggests identity is evolving. Cross-community mural projects now promote shared history and reconciliation. When the border lost its physical presence, it lost some of its power to define people.

Argument 3: Brexit shows borders still matter
Brexit shows how strongly people link borders to identity. In the 2016 UK referendum, 51.9% voted to leave the EU. Lord Ashcroft's poll found that one-third of Leave voters said leaving was the best chance to 'regain control over immigration and its own borders'. Eriksen argues many felt disconnected from power and wanted to return to their own community. For Ireland, Brexit reignited debates about the border, sovereignty, national identity and possible reunification - showing how quickly the border can become a focus of identity again.

Counter-argument: identity goes beyond borders
Other forces shape identity at least as much as borders. Globalisation exposes us to many cultures; Sean Moncrieff wrote in 2019 that Irish identity is being changed less by immigrants than by Americanisation - 'We're building Starbucks.' New Irish identities such as Black-Irish and Muslim-Irish have developed, and same-sex marriage and abortion reforms, North and South, show changing values among younger generations. The Irish diaspora and GAA clubs around the world show Irish identity existing far beyond any border.

Conclusion
Borders do shape identity. Partition helped create distinct and often opposing identities on the island of Ireland, and Anderson shows that nations imagine themselves as 'limited' by boundaries. But the invisible border since the Peace Process has allowed people to be Irish, British, Northern Irish or several at once, and Eriksen reminds us that identity is dynamic, formed from the inside and the outside. I conclude that borders influence identity but do not define it; identity is fluid and is ultimately defined by people's shared history, culture and choices.

Knowledge (K) - 20 marks: excellent 18-20 (clear and critical understanding; extensive knowledge of the issue); very good 14-17 (logical essay based on comprehensive knowledge, no significant omissions or errors); good 10-13; fair 5-9; weak 0-4.
Evidence (E) - 20 marks: excellent 18-20 (identifies and interrogates convincingly a broad range of relevant, authoritative and credible sources of evidence); very good 14-17; good 10-13 (limited range, over-reliance on unsubstantiated data); fair 5-9; weak 0-4.
Analysis and Synthesis (A) - 15 marks: excellent 13-15 (an excellent argument based on a critical and perceptive analysis of the evidence); very good 10-12; good 7-9; fair 4-6; weak 0-3.
Evaluation (V) - 15 marks: excellent 13-15 (comprehensively integrates comparative/alternative perspectives; draws insightful, independent conclusions and confidently justifies own position); very good 10-12; good 7-9; fair 4-6; weak 0-3.
Cohesion (C) - 20 marks: excellent 18-20 (organisation and management of views is excellent; excellent focus, clarity and construction); very good 14-17; good 10-13; fair 5-9; weak 0-4.
Examiners read the whole essay first, mark it on the criteria, then check the total against the grade bands (H1 90-100: coherent, well-structured, supported by relevant, accurate and varied evidence using comparative evidence, in-depth engagement and comprehensively justified conclusions; down to H8 0-29). Skilful brevity is not penalised and unwarranted length is not rewarded.
source: 2019 State Exam - Section C Discursive Essays, Q6 (b)

prompt:
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a coalition government.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Advantage: A coalition gives wider representation. Two or more parties share power, so the views of more voters are reflected in government. For example, after the 2020 general election Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and the Green Party formed a majority together, and the smaller party won policies in the programme for government in return for joining.
Disadvantage: A coalition can be weak and slow to make decisions. The partners must negotiate and compromise on each policy, so laws can take longer, and the government can collapse if a partner pulls out.
marking_scheme:
Section A, Q1 (a). 5 marks: 3 marks + 2 marks.
First point: very good description 3M; good description 2M; fair description 1M; irrelevant description 0M.
Second point: good description 2M; fair description 1M; irrelevant description 0M.
Note: if the first point is awarded 2M or less, mark the second point out of 3M.

prompt:
Briefly describe a model of participation for young people's involvement in decision-making processes.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Lundy's Model of Participation (Laura Lundy) is based on Article 12 of the UNCRC, the right to be heard. It is non-hierarchical and has four elements in order:
1. Space: children get a safe, inclusive space to express their views.
2. Voice: children get the information they need and are helped to express their views.
3. Audience: their views are passed to someone with the power and responsibility to listen.
4. Influence: their views are taken seriously, acted on where appropriate, and children get feedback explaining the decision.
marking_scheme: Section A, Q1 (c). 5 marks. Very good description 4-5M; good description 2-3M; fair description 0-1M.

prompt:
Describe two criticisms of democratic governments.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. Democracies can produce weak governments. In Ireland, PRSTV often leads to coalitions or minority governments (e.g. the 2016-2020 'confidence and supply' arrangement), which must compromise and can be slow to pass laws.
2. Politicians may focus on winning the next election rather than the national interest. TDs are often accused of 'Parish-Pump Politics', concentrating on local issues in their constituency to get re-elected instead of long-term national policy.

Section A, Q1 (d). 5 marks: 3 marks + 2 marks.
First point: very good description 3M; good description 2M; fair description 1M; irrelevant description 0M.

prompt:
Evaluate the statement: 'Statistics don't lie, but liars use statistics.'
(5 marks)
model_answer: The statement is largely true. Quantitative data can be accurate and reliable, and large data sets are easy to compare. But statistics can be misused to push an agenda. A sample may be too small or unrepresentative (e.g. claiming 85% of Irish people want 'Irexit' after asking only 50 people). Researcher bias can shape the questions, and the way results are presented can create a narrative or leave out key facts. A correlation can also be presented as if it were causation. So we should always check the author, who paid for the research, the sample and the methodology before trusting a statistic.
marking_scheme: Section A, Q1 (e). 5 marks. Very good evaluation 4-5M; good evaluation 2-3M; fair evaluation 0-1M.

prompt:
What is meant by the term 'localisation'?
(5 marks)
model_answer: Localisation means prioritising local resources, economies and communities to achieve social, economic and environmental sustainability. It means relying less on long-distance trade, global supply chains and mass production, and supporting local businesses, farmers and industries instead. The goal is self-sufficient, resilient communities that are less dependent on the global market and live in harmony with nature. For example, buying locally grown food cuts the carbon footprint from transport and creates local jobs.
marking_scheme: Section A, Q1 (f). 5 marks. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Describe one advantage and one challenge of living in a globalised world.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Advantage: Globalisation increases cultural exchange and understanding. Migration, travel and media bring people of different cultures together, which builds tolerance. In Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo, children of over a dozen nationalities play on local GAA teams, showing Appiah's idea that we are 'citizens of the world'.
Challenge: It can lead to cultural homogenisation, a loss of cultural diversity, as dominant (often Western) cultural symbols and values spread and local cultures and ways of life are lost. It can also cause cultural conflict and 'us vs them' attitudes.

prompt:
Give two reasons why developing countries should be given development aid and/or debt relief in order to develop sustainably.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. Many developing countries need immediate help to meet basic human rights needs such as food, healthcare and housing, especially after sudden crises like Covid-19 or natural disasters, or after brutal civil wars that destroyed their infrastructure.
2. Many are still recovering from colonisation and exploitation, and some are trapped by conditional loans with unrealistic interest rates (dependency theory, Andre Gunder Frank). Debt relief frees money for health, education and green development, so they can grow sustainably instead of using up resources to repay debt.

prompt:
Explain the purpose of a programme for government.
(5 marks)
model_answer: A programme for government is a set of plans and actions agreed by the parties forming a new Government. It sets out what the Government hopes to achieve during its term, how it will work together, and its policies on areas such as housing, healthcare and education. In a coalition it is negotiated between the partners, so smaller parties can win commitments in return for joining (e.g. the Green Party in 2020). It also lets voters and the opposition hold the Government to account for its promises.
marking_scheme: Section A, Q1 (j). 5 marks. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Explain why, 'The highest cost is the cost of doing nothing' in relation to Climate Change.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Acting on climate change costs money now, but doing nothing costs far more later. Damage from climate change keeps building up, and it hits the poorest hardest: Sean McDonagh notes that 50 million people in eastern and southern Africa needed food aid in 2016. Delay leads to more biodiversity loss, pollution and disasters that must be paid for anyway, and could undo development progress. Acting early, as in the European Green Deal's plan for a climate-neutral EU by 2050 with a 'just transition', spreads the cost fairly and protects future generations.
marking_scheme: Section A, Q1 (k). 5 marks. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Present two arguments on the issue of whether the right to housing should be enshrined in the Irish Constitution.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
For: In 2015 the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called on Ireland to put ESC rights, such as the right to housing, into the Constitution. This would make the Government legally accountable for tackling homelessness, which has grown sharply, including thousands of homeless children.
Against: Housing is a positive right that needs a lot of resources and is realised progressively, so it is hard to enforce. Critics such as Nozick would argue it forces taxpayers to pay for others' rights, and that spending decisions belong to elected governments, not the courts.

prompt:
Voter suppression is a strategy which discourages or prevents specific groups of people from voting. Give two points about how voter suppression might influence the outcome of an election.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. The result would not reflect the will of all the people. If a specific group, such as a minority community, is stopped from voting, the parties or candidates it supports lose votes and seats, and that group becomes even more under-represented, so its issues are ignored.
2. It reduces the legitimacy of the winning government. A smaller, unrepresentative group of voters decides the outcome, so the government does not have the consent of all the people, which Locke argued a legitimate government needs.

prompt:
In September 2020, The European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights published the findings of a survey of Roma and Travellers in Europe entitled 'Roma and Travellers in Six Countries'. Ireland was one of the six countries included.
Almost every second respondent (44%) experienced at least one form of hate-motivated harassment because of being Roma or Traveller in the 12 months before the survey.

1. It isolates groups so they find it hard to integrate and contribute. When 44% of Roma and Travellers face harassment, they are pushed out of work, education and community life, and society loses their skills and participation.

prompt:
Document A: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2020.
Much of the data in this annual publication was collected before the coronavirus hit many of the countries featured in the survey. However, Reuters repeated key parts of the survey in six countries (UK, USA, Germany, Spain, South Korea, and Argentina) in early April 2020. These responses show increased consumption of traditional sources of news, especially television, but also some online news sources.
YouGov (commissioned by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism) conducted an online survey using something called Active Sampling to understand the impact of the novel coronavirus on the use of media in six countries. Sample sizes were approximately 2,000 in the UK and Germany, and 1,000 elsewhere. Samples in each country were assembled using nationally representative quotas for age, gender, region, and education. Anyone who said that they had not consumed any news in the past month, were filtered out in order to ensure that irrelevant responses didn't adversely affect data quality. This category averaged around 3%.
YouGov conducts its public opinion surveys online using Active Sampling and over the last fifteen years, have carefully recruited a panel of over one million British adults and over 6 million people worldwide to take part in their surveys. These panels are large enough to enable YouGov to select nationally representative samples that reflect the actual breakdown of the population on the key demographics. With Active Sampling only the relevant sample selected has access to the questionnaire via their username and password, and respondents can only ever answer each survey once.

Q. How trustworthy would you say news and information about corona virus COVID-19 from the following is?
TRUST IN DIFFERENT SOURCES OF NEWS AND INFORMATION ABOUT CORONAVIRUS (APRIL 2020) - AVERAGE OF SIX COUNTRIES
Source | Trust (%) | Neither/don't know (%) | Don't trust (%)
Scientists, doctors | 83 | 5 | 2
National health organisations | 76 | 9 | 5
Global health organisations | 73 | 12 | 5
News organisations | 59 | 21 | 18
The national government | 59 | 17 | 23
Ordinary people I know personally | 43 | 26 | 21
Individual politicians | 35 | 29 | 35
Ordinary people that I do not know personally | 17 | 33 | 45
Search engines (e.g. Google, Bing) | 45 | 29 | 18
Video sites (e.g. YouTube, Vimeo) | 29 | 31 | 34
Social media (e.g. Facebook, Twitter) | 26 | 29 | 40
Messaging apps (e.g. WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger) | 24 | 31 | 40

Critique the methodology used in Document A.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Strengths: The samples are large (about 2,000 in the UK and Germany and 1,000 elsewhere) and were built with nationally representative quotas for age, gender, region and education, so the results should reflect each population. Active Sampling means only selected people can answer, using a username and password, and each person answers only once, which protects data quality.
Weaknesses: It was an online survey of people who signed up to a YouGov panel, so people without internet access (often older or poorer people) and people who never volunteer are left out. Only six countries were surveyed (not Ireland), and the table gives an average of all six, which hides big differences between countries. It is a quantitative, closed-question snapshot from early April 2020, so it tells us what people trusted but not why, or how trust changed later in the pandemic.
marking_scheme: Section B, Q2 (a). 10 marks. Very good critique 8-10M; good critique 4-7M; fair critique 0-3M.

prompt:
Document B: Journalism, press freedom and COVID-19 - Issue brief in the UNESCO series: World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development, published for World Press Freedom Day, 2020 by UNESCO.
As the novel coronavirus has reached nearly every country on earth, there has also been mass circulation of falsehoods that have spread as fast as the virus itself. Recognising the danger, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that "our enemy is also the growing surge of misinformation". The World Health Organization has described the "second disease" accompanying the COVID-19 pandemic, as an "infodemic", which is "an over-abundance of information - some accurate and some not - that makes it hard for people to find trustworthy sources and reliable guidance when they need it".
Falsehoods in circulation can be categorised as both disinformation (produced and shared with malicious motivation), and misinformation, when these lies are spread without bad intentions. But in the context of COVID-19, the effects of both can be equally deadly. Statistics to track trends on the scope and spread of the disinfodemic are scarce. However, some figures point to a massive scale.
- Based on an analysis of 112 million public social media posts, in 64 languages, related to the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at the Bruno Kessler Foundation found 40% of posts came from unreliable sources.
- Roughly 1/3 of social media users have reported seeing false or misleading information about the coronavirus, says a study by the Reuters Institute carried out in six countries. Research by Pew suggests that people who receive their news primarily through social media are more likely to be exposed to false content.
- In March 2020, about 40 million problematic posts related to COVID-19 on Facebook were identified (and had warnings placed next to them), according to the company. The company confirmed that hundreds of thousands of pieces of misinformation about the virus that could lead to "imminent physical harm," were also removed.
- Approximately 19 million out of nearly 50 million (38%) tweets related to COVID-19 analysed using artificial intelligence by Blackbird.AI, were deemed to be "manipulated content".
- Newsguard identified 191 websites in Europe and North America that have published false information about the virus.
- The CoronaVirusFacts Alliance has discovered, and disproved, more than 3,500 false or misleading pieces of information, in more than 70 countries and in more than 40 languages.

Graphics which were part of UNESCO's campaign materials for World Press Freedom Day 2020:
Graphic 1: "nurses, doctors and facts are life savers."
Graphic 2: "for your health. please respect social media distancing."
Graphic 3: "information is the air you breathe, lies are like the virus, and a free press is the mask."
Graphic 4: "lies kill facts save."

Comment on the authorship of Document B.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Document B was written by UNESCO, the United Nations agency for education, science and culture, as an issue brief in its series World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development. This makes it authoritative and credible: it is a large, reputable international organisation, and it quotes the UN Secretary-General and the World Health Organization and names the researchers behind each statistic.
However, it was published for World Press Freedom Day 2020 as part of a campaign, together with campaign graphics. UNESCO therefore has an agenda: to promote press freedom and fight misinformation. It may present the evidence in a way that stresses the danger of the 'infodemic' and the value of a free press, so the reader should be aware of possible bias in what is selected and emphasised.
marking_scheme: Section B, Q2 (b). 10 marks. Very good comment 8-10M; good comment 4-7M; fair comment 0-3M.

Critique the use of multiple sources for statistics as used in Document B.

model_answer:

Seven different organisations (the Bruno Kessler Foundation, the Reuters Institute, Pew, Facebook, Blackbird.AI, Newsguard and the CoronaVirusFacts Alliance) all point the same way, so the conclusion that misinformation spread on a 'massive scale' is much stronger than if it rested on one study. The sources also cover different platforms (Facebook, Twitter, websites) and many countries and languages (112 million posts in 64 languages; over 70 countries), giving a fuller global picture.
Negative: The statistics are not directly comparable. Each source uses its own method, time period and definition - 'unreliable sources', 'problematic posts', 'manipulated content', 'false information' - so they cannot be added together or compared fairly. No methodology is given for any of them, and UNESCO admits such statistics are 'scarce'. Some sources may also have a conflict of interest: Facebook is reporting on its own platform and has an interest in showing it is taking action.

Section B, Q2 (c). 20 marks: one positive aspect (10 marks) + one negative aspect (10 marks).
Positive aspect: very good description 8-10M; good description 4-7M; fair description 0-3M.
Negative aspect: very good description 8-10M; good description 4-7M; fair description 0-3M.

model_answer:
One conclusion is that the public sees news organisations and government in a similar way: both are trusted by a majority (59%), but far less than scientists and doctors (83%) or national health organisations (76%). This may be because during the pandemic news organisations mainly reported government briefings, so people linked the two together.
This is a concern for democracy. The media should act as a watchdog that holds government to account. If people trust both equally, they may see the media as close to those in power - what Chomsky calls the 'media elite' in his propaganda model - rather than as an independent check.
However, the figures are not identical underneath. More people distrust the government (23%) than news organisations (18%), and more are unsure about the news (21% v 17%). So government faces more open distrust. Also, about four in ten people do not clearly trust either, and as the figure is an average of six countries, it may hide large national differences.

Document B: Journalism, press freedom and COVID-19 - Issue brief in the UNESCO series: World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development, published for World Press Freedom Day, 2020 by UNESCO.
Graphics which were part of UNESCO's campaign materials for World Press Freedom Day 2020:
Graphic 1: "nurses, doctors and facts are life savers."
Graphic 2: "for your health. please respect social media distancing."
Graphic 3: "information is the air you breathe, lies are like the virus, and a free press is the mask."
Graphic 4: "lies kill facts save."

What statement is Graphic 3 in Document B making about the role of the press in a democratic society?
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Graphic 3 says: 'information is the air you breathe, lies are like the virus, and a free press is the mask.' Its statement is that a free press protects citizens from lies in the same way a mask protects people from a virus.
Accurate information is as essential to a democracy as air is to life: citizens need it to make decisions, take part and hold government to account. Lies spread like a virus, infecting more people the further they travel. A free press acts as the mask: professional journalists check facts and give factual accounts, filtering out falsehoods before they reach us.
This links to the three core ideas about the media in a democracy: freedom of the press (UDHR: the right to impart information 'through any media'), the social responsibility of the press to serve the public good, and its role as a watchdog. The press can only do this if it is free; that is why the graphic was made for World Press Freedom Day. Like a mask, a free press cannot stop every lie, but it greatly reduces the spread.

Document A: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2020.
Much of the data in this annual publication was collected before the coronavirus hit many of the countries featured in the survey. However, Reuters repeated key parts of the survey in six countries (UK, USA, Germany, Spain, South Korea, and Argentina) in early April 2020. These responses show increased consumption of traditional sources of news, especially television, but also some online news sources.
YouGov (commissioned by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism) conducted an online survey using something called Active Sampling to understand the impact of the novel coronavirus on the use of media in six countries. Sample sizes were approximately 2,000 in the UK and Germany, and 1,000 elsewhere. Samples in each country were assembled using nationally representative quotas for age, gender, region, and education. Anyone who said that they had not consumed any news in the past month, were filtered out in order to ensure that irrelevant responses didn't adversely affect data quality. This category averaged around 3%.
YouGov conducts its public opinion surveys online using Active Sampling and over the last fifteen years, have carefully recruited a panel of over one million British adults and over 6 million people worldwide to take part in their surveys. These panels are large enough to enable YouGov to select nationally representative samples that reflect the actual breakdown of the population on the key demographics. With Active Sampling only the relevant sample selected has access to the questionnaire via their username and password, and respondents can only ever answer each survey once.

Document B: Journalism, press freedom and COVID-19 - Issue brief in the UNESCO series: World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development, published for World Press Freedom Day, 2020 by UNESCO.
As the novel coronavirus has reached nearly every country on earth, there has also been mass circulation of falsehoods that have spread as fast as the virus itself. Recognising the danger, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that "our enemy is also the growing surge of misinformation". The World Health Organization has described the "second disease" accompanying the COVID-19 pandemic, as an "infodemic", which is "an over-abundance of information - some accurate and some not - that makes it hard for people to find trustworthy sources and reliable guidance when they need it".
Falsehoods in circulation can be categorised as both disinformation (produced and shared with malicious motivation), and misinformation, when these lies are spread without bad intentions. But in the context of COVID-19, the effects of both can be equally deadly. Statistics to track trends on the scope and spread of the disinfodemic are scarce. However, some figures point to a massive scale.
- Based on an analysis of 112 million public social media posts, in 64 languages, related to the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at the Bruno Kessler Foundation found 40% of posts came from unreliable sources.

Research by Pew suggests that people who receive their news primarily through social media are more likely to be exposed to false content.
- In March 2020, about 40 million problematic posts related to COVID-19 on Facebook were identified (and had warnings placed next to them), according to the company. The company confirmed that hundreds of thousands of pieces of misinformation about the virus that could lead to "imminent physical harm," were also removed.

Extra material for part (g):
Ireland at UN @irishmissionun - Oct 21: "Today the United Nations launches #PledgetoPause and calls on everyone to pause and #takecarebeforeyoushare online. A small share can have big consequences for our world. Will you join us?"
Campaign graphic - Question: What spreads across the globe exponentially, can be passed on unwittingly, is potentially deadly if you come into contact with it but measures can be taken by you to stop it from spreading further? Answer: Misinformation.

Drawing on both documents, evaluate the necessity for a campaign such as this about misinformation.
(50 marks)
model_answer:
In my view a campaign such as #PledgetoPause is necessary, because the scale and danger of misinformation are clear from both documents, but it is not enough on its own.
The scale of the problem: Document B shows misinformation spread 'as fast as the virus itself'. 40% of 112 million social media posts came from unreliable sources, 38% of COVID-19 tweets were manipulated, and Facebook flagged about 40 million problematic posts in one month. The CoronaVirusFacts Alliance disproved over 3,500 false claims in more than 70 countries. A problem this large needs a global response like a UN campaign.
The danger: Both misinformation and disinformation 'can be equally deadly'. Facebook removed posts that could cause 'imminent physical harm', and the WHO warned the 'infodemic' makes it hard to find reliable guidance when people need it most.
Why the campaign targets the right behaviour: Document B explains that much false information is misinformation, spread 'without bad intentions'. The campaign's riddle makes the point that misinformation, like a virus, 'can be passed on unwittingly'. Asking ordinary users to pause before they share targets exactly this. Document A supports this: only 17% trust ordinary people they do not know and only 26% trust social media, yet people still share content there, so a small pause can stop a lot of harm.
Limits: A voluntary pledge relies on individuals. It will not stop disinformation, which is spread deliberately with 'malicious motivation'. Document A also shows that most people already distrust social media, so the campaign may mostly reach those who are careful anyway. Stronger action is needed too: platforms flagging and removing posts (as Facebook did), fact-checkers, and a free press, which UNESCO calls 'the mask' against lies. People most trust scientists and doctors (83%) and health organisations (73-76%), so the campaign should point people towards those sources.
Conclusion: The evidence of a massive, deadly 'infodemic' shows a campaign like #PledgetoPause is necessary and cheap, and it builds personal responsibility. But it works best as one part of a wider response that includes platform action, fact-checking and support for a free, trusted press.

prompt:
'This crisis shows we need a social contract to protect all our people.'
Headline in the Irish Independent [29 March 2020]
Do you believe there is a need to re-draft the social contract in Ireland, in the context of a post-pandemic society?
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The social contract is an agreement among members of society to give up some individual freedom in return for protection from the ruler or state. Thomas Hobbes and John Locke both used the idea, but in different ways. During the Covid-19 pandemic the Irish state asked citizens to give up freedoms to protect everyone, and it spent heavily to support them. The crisis also exposed groups the contract does not protect well. In this essay I will argue that Ireland does need to re-draft its social contract after the pandemic, so that it protects all people, especially in housing and inequality, using Hobbes, Locke and John Rawls.

The pandemic showed the social contract working
In the pandemic the state acted much as Hobbes would expect. Hobbes believed people give up freedoms to a strong state in return for security, because life without it would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. Irish citizens accepted limits on the right to move freely, a qualified right that can be restricted to protect the common good. The state also protected people financially: EU social protection spending rose by over 8% in 2020, its largest rise in ten years, and Ireland spent €11,348 per person on social protection in 2021, tenth in the EU. The CSO found that without social welfare almost four in ten people would be in poverty. This suggests that, in a crisis, the contract can protect people.

But it does not protect all our people
Locke argued a government is legitimate only if it keeps the trust and consent of the people and protects their rights. Many Irish people would say the contract is failing them. Over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023, more than 3,000 of them children. Homelessness rose by 178%, and a joint Oireachtas committee criticised the Government's reliance on the private sector for social housing. In 2019 the Ombudsman for Children's report 'No Place Like Home' recommended examining a right to housing in the Constitution. Young people protested in the Winter of Housing Discontent in 2021. Other groups, such as people in Direct Provision, waited an average of 24 months in centres, with families sharing a single room. When a state cannot house its children, it is fair to say it has not met its side of the contract.

A fairer contract: Rawls
John Rawls argued for a social contract based on 'justice as fairness'. People are born into a 'social lottery' they did not choose, so inequalities should only be allowed if they benefit the least well off. Before taxes and benefits, Ireland has the most unequal income distribution in the EU, though the ESRI found our tax system does more than any other in Europe to reduce this. A post-pandemic contract built on Rawls would keep the stronger safety net created during Covid, introduce the living wage (60% of the median wage) and treat housing as a right rather than a market product.

The counter-argument
Robert Nozick would reject this. He favoured a minimal state providing only law and order, and saw taxing earnings to redistribute wealth as 'forced labour'. Others argue the pandemic proved the existing contract works: the Government already has plans such as Housing for All (2022), with schemes like cost-rental homes at least 25% below market rents and Housing First tenancies. On this view, we need better delivery, not a new contract. Hobbes, too, would warn that endless re-negotiation weakens the stability that the contract exists to protect.

Evaluation
I find the argument for re-drafting stronger. The pandemic showed that the state can act quickly and spend at scale when it decides people must be protected. If that is possible in an emergency, it is possible for homelessness, which has been a long-running emergency for thousands of families. Existing plans have not stopped numbers rising, which suggests the problem is the terms of the contract, not just delivery. A new contract does not mean a bigger state for its own sake; it means writing clear commitments, such as a constitutional right to housing, so the state can be held to account.

Conclusion
The Irish Independent headline was right: the crisis showed we need a social contract that protects all our people. Hobbes explains why citizens accepted restrictions, but Locke reminds us that the state keeps its legitimacy only while it protects the rights of all. Using Rawls, I conclude that a post-pandemic social contract should be re-drafted around fairness to the least well off, starting with housing.

prompt:
Evaluate the statement from the Climate Finance Shadow Report 2020 published by Oxfam, which states that:
'Climate change could undo decades of progress in development and dramatically increase global inequalities.'
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course and/or refer to two or more relevant international agreements/organisations (e.g. United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, Paris Climate Agreement 2016, the World Bank, etc.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Oxfam's Climate Finance Shadow Report 2020 warns that climate change could undo decades of development progress and dramatically increase global inequality. Development has made real gains: under the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015) world hunger was cut in half and extreme poverty fell by nearly half. In this essay I will evaluate Oxfam's claim using evidence on how climate change affects poor countries, the ideas of Gro Harlem Brundtland, Andre Gunder Frank, Vandana Shiva and Sean McDonagh, and international responses such as the Sustainable Development Goals and the European Green Deal. I will argue the statement is largely accurate, unless rich countries take much stronger action.

Climate change hits the poorest hardest
The countries least responsible for emissions suffer most. Sean McDonagh points out that 50 million people in eastern and southern Africa needed food aid in 2016, and says 'the cry of the poor for social justice is mirrored in the cry of the earth'. Many poor countries depend on farming and natural resources, and they have weak infrastructure, so droughts, floods and crop failures push people back into hunger. The UN lists 46 Least Developed Countries that are 'highly vulnerable to economic and environmental shocks'. When a harvest fails, children leave school and families sell assets, so the gains of decades can be lost in a season. This supports Oxfam's view that progress could be undone.

Climate change deepens existing inequality
Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory argues that underdevelopment results from the exploitation of periphery states by core states. Climate change fits this pattern: the core grew rich by burning fossil fuels, while the periphery pays the cost. The Brundtland argument about fairness makes the same point: the Global North grew freely, yet developing countries are now told to limit growth, while rich countries still produce disproportionately high emissions. Environmental damage linked to global corporations adds to this: the 2015 Indonesian fires caused by clearing land for palm oil released greenhouse gases almost equal to Indonesia's emissions for a whole year.

Gender inequality is also widened. Vandana Shiva's ecofeminism argues that women, the traditional environmental stewards, are pushed into powerlessness and poverty when the environment is damaged. Oxfam (2023) found women earn 24% less than men globally and 75% of women in developing regions work in the informal economy, so they have little protection when climate shocks hit. Climate change therefore increases inequality between and within countries.

The counter-argument: international action
Others argue the statement is too pessimistic because the world is responding. The 17 Sustainable Development Goals apply to all countries and include SDG 13 (climate action) and SDG 10 (reduced inequalities), recognising that poverty, inequality and climate change are interconnected. The European Green Deal (2019) aims to make the EU climate-neutral by 2050; the European Climate Law makes a 55% emissions cut legally binding, and the 'just transition' is designed to leave no one behind. Neoliberals also argue that technology and market forces will make clean energy cheaper.

Evaluating these responses
These responses are real but limited. Yanis Varoufakis calls the Green Deal 'a colossal exercise in greenwashing', pointing out that the EU still supported a multi-billion-euro gas pipeline. Governments often choose short-term economic gain over long-term sustainability and still subsidise fossil fuels. Critics of the free-market view note that markets put short-term profit first and wealth does not 'trickle down'. Brundtland's model is a moral guide rather than a set of policies, and it only works if all countries take part. Climate finance from rich countries, which Oxfam's report examines, is exactly where the gap between promises and delivery matters most.

Conclusion
I largely agree with Oxfam. The evidence shows that climate change falls hardest on the poorest countries and on women, and dependency theory explains why the costs land on those who did least to cause it. International agreements like the SDGs and the Green Deal show what could be done, but as long as action is slow and greenwashed, climate change could well undo decades of progress. The statement is best read as a warning: it will come true unless rich countries meet their responsibilities.

prompt:
'It is not just COVID that's killing people, it is under-privilege; it's lack of access, it's years living with health conditions that haven't been properly managed because of the colour of your skin or your ethnicity or your social group.'
Dr Mike Ryan, Executive Director, WHO Health Emergency Programme, 2020.
Evaluate Dr Ryan's statement in relation to the threat to life posed by global inequalities and discrimination in societies around the world.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Dr Mike Ryan of the WHO argues that Covid-19 did not kill people equally: poverty, lack of access to healthcare and discrimination based on skin colour, ethnicity or social group made some people far more likely to die. In this essay I evaluate his statement using evidence on child survival, vaccine access and discrimination, together with the ideas of Martha Nussbaum, Andre Gunder Frank and John Rawls. I will argue that his statement is accurate: inequality and discrimination are a direct threat to the right to life.

Global inequality and the right to life
Article 6 of the UNCRC gives every child 'the inherent right to life' and says states must ensure survival and development 'to the maximum extent possible'. Yet survival depends heavily on where you are born. UNICEF reports that in 2021 one in 26 children worldwide died before age five, but in Sub-Saharan Africa it was one in 14, fifteen times higher than in high-income countries. In South Sudan, under-five mortality is 98.7 per 1,000 live births, 1.4 million young children face malnutrition, and 51% of children use water from limited or unimproved sources. These deaths come from malaria, pneumonia and vaccine-preventable disease: conditions that are managed elsewhere. This is exactly Ryan's point about 'lack of access'.

Covid-19 made this inequality visible. On 17 June 2021, North America and Europe had administered 68 vaccine doses per 100 people, while Sub-Saharan Africa had fewer than 2 per 100. The same virus was far more dangerous for people in poor countries, because of where they were born, not because of the virus itself.

Why the gap exists
Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory explains why poor countries lack access. Wealth flows from periphery states to core states, and the periphery stays poor. The DRC has some of the world's richest mineral deposits, including cobalt for smartphones and electric cars, yet it is one of the poorest countries: 7 in 100 children die before age five and 33 million rural people lack safe drinking water. Conditional loans can make this worse: in Sierra Leone, IMF conditions required cuts to health spending while the country was still dealing with the effects of Ebola.

Discrimination within societies
Ryan also refers to skin colour, ethnicity and social group, and this applies within wealthy countries too, including Ireland. An Oireachtas Joint Committee (2021) found that Travellers live in 'deficient and substandard living conditions and homelessness which have severely detrimental effects on both mental and physical health'. The EU Fundamental Rights Agency (2020) found 44% of Roma and Travellers had experienced hate-motivated harassment in the previous year. In Ireland's housing crisis, the hardest hit are people on low incomes, people with disabilities and those with less social capital. Overcrowding and poor housing make it harder to isolate and recover from illness, so social class becomes a health risk.

Theorists
Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach supports Ryan. She argues everyone needs a social minimum of capabilities for a dignified life, starting with 'Life: being able to live a full, healthy life' and 'Health: being able to enjoy health, shelter and nourishment'. Having a right to health on paper means little if you cannot reach a clinic or a vaccine. John Rawls's 'social lottery' makes the same point: the country, family and wealth you are born into are not chosen, so a just society should arrange inequalities to benefit the least well off.

Counter-argument
Some would argue Ryan overstates the role of discrimination. There has been remarkable progress: child mortality fell from one in 11 in 1990 to one in 26 in 2021. Some deaths in places like South Sudan and the DRC are caused mainly by conflict and weak or corrupt governance, not by discrimination by richer societies. Supporters of modernisation theory argue that growth and technology will close the gap over time.

Evaluation and conclusion
The progress is real, but it does not disprove Ryan. The huge gaps that remain follow the lines of wealth, ethnicity and class, and conflict and weak governance are themselves linked to poverty and exploitation. Covid-19 vaccine figures show that when a life-saving resource was scarce, it went to the rich first. I conclude that Ryan's statement is accurate: inequality and discrimination turn treatable conditions into deadly ones, and protecting the right to life requires tackling them, not just the virus.

prompt:
"Difference is of the essence of humanity. Difference is an accident of birth and it should therefore never be the source of hatred or conflict. The answer to difference is to respect it. Therein lies a most fundamental principle of peace - respect for diversity."
Quote from: John Hume (1937-2020), Nobel Peace Prize winner and Northern Ireland politician.
Compare the view of John Hume on diversity with Kwame Anthony Appiah's theory of cosmopolitanism.
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
John Hume, the Nobel Peace Prize winner who helped bring peace to Northern Ireland, argued that difference is 'an accident of birth', that it should never cause hatred, and that respect for diversity is 'a most fundamental principle of peace'. Kwame Anthony Appiah's theory of cosmopolitanism also celebrates difference while stressing what all humans share. In this essay I compare their views, using Northern Ireland, Ballyhaunis in Co. Mayo and anti-immigrant tensions in Ireland as evidence, and contrasting both with Samuel Huntington. I will argue that their views are very similar, but that Appiah goes further by stressing conversation and moral concern beyond national borders.

Similarity 1: difference is natural and should be respected
Hume says difference is 'of the essence of humanity'. Appiah agrees: cosmopolitanism recognises 'universal strands' connecting all humans but also celebrates differences. A cosmopolitan person values different forms of social and cultural life, within and between countries, as long as human rights are respected. Appiah does not ask people to put their differences aside: we 'bring them to the table', 'united by common morals and separated through the richness of diversity'. This is close to Hume's 'the answer to difference is to respect it'.

Similarity 2: identity is not fixed
Hume's phrase 'an accident of birth' suggests nobody chooses their identity, so nobody should be punished for it. Appiah, born in London to a Ghanaian father and an English mother, argues identities are partly invented: you can 'take up your roots' and choose parts of local life wherever you settle, and people can hold multiple identities. Both reject the idea that one identity must defeat another.

Evidence: Northern Ireland
Hume's view was shaped by conflict between unionists and nationalists. The Belfast/Good Friday Agreement (1998) put respect for diversity into practice through power-sharing: the First Minister and Deputy First Minister come from the two communities and have equal powers, and special voting procedures stop one community dominating. This is Hume's principle in institutional form. But the Executive collapsed in 2017 over an Irish Language Act and again in 2022 over the Northern Ireland Protocol, which shows that respecting difference is hard to sustain when identities are tied to borders. Appiah notes that 'most identities grow from conflict' and that borders are often drawn after conflict.

Evidence: Ballyhaunis
In Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo, 20 ethnic minorities make up over 50% of the population. The local GAA club, where children of over a dozen nationalities play together, together with festivals and language exchanges, built tolerance and social cohesion. This supports both thinkers: difference, when respected, enriches a community. It is a clear example of Appiah's cultural hybridisation, where cultures blend and new forms are created.

Difference 1: conversation, not just tolerance
Here Appiah goes beyond Hume. Hume calls for respect; Appiah calls for conversation. Shared conversation lets us 'borrow good ideas' from others and helps us 'agree how to disagree'. For Appiah, respect is the starting point, but real cosmopolitanism means engaging with and learning from others. As the Ghanaian saying puts it, 'In a single polis there is no wisdom.'

Difference 2: concern beyond our borders
Hume's quote comes from a divided society and focuses on peace within it. Appiah's 'cosmopolitan patriotism' extends moral concern to all of humanity: we should care for all humans, not just our own community, and 'remember that you are citizens of the world'. He believes globalisation makes this more relevant than ever. Appiah also stresses that global citizenship does not mean one world government.

Counter-view: Huntington
Samuel Huntington would challenge both. He argued that cultures form 'fault lines' and an 'us vs them' mentality, making conflict likely. Anti-refugee protests in Ireland, threats to burn hotels housing refugees and the November 2023 riots in Dublin suggest difference can indeed become 'the source of hatred'. However, this does not disprove Hume or Appiah: they describe how we ought to respond to difference, and Ballyhaunis shows it can work.

Conclusion
Hume and Appiah share the belief that difference is natural and must be respected, and both see this as the basis for peace. Hume's view is rooted in ending a local conflict through respect and shared institutions, while Appiah offers a wider, global theory based on conversation and concern for all humanity. I conclude that Appiah's cosmopolitanism builds on the principle Hume put into practice, and that together they offer a stronger answer to division than Huntington's 'us vs them'.

prompt:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, as governments have scrambled to protect their populations many human rights and civil liberties taken for granted have been restricted or taken away.
Discuss the challenge for governments of maintaining the balance between the rights of the individual and the rights of the majority in a democratic country.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
In a democracy, governments must protect the rights of each individual while also acting for the good of the majority. Sometimes these clash. During Covid-19, rights such as the freedom to move freely and to assemble were restricted to protect public health. In this essay I discuss this challenge using three examples - pandemic restrictions, hate speech and the right to protest - and the ideas of Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Robert Nozick. I will argue that individual rights can sometimes be limited for the majority, but only when the limit is necessary, lawful, temporary and open to challenge.

Example 1: Covid-19 restrictions
Most human rights are inalienable, but some are qualified rights: an authority can interfere with them in the interest of the wider community, if it meets a social need and protects the common good. The right to move freely, limited during Covid-19, is the clearest example. The challenge is proportionality. Restrictions saved lives, but they also closed schools, stopped protests and kept families apart. A government must show that each limit is needed and must lift it when the danger passes.

Hobbes would strongly support the restrictions. He believed people enter a social contract, giving up freedoms to a strong sovereign in return for security, because without it life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. For Hobbes, the aim of government is peace and stability, not individual freedom, so emergency powers are fully justified.

Example 2: hate speech versus free speech
Freedom of expression is protected by Article 19 of the UDHR. But hate speech can lead to discrimination or violence and stop targeted groups taking part in society. IHREC's 2019 report found the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 ineffective, and the Government brought in the Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Bill. Supporters say the old law had been outstripped by the internet. Critics say the Bill goes too far and could censor politically incorrect views. This shows the balance runs both ways: here limiting one person's speech protects the rights of minorities, not just the majority.

Example 3: the right to protest
Peaceful protest is protected by the Irish Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. It lets people who cannot vote, such as under-18s in Greta Thunberg's Fridays For Future strikes, 'speak truth to power'. But protests can also be used to spread fear: anti-refugee protests in Ireland included threats to burn hotels housing refugees, and far-right riots took place in Dublin in November 2023. Governments must protect the right to protest without allowing it to threaten others' safety.

Locke and Nozick: the other side
John Locke offers a strong counter-view to Hobbes. He believed people have natural rights to life, liberty and property that no government can take away, and that government is legitimate only while it keeps the consent of the people. If a government abuses its power, citizens have a right to resist. Locke's ideas suggest that emergency powers must be limited and accountable. Robert Nozick, a libertarian influenced by Locke, would go further: he believed the state should be minimal and should interfere as little as possible in individual lives. He would be wary of governments using a crisis to expand their power.

Evaluation
The danger of the Hobbesian approach is clear from non-democratic states. In Iran, unelected institutions restrict civil liberties and suppress opposition in the name of protecting the system. A democracy is different because of checks and balances: the separation of powers lets courts review laws, the Oireachtas debates emergency measures, and bodies such as IHREC monitor rights. These checks are what make it possible to limit individual rights for the majority without sliding into authoritarianism.

Conclusion
Balancing individual and majority rights is one of the hardest challenges for a democratic government. Covid-19 showed that some rights must sometimes be set aside to protect everyone, as Hobbes would argue. But Locke reminds us that a government keeps its legitimacy only while it respects natural rights and the consent of the people. I conclude that the balance is best kept when restrictions are necessary, proportionate, temporary and subject to the courts, the Oireachtas and a free press.

prompt:
In the European Union, women are paid 14.1% less per hour than men on average. This equals almost two months of salary in a year.
This is why the European Commission marks 10 November as a symbolic day to raise awareness about the fact that female workers in Europe still earn on average less than their male colleagues.
Discuss whether the gender pay gap is a complex issue, which goes far beyond the issue of equal pay for equal work.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The gender pay gap is the difference in average gross hourly earnings between women and men. In the EU women are paid 14.1% less per hour, almost two months' salary a year; in Ireland the gap was 14.4% in 2020. Paying a woman less than a man for the same job is already illegal under the Employment Equality Acts. So the gap that remains must come from something deeper. In this essay I will argue that the gender pay gap is a complex issue that goes far beyond equal pay for equal work, using evidence from the EU and Ireland and the ideas of Sylvia Walby, Kathleen Lynch and Martha Nussbaum.

Part-time and unpaid work
The European Parliament identifies part-time and unpaid work as a key cause. In the EU, 28% of women work part-time compared with 8% of men (Eurostat 2020), and in 2018 a third of employed women had a career break for childcare, compared with just 1.3% of men. These patterns are not about unequal pay for the same work; they are about who does the caring. Kathleen Lynch calls this affective inequality: care and emotional labour are unpaid or undervalued because they are seen as 'natural' for women. In Ireland, 195,263 people were unpaid carers in 2016, over 60% of them women, worth €10 billion a year to the State.

Fewer women at the top
Women made up almost half of EU employees in 2020 but only 34% of managers, and female managers earned 23% less per hour than male managers. The gap is larger in higher-paid jobs. Lynch describes 'care commanders', usually men, who hold power and resources, and 'footsoldiers', usually women, who do the care work as nurses, teachers and childcare workers. Jobs dominated by women tend to be lower paid.

Patriarchy in society
Sylvia Walby's theory of patriarchy explains why these patterns persist. She identifies six structures, including the household, where women do most domestic and care work, and paid work, where women are concentrated in low-paid, low-status jobs and under-represented in leadership. Public patriarchy is built into the labour market, the state and education. In Ireland, women made up only about 22% of TDs after 2016, so decisions on childcare and pay are mostly made by men. As Walby puts it, 'Liberated from the home, women now have the whole of society in which to be exploited.'

A gap that lasts a lifetime
The gap grows with age. The gender pension gap was over 28% in the EU in 2020, putting women at greater risk of poverty in old age. The OECD found a 'motherhood pay gap': women earn 22% less on average, and 33% less if they have children. Globally, Oxfam reports women earn 24% less than men and do at least twice as much unpaid care work.

Counter-argument
Some argue the gap is not discrimination at all but the result of choice. Forbes (2016) called it a 'myth' based on statistical manipulation. Claudia Goldin of Harvard found that women often seek flexibility, which leads to part-time, lower-paid jobs, while men reach higher corporate positions. Differences in qualifications and experience also play a part.

Evaluation
This counter-argument actually supports the view that the issue is complex. The 'choices' women make are shaped by social expectations - women as carers, men as breadwinners - by the cost of childcare and by workplaces built around the full-time male worker. Martha Nussbaum's capabilities approach asks what people are actually able to do and be. A woman who cannot afford childcare is not freely choosing part-time work. Policies show the issue needs more than equal-pay laws: in December 2022 the EU agreed companies must disclose pay information, and in 2022 Ireland increased paid parental leave to seven weeks for both parents to encourage shared caring.

Conclusion
Equal pay for equal work is already the law, yet the gap remains. Evidence on part-time work, career breaks, management, pensions and motherhood shows the causes lie in how care is shared, how work is valued and who holds power. Walby's patriarchy and Lynch's affective inequality explain why. I conclude that the gender pay gap is a complex issue that can only be closed by tackling unpaid care, childcare costs and the structures of patriarchy, not just pay rates.
