prompt:
State and explain one example of how the system of checks and balances works in Irish democracy.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Checks and balances means each branch of government (executive, legislature and judiciary) has powers that can control the others, so no one part becomes too powerful. One example is the Seanad. When the Dáil passes a Government bill, the Seanad can debate it, amend it and delay it becoming law. The President can also refer a bill to the Supreme Court to test if it is constitutional before signing it. This stops the Government using its Dáil majority to rush through laws without scrutiny.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may refer to: separation of powers; the role of the media as a watchdog; an example of checks and balances in action. Very good explanation 4-5 marks; good explanation 2-3 marks; fair explanation 0-1 marks.

prompt:
Make two points about the right to peaceful protest as a means of political participation.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Point 1: Peaceful protest is protected as part of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly (UDHR, the Irish Constitution and the ECHR). It lets people who cannot vote, such as under-18s, take part in politics. For example, Greta Thunberg's Fridays For Future climate strikes brought over 10,000 students onto the streets of Dublin in 2019.
Point 2: Protest can bring social and political change by focusing attention on an issue and forcing debate, as in the US Civil Rights protests led by Martin Luther King. However, the right is limited: the state can restrict protest to protect public safety.
marking_scheme: 3 marks + 2 marks. Responses may refer to: Article 20 UDHR - freedom of assembly; national security/public safety; protest as freedom of expression; a relevant example; social and political change. First point: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Second point: good 2M, fair 1M. If the first point gets 2M or less, mark the second point out of 3M.

prompt:
Explain the message portrayed in this cartoon. Which key thinker would you associate with this view?
[The cartoon carries the words: 'NO ONE IS GOING TO GIVE YOU THE EDUCATION YOU NEED TO OVERTHROW THEM.' Source: Assata Shakur, Assata: An Autobiography.]
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Message: Education is political. Those who hold power control the education system, so it is used to pass on their ideas and keep things as they are. People who are oppressed will not be taught how to question or challenge that power; they have to gain critical thinking for themselves.
Key thinker: Paulo Freire. He said traditional 'banking' education fills students with facts and stops them developing critical consciousness. His problem-posing education helps the oppressed see their oppression and act to change it.
marking_scheme: Explanation of the message: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Key thinker: Paulo Freire (or any other relevant thinker) 2M.

prompt:
Briefly explain the function of the Oireachtas Committee System in Irish parliamentary politics.
(5 marks)
model_answer: An Oireachtas committee is a group of TDs, Senators or both, chosen to look at one subject in more depth than the full Dáil or Seanad can. Departmental committees shadow a government department and examine its policy, proposed laws and spending. Thematic committees look at topics such as European affairs. Committees consider bills at the Committee Stage, hold hearings with stakeholders and civil society groups, and publish reports with recommendations. For example, the Public Accounts Committee examines how public money is spent.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may refer to: advisory role; committee members include TDs, Senators or both; the role of civil society groups; an actual example plus description, e.g. the PAC. Very good explanation 4-5 marks; good explanation 2-3 marks; fair explanation 0-1 marks.

prompt:
Critique the use of cartoons as a tool of political speech.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Strengths: Cartoons are a form of freedom of expression. They use humour and simple images, so they are quick to understand and reach a wide audience. They can act as a watchdog by mocking people in power and getting readers to question them.
Weaknesses: Cartoons simplify complex issues and lack nuance. They can rely on stereotyping and frame an issue in a biased way. Taken out of context or shared on social media, satire can be taken seriously and spread misinformation.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good critique 4-5M; good critique 2-3M; fair critique 0-1M.

prompt:
In this Irish Times/IPSOS MRBI poll, voters were asked if they would support or be opposed to certain measures to combat climate change.
What message can the Irish Government take from the answer to the question regarding higher taxes on energy and fuel?
Higher taxes on energy and fuel - share of respondents:
Yes: 14%
No: 82%
(5 marks)
model_answer: The message is that the public strongly opposes paying for climate action through higher taxes: 82% said no and only 14% said yes. People may worry about climate change, but that concern does not turn into willingness to pay more for energy and fuel, especially in a cost-of-living crisis. Increases in carbon tax are therefore politically risky. The Government may need to use other measures, such as grants and a 'just transition' that protects lower-income households, to keep public support.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may refer to: public resistance to paying taxes as a climate action measure; concern over climate change does not seem to translate into enthusiasm to pay to combat it; a relevant example plus explanation, e.g. resistance to Carbon Tax. Very good explanation 4-5 marks; good explanation 2-3 marks; fair explanation 0-1 marks.

prompt:
Name and describe a model of youth participation outside of the school environment used by organisations or governments to capture the voice of young people in decision-making processes.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Model of participation: Lundy's Model of Participation (Laura Lundy).
Description: It is based on Article 12 of the UNCRC (the right to be heard) and is not hierarchical. It has four elements in order. Space: give children a safe, inclusive space to express views. Voice: give them the information they need and help them express their views. Audience: make sure their views reach someone with the power to act. Influence: make sure views are taken seriously, acted on where appropriate, and that children get feedback on decisions.
marking_scheme: Name 2M (a mechanism for youth participation outside of the school environment); description 3M. Possible responses: Hart's Ladder; Shier's Pathways to Participation; Lundy Model of Participation. Description must match the model named: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M.

prompt:
Critique the value of opinion polls.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Positives: Opinion polls are quantitative data. They can survey large samples quickly and cheaply, and results are easy to compare and show in charts. Governments and parties can use them to see what the public thinks.
Negatives: Their value depends on the sample. A small or unrepresentative sample gives misleading results. Closed questions limit answers, so polls lack nuance and show what people think but not why. Question wording can bring in researcher bias, and published polls can influence how people vote.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good critique 4-5M; good critique 2-3M; fair critique 0-1M.

prompt:
Explain the significance of this headline in The Guardian in relation to the climate crisis.
[Headline: 'Clean environment is a human right, UN council agrees. Human rights council also appoints special rapporteur to monitor impact of climate crisis on rights'. The image also shows a protest sign: 'WE ARE THE FUTURE'.]
(5 marks)
model_answer: The headline is significant because it links the climate crisis to human rights. If a clean environment is a human right, states become duty bearers who must protect it, not just a policy choice. A special rapporteur will monitor how climate change affects rights, putting pressure on governments to act. It supports campaigners such as Fridays For Future ('We are the future') who say young and future generations will suffer most. It also fits sustainable development: meeting today's needs without harming future generations.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Critically evaluate this image in the context of the global influence of supranational organisations.
[The image shows the words SUPRANATIONAL ORGANISATIONS surrounded by: UN, EU, OECD, G20, REGULATIONS, BUREAUCRACY (in large bold letters), FREE ENTERPRISE and CIVIL RIGHTS. Source article: 'Supranational bodies and the lack of democratic accountability'.]
(5 marks)
model_answer: The image suggests that supranational bodies such as the UN, EU and G20 create layers of regulation and bureaucracy that can threaten civil rights, free enterprise and democracy. This has some truth. Member states pool sovereignty, and decisions are made by people citizens did not elect, such as the European Commission. In the IMF, votes depend on money, so the US has 16.5% of the vote. However, the image is one-sided. These bodies also protect rights and tackle global problems no state can solve alone, such as climate change.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Possible responses: civil rights are endangered; reduces the sovereignty of nation-states; more bureaucracy, less democracy. Very good explanation 4-5 marks; good explanation 2-3 marks; fair explanation 0-1 marks.

prompt:
Describe the selection method used by Northern Ireland's power-sharing executive to appoint MLAs (Members of the Legislative Assembly) to ministerial roles.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), ministries are given out using the D'Hondt system. This is a mathematical formula based on each party's number of seats. Parties pick ministries in turn, and after each pick their total is recalculated, so the larger parties choose first but all large parties from both communities get a share. This creates a mandatory coalition. The First Minister and Deputy First Minister come from the two communities, have equal powers and must agree on all decisions.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may refer to: the 'D'Hondt' system; appointment of the First Minister and Deputy First Minister; special arrangement for the appointment of the Minister for Justice. Very good description 4-5M; good description 2-3M; fair description 0-1M.

prompt:
Critically evaluate this image in the context of the growing power and influence of social media.
[A cartoon (Brian Adcock, 'Earth selfie'). Caption: 'Catastrophic climate warning from UN'. Speech bubble: 'Maybe people will notice if I tweet a selfie'.]
(5 marks)
model_answer: The cartoon suggests that serious warnings from official bodies like the UN are ignored, while people pay attention to selfies on social media. Social media now shapes what the public thinks is important (agenda setting), and people live in echo chambers where trivial content gets more attention than facts. However, social media can also be positive. It has no gatekeepers, so campaigners can reach millions; Greta Thunberg's Fridays For Future used it to organise climate strikes in over 200 countries. The risk is that it also spreads misinformation.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good evaluation 4-5M; good evaluation 2-3M; fair evaluation 0-1M.

prompt:
What is the purpose of a political party?
(5 marks)
model_answer: A political party brings together people who share the same political ideas or ideology, for example on the left or right. It nominates candidates for elections and tries to get as many as possible elected, ideally enough to form a government (a majority in the Dáil). Once elected, its members try to put the party's policies into law. In a coalition, parties negotiate a programme for government, as Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and the Greens did in 2020. Opposition parties hold the Government to account.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Possible responses: brings together people with the same political ideas; nominates candidates for public office and tries to get as many of them as possible elected; once elected, these officials try to achieve the goals of their party through legislation and programme initiatives. Very good 4-5M; good 2-3M; fair 0-1M.

prompt:
Name one non-democratic country and briefly explain how it is governed.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Name of country: Iran.
Explanation: Since the 1979 revolution, Iran has been an Islamic Republic that mixes elections with religious control. Citizens elect a president and parliament, but the unelected Guardian Council can disqualify candidates it thinks are not loyal. Ultimate power lies with the Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who controls the judiciary, media and security forces. These are used to suppress opposition and restrict civil liberties, so the system is largely authoritarian.
marking_scheme: Name of one non-democratic country 2M. Explanation of how it is governed 3M. The explanation must match the country named.

prompt:
Section B - Data-based question. Read the documents below and answer the question.

Document B: Reports of racism in Ireland: Data from iReport.ie - Annual Report 2020, Irish Network Against Racism (INAR) authored by Dr Lucy Michael (2021).

The iReport compiles its data from information submitted by: people who have been subjected to racism; frontline anti-racist organisations; trade unions and other organisations committed to combating racism; and by the general public. It uses iReport.ie, an online racist incident reporting system, which can be found at www.iReport.ie.
The reporting mechanism is designed to be as inclusive of all communities as possible, and one which strives to overcome many of the barriers to reporting. To overcome these barriers, the iReport.ie reporting form guarantees confidentiality, is short and easy to use, is written in plain English, and can be filled in anonymously, if the person so wishes.

Methodology - iReport.ie reporting system: how it works:
- Those affected, witnesses and supporters can report all forms of racism online at www.iReport.ie: discrimination at work; discrimination in access to services; racist speech (political, in the media and online); racist crime; graffiti. Photos, videos and screen grabs can be uploaded with your report.
- Data on racism is collected and published in annual reports.
- Information influences and lobbies for change with: UN, ODIHR and European bodies; Irish government and policy makers; unions, NGOs, organisations; media and public; community action.
- 'Don't ignore racism, report it! See it. Send it. End it.'

Racism in Ireland 2020 - iReport reports of racism (infographic):
- Victims - Gender: men were 35% more likely to be a victim of assault; men and women were equally likely to be a victim of other abuse.
- Victims - Age: under 18s are victims in 10% of reports and 15% of assaults.
- Impact: psychological impacts and social isolation resulting from racist abuse and violence have more than doubled, as have financial impacts for people forced to leave jobs and move homes.
- Crime (groups targeted): 33% of African descent; 16% South Asian; 16% Chinese/Other Asian; 17% Muslim.
- Discrimination (groups targeted): 33% of African descent; 20% Muslim; 13% South Asian; 11% Irish Traveller.
- INAR definition of a racist incident: 'A racist incident is any incident which is perceived to be racist by the victim or any other person.'
- Under-reporting - not reported anywhere: 28% of crime; 52% of discrimination; 60% of hate speech; 67% of other incidents.
- Perpetrators: 83% of racist crime and abuse was by white Irish people; 50% were strangers not known to their victims; 38% were acting alone; 25% of assaults were committed by groups of 5+; 80% of incidents were perpetrated by adults; less than 5% of perpetrators were under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
(www.inar.ie - Adapted)

(a) Comment on the definition of a racist incident adopted by INAR in Document B.
(10 marks)
model_answer:
INAR defines a racist incident as 'any incident which is perceived to be racist by the victim or any other person'.
Strength: This is a broad, victim-centred definition. Victims do not have to prove what was in the perpetrator's mind, so they feel believed and are more likely to report. Witnesses ('any other person') can also report. This matters because under-reporting is high: 60% of hate speech is not reported anywhere. A broad definition captures micro-aggressions, like those in Document A, which may never be a crime.
Weakness: The definition is very subjective. The same incident can be seen differently by different people, so the data may include incidents that others would dispute. This could be used to question the reliability of the figures, so the data would need to be backed up by other sources.
marking_scheme: 10 marks. Very good comment 8-10M; good comment 4-7M; fair comment 0-3M.

- Under-reporting - not reported anywhere: 28% of crime; 52% of discrimination; 60% of hate speech; 67% of other incidents.
- Perpetrators: 83% of racist crime and abuse was by white Irish people; 50% were strangers not known to their victims; 38% were acting alone; 25% of assaults were committed by groups of 5+; 80% of incidents were perpetrated by adults; less than 5% of perpetrators were under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
(www.inar.ie - Adapted)

Census 2022 questions (www.census.ie):
Question 11: What is your ethnic group/background? Choose ONE section from A to D, then mark the appropriate box.
A White: 1 Irish; 2 Irish Traveller; 3 Roma; 4 Any other White background.
B Black or Black Irish: 5 African; 6 Any other Black background.
C Asian or Asian Irish: 7 Chinese; 8 Indian/Pakistani/Bangladeshi; 9 Any other Asian background.
D Other, including mixed group/background: 10 Arabic; 11 Mixed, write in description; 12 Other, write in description.
Question 12: What is your religion, if any? Mark one box only: 1 No religion; 2 Roman Catholic; 3 Church of Ireland; 4 Islam; 5 Orthodox Christian; 6 Presbyterian; 7 Other, write in your religion.

(g) Based on the evidence presented in both documents and the Census questions below what conclusions can be made about the evolving nature of Irish identity?
(50 marks)
model_answer:
Conclusion 1: Irish identity is becoming more multicultural. Irishness is no longer defined only by being white and Catholic. Document A shows a generation of black Irish people who are 'first-generation Irish', born and raised here. Tamilore Awonusi wants her children to say they are from Ireland 'with no questions asked'. The Census now offers 'Black or Black Irish' and 'Asian or Asian Irish', and adds options such as 'Indian/Pakistani/Bangladeshi', 'Arabic' and 'Mixed'. The State itself accepts that you can be Irish and of another background. Census 2022 also showed 12% of residents are non-Irish.
Conclusion 2: Identity is fluid, not fixed. Mary Adekoya says 'you can be two things at once'. This fits Appiah's cosmopolitanism: people can have multiple identities and be 'citizens of the world'. It also fits Anderson's idea that the nation is an 'imagined community' that can grow to include new members.
Conclusion 3: Ireland is becoming more secular. The religion question changed from 'What is your religion?' (2016) to 'What is your religion, if any?' (2022), and 'No religion' is now the first box. It also lists Islam and Orthodox Christian, showing growing diversity of belief.
Conclusion 4: The change is not accepted by everyone. Document B shows 83% of racist crime and abuse was by white Irish people, and groups such as people of African descent (33%), Muslims and Travellers are targeted. The question 'where are you really from?' shows that many still see Irishness as tied to skin colour. Eriksen would say that rapid change can make some people hold more tightly to their 'own'.
Overall, Irish identity is evolving from a narrow, ethnic and religious identity to a more diverse, civic one, but racism shows the change is still contested. Education, better media representation and laws against hate are needed so that all who live here can feel fully Irish.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
'The clash of civilisations theory best describes the current state of the world.' Discuss.
[In your answer refer to the ideas of Samuel Huntington and one other theorist of your choice. Your answer should also include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: Samuel Huntington argued that after the Cold War the main source of conflict would be between civilisations - groups defined by shared culture, religion and tradition - and that conflict would happen along 'cultural fault lines'. This essay argues that his theory explains some current divisions, such as the rise of 'us versus them' politics, but it does not best describe the world. Using Edward Said's critique and evidence from Ireland and abroad, I will argue that economic and political causes, and growing global cooperation, matter more.

Argument 1 - Evidence that supports Huntington: Huntington divided the world into seven major civilisations, including Western, Islamic, Sinic and Orthodox, and said the most serious fault line is between the West and the Muslim world. Some events seem to fit. He would point to the 2015 terrorist attacks in Paris as a rejection of a modern, secular republic, and to the Israel-Palestine conflict. He also said globalisation makes people more aware of differences, which strengthens identity and conflict. The rise of nationalist and populist movements fits this: far-right parties in Hungary, Poland and Italy have fuelled anti-immigrant feeling, and the Brexit vote of 2016 (51.9% Leave) was linked by many to fear of immigration.

Argument 2 - 'Us versus them' in Ireland: Ireland shows similar tensions. In 2022 and 2023 there were anti-refugee protests in East Wall and Ballybrack under slogans like 'Ireland is Full', and threats to burn a hotel housing refugees. A 2023 Virgin Media poll found 56% believed Ireland had accepted too many refugees, at a time when Ireland housed about 74,000 asylum applicants compared to 7,500 in 2021. Huntington would see this as a clash between a host culture and outsiders.

Argument 3 - Said's critique: Edward Said argued that Huntington's theory is 'reductive', a dangerous oversimplification. It treats civilisations as 'monolithic' blocks and ignores the huge diversity inside them. Through Orientalism, the West has portrayed the East as exotic, savage and inferior, and the media spread these stereotypes, for example by linking Islam with terrorism. Said said Huntington's theory feeds Islamophobia and keeps alive the very 'us versus them' mentality it describes. Looking at the Irish case through Said's eyes, the protests were driven less by a clash of cultures than by a devastating housing crisis, stagnant wages and disinformation spread on social media - economic and political factors, not fixed civilisational differences.

Argument 4 - Cooperation and cosmopolitanism: The world is also more connected than Huntington allowed. The United Nations brings countries from every region together on climate change, poverty and conflict, and bodies like the UNDP work in about 170 countries. Kwame Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitanism suggests people can value their own culture and still see themselves as 'citizens of the world'. In Ireland, tens of thousands marched in the 'Ireland for All' rally in Dublin in February 2023, a broad coalition welcoming refugees. In Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo, more than 20 ethnic minorities live together and the GAA club unites children of many nationalities. These are not signs of an inevitable clash.

Evaluation: Huntington is useful for explaining why identity politics and polarisation are growing, and some fault lines are real. But conflict inside civilisations - such as the storming of the US Capitol in January 2021, which showed deep divisions within the West itself - shows that civilisation is not the main dividing line. Inequality, echo chambers on social media and loss of trust in institutions explain today's polarisation better.

Conclusion: The clash of civilisations theory describes part of the world, but not the whole. Said shows it is too simple and risks becoming self-fulfilling. The current state of the world is better described as a struggle between polarisation, driven largely by economic insecurity, and growing cooperation and cultural mixing.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
How universal is the UDHR? Discuss.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris in 1948. Universality - the idea that rights apply to everyone, whatever their culture - is called by the UN 'the cornerstone of international human rights law'. This essay argues that the UDHR is universal in principle and in its global support, but not fully universal in practice, because of cultural challenges and failures by states, including Western ones. I will draw on Samuel Huntington, Edward Said and Amartya Sen.

Argument 1 - The UDHR is a Western concept: Some academics argue the UDHR comes from European Enlightenment ideas of Locke and Rousseau. Eleanor Roosevelt compared it to the Magna Carta and the US Declaration of Independence. In 1948 the UN was dominated by Western interests, and much of Africa was still under colonial rule. Saudi Arabia abstained, saying Article 16 (freedom to marry) and Article 18 (freedom of religion) went against Islamic teaching. In 1990, 54 Muslim countries adopted the Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam, based on sharia law, which gives weaker protection to women and minorities. Samuel Huntington argued that the idea of a universal culture is itself Western, and that Western belief in its universality 'is false; it is immoral; and it is dangerous'.

Argument 2 - The UDHR is not only Western: Against this, the UDHR was drafted by representatives from Chile, China, Egypt, India, Pakistan, Lebanon and others. Two-thirds of the 48 votes in favour came from non-Western nations, and no country voted against it. Ideas of justice and dignity appear in ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt and China, and in Buddhism, Hinduism, Confucianism and Islam. Later treaties built on it have near-global support: the ICESCR has 171 states parties. Edward Said would warn that calling rights 'Western' can itself be a form of 'us versus them' thinking, which treats non-Western cultures as monolithic and ignores voices within them that demand rights.

Argument 3 - Cultural imperialism and relativism: Critics say the West uses human rights as a 'weapon', for example through IMF and World Bank conditional aid. Cultural relativists say rights should be understood in each culture's context. But relativism can excuse abuse. Apartheid in South Africa was defended as part of the country's own system, yet it was a clear violation of human dignity. This suggests some rights must be universal.

Argument 4 - Universal on paper but not in practice: Even where it is accepted, the UDHR is not applied equally. China and North Korea point to Western hypocrisy, such as police brutality in the US shown by the killing of George Floyd in 2020, and poor treatment of migrants in detention centres. The West trades with China despite the treatment of Uighur Muslims and the erosion of democracy in Hong Kong. Some leaders, such as Malaysia's Mahathir Mohamad, argued political rights could be set aside for development. Amartya Sen disagreed: development is the 'removal of unfreedoms', and 'economic growth without investment in human development is unsustainable - and unethical'. Freedom House data also shows the number of people living in a 'free world' has fallen.

Evaluation: Huntington is right that the UDHR has Western roots and that cultures disagree on some rights, especially on women and religion. But the global drafting, the voting record and wide ratification show it is far more than a Western document. The biggest threat to universality is not culture but the failure of states, Western and non-Western, to apply it.

Conclusion: The UDHR is universal in its aim and in the support it receives, but only partly universal in practice. Its universality must be defended by holding all states, including the West, to the same standard.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
Rich countries pledging money to poor countries to address the challenges of the climate crisis was one of the key outcomes of COP26 in 2021.
Critically evaluate these pledges as a measure that addresses sustainable development in the context of the climate crisis facing the world today.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course and/or refer to two or more relevant international agreements/organisations (e.g. United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, Paris Climate Agreement 2016, the World Bank, etc.)]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: Sustainable development, as defined in the Brundtland Report, is 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. The climate crisis threatens this, and it hits the poorest countries hardest. At COP26 in 2021 rich countries pledged money to help poor countries cope. This essay argues that these pledges are necessary and fair, but on their own they are not enough: they must be delivered, must not create new dependency, and must come with real cuts in emissions by rich countries. I will refer to Gro Harlem Brundtland, Andre Gunder Frank, the SDGs and the World Bank.

Argument 1 - The pledges are a matter of justice: Brundtland's model accepts that the Global South must develop economically, but in balance with the environment and social justice. There is an unfairness argument: the Global North grew freely through industrialisation and still produces disproportionately high carbon emissions, while developing countries are now told to limit growth. Climate change hits the poor hardest - 50 million people in eastern and southern Africa needed food aid in 2016. Oxfam warned in 2021 that 'climate change could undo decades of progress in development and dramatically increase global inequalities.' Climate finance is therefore a way for rich countries to take responsibility, supporting SDG 13 (climate action) and SDG 1 (no poverty).

Argument 2 - The risk of dependency: Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory warns that money from the core can keep the periphery dependent. The IMF and World Bank have given loans with strict conditions (conditional aid) that put neoliberal policies ahead of social welfare. The World Bank has even funded large dams in India and Brazil that displaced communities and damaged ecosystems. If climate finance comes as loans with conditions, poor countries could end up in more debt and less in control of their own development. Frank would say the problem is the unequal global system itself, not a lack of money.

Argument 3 - Pledges are not delivery: Governments often choose short-term gain over long-term sustainability, and some still subsidise fossil fuels. Agreement is hard between countries with different priorities. Even the EU's own European Green Deal, which aims for a climate-neutral economy by 2050 with legally binding 55% emissions cuts, was called 'a colossal exercise in greenwashing' by Yanis Varoufakis. If rich countries do not cut their own emissions, money alone will not stop the crisis. A pledge is only a promise.

Argument 4 - Who benefits on the ground: Sustainable development also needs social justice. Oxfam (2023) shows the majority of the world's poor are women, who do at least twice as much unpaid care work as men. Industrialisation and environmental damage often push women, the traditional environmental stewards, into poverty. Climate finance should reach local communities and support a rights-based approach, as the UNDP advocates, not just large projects.

Counter-argument: Neoliberals argue that market forces and new technology, not aid, will make clean energy cheaper and solve the crisis. But markets put short-term profit first, and poorer countries struggle to compete with richer producers.

Conclusion: The COP26 pledges are an important recognition that rich countries owe a debt to poorer countries in the climate crisis, and they can support the SDGs. However, they only address sustainable development if they are delivered in full, given as grants that do not deepen dependency, reach the most vulnerable, and are matched by real emissions cuts in the Global North.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
"The sheer amount of children being made homeless in Ireland today is a case of State failure and the violation of the basic human rights of the Irish state's most vulnerable citizens, its children." Source: The Irish Examiner, October 2021, by Dr Rory Hearne.
Critically evaluate the statement above in relation to children's rights in Ireland.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: Ireland signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) in 1992, promising to respect, protect and fulfil children's rights 'to the maximum extent of their available resources'. Article 27 gives every child the right to food, clothing and a safe place to live. This essay largely agrees with Dr Hearne: rising child homelessness shows the State has failed as a duty bearer. However, the State has taken some steps, and the causes are complex. I will use John Locke, John Rawls and Robert Nozick.

Argument 1 - The scale of the problem: The figures are stark. The Children's Rights Alliance reports that the number of homeless children rose from 2,327 (December 2020) to 2,451 (2021) and 3,442 (2022). Focus Ireland reports over 11,000 people homeless in January 2023, and 1,387 young people aged 18 to 24 were homeless in December 2022. A further 3,580 children were living in Direct Provision in November 2022. Homelessness has risen by 178%, and the official figures leave out rough sleepers and hidden homelessness. Homeless children lack space to play (Article 31) and struggle with school, so one failure affects many rights.

Argument 2 - A failure of the social contract: John Locke said people agree to a social contract so the state will protect their natural rights to life, liberty and property. If the state fails to protect its most vulnerable citizens, it breaks that contract. John Rawls argues that inequalities should be arranged to benefit the least well off; children born into poverty lose the 'social lottery' and the State should correct this. By relying on the private sector for social housing, as a joint Oireachtas committee criticised, the State has left these children unprotected. Ireland has no constitutional right to housing, even though the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for one in 2015.

Argument 3 - What the State has done: To be fair, the State has acted. The Ombudsman for Children's report 'No Place Like Home' (2019) set out actions to end child homelessness. The Government published the National Youth Homelessness Strategy in November 2022 after consulting young people, and the Housing for All plan includes cost rental homes and help for first-time buyers. Under progressive realisation, economic and social rights can be achieved over time. However, monthly figures still show more young people in emergency accommodation, so progress is too slow.

Counter-argument - Nozick: Robert Nozick would reject the idea that housing is a right the State must provide. He believed in a minimal state that only provides law and order, and saw taxing people to redistribute wealth as 'forced labour'. On this view, homelessness is not a State failure. But this ignores that children cannot provide for themselves; they depend on adults and the State as duty bearers.

Evaluation: Homelessness has structural causes - lack of affordable housing, poverty and unemployment - and personal causes such as family breakdown. Not all are under State control. But Ireland is a wealthy country, and the UNCRC requires action to the 'maximum extent' of resources. The scale and growth of child homelessness show that resources have not been used well enough.

Conclusion: The statement is largely accurate. Child homelessness in Ireland is a violation of children's rights under the UNCRC and a failure of the social contract. Real change would need a constitutional right to housing, far more social housing and full use of the Ombudsman for Children's recommendations.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
In the context of the findings of the CSO survey and the theories of Sylvia Walby, evaluate whether contemporary Irish society is a patriarchy.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national context to support your argument.]
CSO Pulse Surveys - Life at Home, May-June 2021:
- 64% of women said they are mostly responsible for household chores compared to 12% of men.
- 62% of men said they are mostly responsible for home and garden maintenance compared to 15% of women.
- Of respondents living with a same sex partner, 51% reported a balance of household chores compared to 42% of those living with an opposite sex partner.
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: A patriarchy is a system in which men hold most power and resources, marginalising women. Sylvia Walby argues patriarchy works through six structures and has moved from 'private patriarchy' in the home to 'public patriarchy' in wider society. This essay argues that contemporary Ireland is still a patriarchy, though a weakening one. Women have made major gains in law and politics, but the CSO survey and other data show inequality in the home, work, politics and safety.

Argument 1 - The household (private patriarchy): The CSO Pulse Survey shows 64% of women say they are mostly responsible for household chores, compared to only 12% of men. Walby says women's unpaid domestic labour supports capitalism by freeing men for paid work. Kathleen Lynch's idea of affective inequality supports this: care work is unpaid and mostly done by women. In Census 2016, 195,263 people were unpaid carers, over 60% of them women, work worth €10 billion a year to the State. Ireland's Constitution, Article 41.2, still refers to a woman's place in the home. The survey also shows gender roles are learned, not natural: 51% of same-sex couples reported a balance of chores compared to 42% of opposite-sex couples.

Argument 2 - Paid work: Walby's second structure is paid work. Irish women earned 14.4% less than men on average in 2020, with a bigger gap in higher-paid jobs. Across the EU, 28% of women work part-time compared to 8% of men, and in 2018 a third of employed women had a career break for childcare compared to 1.3% of men. Women are 34% of EU managers. This links back to the home: women's care burden limits their careers.

Argument 3 - The state, violence and culture: Women are under-represented in the state. After 2016 women made up only 22.2% of TDs, and Ireland was tenth lowest in the EU. Women's Aid (2021) found one in four Irish women who have been in a relationship experienced domestic violence - Walby's fourth structure. Walby also sees the media as a 'patriarchal cultural institution' that reinforces gender stereotypes.

Counter-arguments: There has been real progress. The 8th Amendment was repealed in 2018 by 66.4% to 33.6%. Paid parental leave was extended to seven weeks for both parents in 2022, encouraging shared care, which supports Martha Nussbaum's idea of a social minimum of capabilities for all. Gender quotas have increased the number of women candidates. Some, like Claudia Goldin, argue the pay gap reflects choices such as part-time work rather than discrimination. Men also face pressures: they were 76% of suicides in 2019. However, Walby would answer that these 'choices' are shaped by patriarchal structures, and the CSO survey shows they are not freely chosen when women still carry most of the housework.

Evaluation: Ireland has moved from private towards public patriarchy, just as Walby predicted: 'Liberated from the home, women now have the whole of society in which to be exploited.' Women can now work and vote, but they still face a pay gap, under-representation in politics, violence and an unequal share of unpaid work.

Conclusion: Contemporary Irish society is still a patriarchy, though it is changing. The CSO data shows the household remains the clearest example. Ending patriarchy will need shared care, affordable childcare, more women in politics and a change in cultural attitudes.

prompt:
Discursive essay.
Critically assess what it means for European Union (EU) member states to agree to implement economic, social and cultural rights.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to relevant treaties/conventions/agreements/charters and/or the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: Economic, social and cultural (ESC) rights include the rights to adequate housing, education, food, work and to take part in cultural life. They are positive rights: the state must provide something. All EU member states are bound by the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR, 1966) and by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. This essay argues that agreeing to these rights commits states to real duties, especially spending, but that weak enforcement and austerity often leave a gap between promise and reality. I will use Robert Nozick, John Rawls and Martha Nussbaum.

Argument 1 - A legal commitment: By ratifying the ICESCR, states promise to realise rights 'to the maximum extent of their available resources'. The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights monitors them. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights came into force in December 2009 with the same legal power as any EU treaty. EU membership has brought real social rights: better workers' rights, equal treatment of men and women at work and limits on working hours. So agreeing to ESC rights means states accept outside scrutiny of how they treat their people.

Argument 2 - It means spending and taxing: ESC rights need resources, so the tax a state collects directly affects services such as health, housing and education. In Ireland the top 10% of earners pay over 50% of income tax, and the ESRI says no tax system in Europe does more to reduce household inequality. John Rawls would support this: inequalities should be arranged to benefit the least well off. Martha Nussbaum argues rights only matter if people actually have the capabilities to live a dignified life.

Argument 3 - Weak enforcement and progressive realisation: ESC rights are realised progressively over time, which makes it hard to hold states to account. When the UN Committee examined Ireland in 2015, it called for more spending on health, education and housing and for the right to housing to be put in the Constitution. Ireland has still not done this, and child homelessness rose to 3,442 in December 2022. Pressure on abortion rights may have influenced the 2018 referendum, which shows monitoring can have some effect. But globally, over 160 million children are still in child labour despite the right to education, a gap between rhetoric and reality.

Argument 4 - Austerity and the EU itself: EU membership can also limit ESC rights. When Greece's economy collapsed in 2009, IMF-backed austerity cut public services and caused severe hardship. Yanis Varoufakis argues the EU's commitment to austerity limits its power to improve lives, even in plans such as the European Green Deal and its 'just transition'. This suggests economic rules can come before social rights.

Counter-argument - Nozick: Robert Nozick would say positive rights are unfair because they force some people to pay for others, and he compared taxation for redistribution to 'forced labour'. On this view, implementing ESC rights violates individual freedom and property. However, without ESC rights, civil and political rights mean little to someone without a home or education.

Conclusion: For EU member states, agreeing to ESC rights means accepting legal duties, outside monitoring and the need to raise and spend money for the common good. In practice, progressive realisation, weak enforcement and austerity mean these rights are often unevenly delivered. The commitment is real, but it only matters if states act on it with the resources they have.

prompt:
Give one positive and one negative aspect of coalition governments.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Positive: A coalition represents a wider range of views and people. For example, after the 2020 election Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael governed with the Green Party, so Green voters' views shaped the programme for government.
Negative: Parties must compromise on their election promises, and a small junior partner can have more power than its votes justify, because the larger parties need its seats to keep a majority.

prompt:
Describe what it means for states to agree to act to implement rights to the 'maximum extent of their ability.'
(5 marks)
model_answer: It means the state, as duty bearer, must do everything in its power to make sure rights holders enjoy their rights. Immediate obligation: the state must take concrete, targeted steps now, ensure rights without discrimination and a minimum level of rights for all. The World Migration Report (WMR) is IOM's flagship publication, having been produced biennially since 2000. The WMR responds to a clear and growing need for rigorous, balanced, and evidence-based research and analysis on migration at a time of heightened interest in the topic.
Key migration data at a glance:
- International migrants: 281 million international migrants globally in 2020, or 3.6 per cent of the world's population (up from 272 million, or 3.5%, in 2019).
- Females: 135 million international female migrants globally in 2020, or 3.5 per cent of the world's female population (up from 130 million, or 3.4%, in 2019).
- Males: 146 million international male migrants globally in 2020, or 3.7 per cent of the world's male population (up from 141 million, or 3.6%, in 2019).
- Labour migrants: 169 million migrant workers globally in 2019 (up from 164 million globally in 2017).
- Missing migrants: around 3,900 dead and missing globally in 2020 (down from almost 5,400 in 2019).
Displaced persons: 89.4 million people were living in displacement globally at the end of 2020 (includes refugees, asylum seekers, displaced Venezuelans and IDPs), up from 84.8 million in 2019.
- Refugees: 26.4 million refugees globally in 2020 (up from 26 million in 2019).
- Asylum seekers: 4.1 million asylum seekers globally in 2020 (down from 4.2 million in 2019).
- Displaced Venezuelans: 3.9 million Venezuelans displaced globally in 2020, not including those who were refugees or asylum seekers (up from 3.6 million in 2019).
- Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs): 55 million IDPs globally in 2020: 48 million due to conflict and violence; 7 million due to disasters (up from 51 million in 2019).

Document B: Online articles (edited), The New Humanitarian: 'Migration and forced displacement', December 2021 (Eric Reidy, Migration Editor) and '25 years of journalism from the heart of crises', June 2022.
For the second year in a row, global mobility was shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic in unprecedented ways in 2021. Cross-border travel by people with passports and visas isn't expected to return to pre-pandemic levels until 2024. Meanwhile, the number of those forcibly displaced due to climate disasters, conflicts, and violence - both within their countries and internationally - has continued to climb, from 82.4 million at the end of 2020 to more than 84 million by June 2021, according to the UN's refugee agency UNHCR.
Numbers for the second half of the year are not yet available, but climate crisis-linked flooding has displaced hundreds of thousands in China, Malaysia, South Sudan, and elsewhere across the globe since the beginning of October. The second-order effects of the pandemic are exacerbating factors - from economic stagnation to political instability - that push people to migrate.
The inequitable distribution of COVID-19 vaccines is likely contributing to the dynamic by paving the way for poorer countries to be left behind while the economies of wealthier countries with higher vaccination rates rebound more quickly.
Migration routes from the US-Mexico border to the Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama have seen increased movement compared to last year. The upsurge is coinciding with the intensification of efforts by Western countries to limit access to asylum and the ability of those seeking safety and opportunity to reach their territories. The chaotic airlift that accompanied the US and NATO withdrawal from Afghanistan as the Taliban retook power in Kabul in August provided perhaps the most unforgettable images of global mobility inequality of the year - with people clinging to US military planes as they took off. Around 113,000 Afghans were able to leave Afghanistan during the two-week evacuation. Thousands fleeing the fallout are crossing into neighbouring Iran every day. But restrictive policies have a domino effect, and Iran - which along with Pakistan has hosted the vast majority of Afghan refugees for decades - has deported around 360,000 since August.
Displacement and migration are consequences of the crises we report on at The New Humanitarian. And often, the governance - or mismanagement - of migration creates additional negative humanitarian and human rights consequences for those compelled to move.

We're documenting the threats to humanitarian responses in the country and providing a platform for those bearing the brunt of invasion. Our goal is to bring you the truth when disinformation is rampant. (June 2022)

Using evidence from both documents, outline the significant rise in internally displaced persons (IDPs).
(20 marks)
model_answer:
IDPs are people forced to flee their homes who stay inside their own country.
Document A: there were 55 million IDPs globally in 2020, up from 51 million in 2019. That is a rise of 4 million in one year (4 / 51 x 100 = about 8%). IDPs are by far the largest displaced group - 55 million of the 89.4 million people living in displacement, which is more than half (55 / 89.4 x 100 = about 62%), and about twice the 26.4 million refugees. Of the 55 million, 48 million were displaced by conflict and violence and 7 million by disasters.
Document B: the number forcibly displaced 'both within their countries and internationally' kept climbing, from 82.4 million at the end of 2020 to more than 84 million by June 2021. Climate-linked flooding displaced hundreds of thousands more in China, Malaysia and South Sudan from October 2021. Pandemic effects such as economic stagnation and political instability also pushed people to move.
Conclusion: both documents show the rise in IDPs is large and continuing, driven mainly by conflict but increasingly by the climate crisis. Because COVID-19 made cross-border travel harder and Western countries limited access to asylum, more displaced people may be stuck inside their own country.

Comment on the 'negative humanitarian and human rights consequences' that can result from the mismanagement of migration.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
When migration is badly managed, people who are already vulnerable suffer further harm.
1. Loss of life and dignity: The chaotic airlift from Kabul showed people clinging to military planes as they took off. Document A records around 3,900 migrants dead and missing in 2020. People forced onto dangerous routes, like the Darién Gap, risk their lives.
2. Deportation and loss of protection: Iran has deported around 360,000 Afghans since August. Article 14 of the UDHR gives everyone the right to seek asylum from persecution, but restrictive policies push people back towards danger.
3. Poor shelter and overcrowding: In Ireland, Direct Provision was meant to be short term, but whole families often share a single room with no cooking facilities, and the average stay is 24 months - some people stayed up to 12 years.
4. Loss of rights to work and education: Asylum seekers in Ireland had no right to work until 2018 and have limited access to further and higher education, so they cannot build a life.
5. Effects on children: Children born into Direct Provision make up 30% of residents, and the long-term effects on their development are unknown.
These consequences break human rights that are meant to be universal. The EU and its member states have legal obligations to people at their borders, so border control must still give safe alternatives to people seeking protection.

prompt:
Using contemporary examples discuss the effectiveness, or not, of peaceful protests as a key tool for citizens to bring about political change in democratic societies today.
[Your answer should refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The right to peaceful protest comes from freedom of expression and freedom of assembly (Articles 19 and 20 of the UDHR). It is protected in the Irish Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. Protest lets citizens 'speak truth to power', and it is especially important for people who cannot vote, such as under-18s. In this essay I will argue that peaceful protest is an effective tool for political change, but mainly when it is combined with other tools such as lobbying, the courts and elections. I will use the ideas of John Locke, Thomas Hobbes and Paulo Freire.

Point 1: Protest puts issues on the agenda - Fridays For Future
Greta Thunberg's school strike in 2018 grew into Fridays For Future. On 15 March 2019 more than 1.4 million students took part in over 2,000 protests in more than 125 countries - the biggest global climate action in history. In Dublin more than 11,000 marched on Dáil Éireann. The Irish students demanded that Ireland declare a national climate emergency and scale up investment in renewable energy. The movement also started a campaign to lower the voting age to 16. This shows protest can set the agenda: the more attention an issue gets, the more important society thinks it is. However, many demands, such as a carbon-free Ireland by 2030, have not been met. Protest raised awareness, but governments still choose short-term economic gain.

Point 2: Protest combined with other action - LGBTQ+ rights in Ireland
Ireland's first Pride parade in 1983 followed the killing of Declan Flynn and highlighted violence against gay people. Protest alone did not change the law. David Norris also went to court and won at the European Court of Human Rights in 1988. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1993, and in 2015, after lobbying and campaigning, 62% voted Yes to same-sex marriage. This shows peaceful protest is most effective as part of a wider campaign. John Locke would support this. He believed government rests on the consent of the people and that citizens may resist government that does not serve the general good. Peaceful protest is a way of showing that consent is being withdrawn.

Point 3: Protest that has not yet won change - housing
In 2021 the National Homeless and Housing Coalition organised the Winter of Housing Discontent protest in Dublin. Yet over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023, more than 3,000 of them children. The Government launched Housing for All, but critics say it does not tackle the root causes. Here protest raised awareness but did not quickly change policy. Paulo Freire would say protest is a form of praxis - action combined with reflection - that helps the oppressed become conscious of injustice. Even if change is slow, protest builds critical consciousness.

Counter-argument
Thomas Hobbes would reject protest. For Hobbes, once citizens sign the social contract they give up the right to question the sovereign, and protest threatens stability and risks chaos. Some recent events support this worry: anti-refugee protests in Ireland included threats to burn hotels housing refugees, and in November 2023 there were riots on O'Connell Street, Dublin. These were not peaceful, and they show protest can be used to spread fear rather than to protect rights. However, these events break the condition of being peaceful, so they do not prove peaceful protest is wrong.

Conclusion
Peaceful protest is an effective tool for political change, but rarely on its own. It works best at raising awareness and forcing debate, as Fridays For Future did. Lasting change usually comes when protest is joined with court cases, lobbying and votes, as the LGBTQ+ campaign shows. I agree with Locke more than Hobbes: in a democracy, peaceful protest is a sign of a healthy social contract, not a threat to it.

prompt:
Fr Peter McVerry (from the Peter McVerry Trust - a national housing and homelessness charity) recently said, "It is the responsibility of the Irish government to meet the basic needs of its citizens." (adapted, Irish Times, 24 September 2022)
Do you agree with this statement? Discuss.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Basic needs include food, shelter, healthcare and education. Article 25 of the UDHR gives everyone the right to an adequate standard of living, including food, clothing, housing and medical care. I agree with Fr McVerry that the Irish government has the main responsibility to meet these needs, but the Government is not fully meeting it, especially in housing. I will use evidence on homelessness and the welfare system, and the ideas of Thomas Hobbes, John Rawls, Robert Nozick and Martha Nussbaum.

Point 1: The social contract - homelessness
For Hobbes, citizens give up some freedoms in return for protection from the state. If the state does not protect its citizens, it fails its side of the contract. Focus Ireland reported over 11,000 people homeless in January 2023, more than 3,000 of them children. There has been a 178% increase in homelessness, and monthly figures do not even count rough sleepers or hidden homelessness. The Government published a National Youth Homelessness Strategy in November 2022, but more 18-24 year olds are still in emergency accommodation. In 2019 the Ombudsman for Children's report 'No Place Like Home' recommended examining a right to housing in the Constitution. This evidence suggests the Government has not met its obligation to protect citizens.

Point 2: Rights and progressive realisation
Ireland has signed the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). In 2015 the UN committee called on Ireland to put rights such as housing into the Constitution and to spend more on health, education and housing. These rights are subject to 'progressive realisation' - they can be achieved over time - but the state must keep making progress 'to the maximum extent of its available resources'. Martha Nussbaum argues every citizen needs a 'social minimum' of capabilities, such as health and shelter, for a dignified life. A child growing up in emergency accommodation does not have this social minimum.

Point 3: The welfare state works when it is used
There is evidence that government action does meet basic needs. The CSO found in 2022 that without social welfare almost four in ten people would be in poverty. Ireland spent €11,348 per person on social protection in 2021, 10th in the EU. The ESRI found that no tax system in Europe does more to reduce household income inequality. Schemes like the School Meals Programme (228,007 children in 2021/22) and free schoolbooks show the state meeting needs directly. John Rawls supports this: inequalities are only fair if they benefit the least well off, and the state should redistribute to protect people who lose out in the 'social lottery' of birth.

Counter-argument
Robert Nozick would disagree with McVerry. He believed in a minimal state that only provides law and order. Taxing people to pay for others' needs is, for Nozick, a kind of 'forced labour', and positive rights are unfair because some people pay for others. Some people argue welfare creates a sense of entitlement, and that families, charities and the free market should meet more needs. However, charities like Focus Ireland and the Peter McVerry Trust cannot build housing at the scale needed, and the market has not delivered affordable homes - in 2021 over 25% of households rented privately, often with insecure tenure and high rents.

Conclusion
I agree with Fr McVerry. Only the government has the resources and power to guarantee basic needs for everyone. The welfare system shows this works when the state acts, but the housing crisis shows the Government is falling short. Nozick's minimal state would leave the most vulnerable without shelter. As Hobbes and Rawls suggest in different ways, a government that does not protect its least well-off citizens is not keeping its social contract.

prompt:
Are social class and wealth rewarded in Ireland's education system? Discuss.
[Your answer should include examples and evidence from a national context to support your argument. You should also refer to the views of two theorists you have studied, at least one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Article 42 of Bunreacht na hÉireann says the State shall provide for free primary education, and Article 28 of the UNCRC says education should be available on the basis of equal opportunity. In theory, then, social class and wealth should not matter. In this essay I will argue that, in practice, wealth and class are still rewarded in Irish education, through hidden costs, voluntary contributions and the advantages of cultural capital. I will use Kathleen Lynch and Pierre Bourdieu, and Robert Nozick as a counter view.

Point 1: 'Free' education is not free
The Irish Times reported in 2022 that the average cost per secondary school child was €1,518, and €1,195 per primary child. 66% of parents said back-to-school costs were a financial burden, and 29% went into debt, with an average debt of €339. 75% of primary and 95% of secondary parents must buy crested or branded uniforms. The article concluded that making education free 'remains one of the most important unfulfilled policy goals of the Irish State'. Families with more money can easily pay these costs, while poorer families struggle, so wealth gives an advantage from the start.

Point 2: Voluntary contributions and unequal schools
The St Vincent de Paul 'Closing the Gap' report (2023) found 87% of parents had to cut back or delay spending to pay the voluntary contribution, and some students felt shame at school if they did not pay. Wealthier communities can pay more, so schools in richer areas have more resources, while disadvantaged areas struggle to provide supports. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (2022) was concerned about 'persistent barriers' for disadvantaged children and recommended banning priority for children or grandchildren of past pupils in oversubscribed schools - a rule that favours established, often better-off families. School league tables, which rank schools by how many students go to university, reward this advantage further.

Point 3: Cultural capital (Bourdieu) and equality of condition (Lynch)
Pierre Bourdieu argued that class depends not only on money but on social and cultural capital. Middle-class parents pass on language, knowledge and confidence that help children succeed at school, so education reproduces class inequality - success leads to better-paid jobs, which pay for private education for the next generation. Kathleen Lynch agrees. She writes that 'we need to have a significantly more equal distribution of wealth and income to have substantive equality of opportunity in education'. For Lynch, unless we tackle class inequality outside school, there can be no real equality inside school. The Equal Status Acts only give equality of access, not equality of outcome.

Counter-argument
The state does take steps to reduce inequality. Donogh O'Malley introduced free secondary education in 1966, when only 6% of people had gone beyond primary school under British rule. Today schemes such as the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance, the Free Primary Schoolbooks Scheme and the School Meals Programme (228,007 children in 2021/22) help low-income families, and SUSI grants and the HEAR scheme support access to college. Robert Nozick would go further: he would support a market-based system where families pay for the education they choose, with means-tested help for the poor, arguing that competition improves quality. But Nozick's view would reward wealth even more openly, which is the problem this essay identifies.

Conclusion
Ireland has made real progress, but social class and wealth are still rewarded. Hidden costs, voluntary contributions and cultural capital mean that richer students start ahead and often stay ahead. I agree with Lynch: schemes help, but true equality in education needs a more equal society, and the State must fully deliver on its promise of free education.

prompt:
A report published by the Mercy Corps ('The Weaponization of Social Media: How social media can spark violence and what can be done about it') found that, "Social media has emerged as a powerful tool for communication, connection, community and, unfortunately, conflict."
Critically evaluate the changing nature of contemporary media.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of one named theorist you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Media used to mean traditional media - newspapers, radio and television - controlled by editors and owners who acted as gatekeepers. Today new media, especially social media, lets anyone create and share information instantly. In this essay I will argue that this change has strengthened democracy in some ways, by giving a voice to ordinary people, but has also created serious dangers, including disinformation and conflict. I will use Noam Chomsky's propaganda model, with evidence from Ireland and abroad.

Point 1: Communication and connection - citizen journalism
Social media has made citizen journalism possible. Ordinary people can record and share events with no gatekeepers. During the Arab Spring and the war in Syria, citizens shared footage that mainstream media could not get, and it remains vital where news is censored. Citizen journalism amplifies minority voices that were silenced by mainstream media and shifts the balance of power away from traditional media. This challenges what Chomsky described in Manufacturing Consent: that corporate media 'serve, and propagandize on behalf of, the powerful societal interests that control and finance them'. Social media can break through his 'filters' of ownership and advertising.

Point 2: Conflict - misinformation and disinformation
The Mercy Corps warning is supported by evidence. False claims on social media that the HPV vaccine causes infertility led some parents to refuse the vaccine. In Ireland, social media spread false rumours about migrants, feeding anti-refugee protests and the riots on O'Connell Street in November 2023. Social media also creates echo chambers, where people only meet opinions like their own. The Reuters Digital News Report 2019 found 61% of Irish people were very or extremely worried about made-up stories. Citizen journalists are untrained and publish quickly without careful editing, which can give a platform to far-right, anti-immigration views.

Point 3: New owners, old problems
The change in media has not ended the power of owners - it has moved it. Google, Facebook, Amazon and Netflix are US-owned multinational corporations that invest little in Irish content. In traditional media, Reporters Without Borders said in 2019 that highly concentrated ownership was the 'single largest threat' to press freedom in Ireland, with Denis O'Brien's group owning about 40%. Chomsky would argue that platforms still sell users as a product to advertisers, so profit, not truth, decides what we see. His 'common enemy' filter can also be seen when online content targets immigrants or Travellers.

Counter-argument and regulation
Some argue social media should not be regulated, because traditional media should not 'set the agenda' and regulation could silence minorities and unpopular views. Trust in traditional news is still fairly high - 74% of Irish people trusted 'most news' in 2022, mainly RTÉ - and Facebook as a news source fell from 67% (2018) to 63% (2022), so traditional media still matters. Governments have also begun to respond: the EU Digital Services Act and Ireland's Online Safety and Media Regulation Act, which created a Media Commission with binding online safety codes. This shows the dangers can be managed, but regulation must protect freedom of expression.

Conclusion
Contemporary media is more open, faster and more participatory than ever, and this has given voices to people who were ignored. But, as Mercy Corps says, the same tools can spark conflict through disinformation and echo chambers. Chomsky's warning about owners and advertisers still applies to the new tech giants. I believe the change is positive overall only if it is matched by regulation, media literacy and a socially responsible press.

prompt:
Critically assess whether international human rights frameworks require updating for the 21st century.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course and/or refer to one or more human rights declaration/treaty/convention.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The modern human rights framework began with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted in 1948 after the Holocaust. It led to treaties such as the European Convention on Human Rights (1950), the ICESCR (1966) and the UNCRC (1989). In this essay I will argue that the core principles - that rights are universal, inalienable and indivisible - are still valid, but the frameworks do need updating in three areas: who they represent, how they are enforced and the new challenges of the digital world. I will use Samuel Huntington, Edward Said, Martha Nussbaum and Amartya Sen.

Point 1: A framework from a Western world?
In 1948 the UN was dominated by Western interests: most of Africa was under colonial rule. Saudi Arabia abstained, saying Articles 16 and 18 went against Islamic teaching, and in 1990, 54 Muslim countries made the Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam. Huntington argued that the Western belief in a universal culture 'is false; it is immoral; and it is dangerous'. Edward Said disagreed with Huntington's 'us vs them' view, arguing cultures are not fixed or monolithic. In fact the UDHR was drafted with representatives from Chile, China, Egypt, India, Lebanon and others, and two-thirds of the 48 votes in favour came from non-Western nations. I believe the principles are genuinely universal, but the system must include more non-Western voices to keep its legitimacy.

Point 2: Weak enforcement of economic and social rights
Economic, social and cultural rights depend on 'progressive realisation', so it is hard to hold states to account. Despite the ICESCR, over 160 million children are still in child labour. In South Sudan, which ratified the UNCRC in 2015, about 1 in 10 children die before their fifth birthday. In Afghanistan, 80% of school-aged girls are out of school under the Taliban. Nussbaum argues rights 'do not go far enough' and that we need a capabilities approach that looks at what people can actually do, while Sen defines development as removing 'unfreedoms'. These ideas suggest frameworks need stronger ways to measure and enforce real outcomes, not just promises.

Point 3: New 21st-century challenges
Some problems did not exist when the frameworks were written. The Children's Rights Alliance found that law and policy had not kept pace with the online world: 25% of children aged 9-17 saw something online that bothered them in a year. Ireland's 1989 incitement to hatred law was 'outstripped by the internet'. Climate change is expected to drive more migration, yet the refugee definition is based on fear of persecution, not climate disasters. The EU Digital Services Act and Ireland's Online Safety and Media Regulation Act show that new rules are needed for new problems.

Counter-argument: frameworks can update themselves
Some argue we do not need new frameworks, because existing ones already evolve. The European Court of Human Rights treats the ECHR as a 'living instrument' that changes with society. In Norris v Ireland (1988) the Court found Ireland's laws against homosexuality broke Article 8 (privacy), leading to decriminalisation in 1993. The Universal Periodic Review also reviews every UN member state every four years. These show the framework can adapt through interpretation.

Conclusion
International human rights frameworks still rest on sound principles, and courts can update them as 'living instruments'. However, weak enforcement of economic and social rights, the rise of online harm and climate displacement, and the need for wider global ownership show they do require updating for the 21st century. I agree with Nussbaum and Sen that rights must be measured by what people can really do, not just by what is written down.

prompt:
Across the world, low and middle-income countries are struggling with a three-pronged crisis: the pandemic, the climate crisis and the increase in food and fuel prices caused by war.
Critically evaluate the view that supranational bodies have an important role to play in tackling problems in developing countries.
[Your answer should include examples and evidence to support your position. You should also refer to two or more relevant supranational bodies e.g. the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Health Organisation (WHO), the United Nations (UN), the European Union (EU) and/or the views of at least one named theorist you have studied.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Supranational and intergovernmental bodies such as the IMF, the World Bank, the WTO and the UN Development Programme (UNDP) were set up to promote stability, trade and development. Developing countries now face a three-pronged crisis of the pandemic, the climate crisis and rising food and fuel prices. In this essay I will argue that these bodies do have an important role, because no developing country can solve global problems alone, but their current methods can make problems worse. I will use Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory, Vandana Shiva and the case study of Sierra Leone.

Point 1: The role they can play - money, expertise and goals
The World Bank gives low-interest loans and grants to tackle poverty; it has funded schools, hospitals and roads in Kenya and India, and the STEP project in Bangladesh trains workers to reduce poverty. The UNDP works in about 170 countries, helps with disaster recovery and supports the Sustainable Development Goals. The UN's Millennium Development Goals helped cut world hunger in half and reduce extreme poverty by nearly half between 2000 and 2015. After Ebola in 2014, the IMF gave Sierra Leone an aid package of about 100 million US dollars. This shows supranational bodies can respond to crises at a scale no single country can.

Point 2: Conditional aid can deepen the crisis
In 2017 the IMF approved a loan of over 220 million US dollars to Sierra Leone, but on condition that it cut public spending on health and education - while it was still recovering from Ebola. Critics say the interest rates are unrealistic and the 'one-size-fits-all' approach ignores local needs. Sierra Leone has an HDI rank of 181 out of 191 and spends just 0.7% of GDP on social protection. Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory explains this: rich 'core' countries use bodies like the IMF and WTO to keep 'periphery' countries dependent through conditional loans and unfair trade. Vandana Shiva adds that the WTO and IMF pushed Indian farmers into monocultures, with disastrous effects on farmers and the environment.

Point 3: Unequal power inside the bodies
Voting in the IMF depends on wealth: the United States has 16.5% of the vote, while the whole African continent has only 6%. In the World Bank, the most powerful members are developed Western nations. In the WTO, larger economies have more bargaining power, so trade liberalisation may benefit developed countries more. The unequal pandemic response shows the cost of this: in June 2021, North America and Europe had 68 vaccine doses per 100 people, while sub-Saharan Africa had fewer than 2. As UN Secretary General António Guterres said, 'Inequality starts at the top: in global institutions. Addressing inequality must start by reforming them.'

Counter-argument
Some argue that developing countries' problems are mainly internal, such as corruption. Human Rights Watch says Sierra Leone has one of the world's highest rates of reported bribery, and the World Bank found fake development projects collecting fees and disappearing. Rostow's modernisation theory suggests aid and investment help countries move through stages to growth, as IMF conditionality helped Poland's economy in the 1990s. However, even here supranational bodies matter: Human Rights Watch recommends that the World Bank and IMF support anti-corruption commissions and stronger labour and environmental laws.

Conclusion
Supranational bodies have a vital role in tackling a global three-pronged crisis, because they hold the resources, expertise and reach that developing countries lack. But their role is only positive if they change. Reforming voting power, ending harsh conditions that cut health and education, and focusing on human development, not just growth, would let them solve problems rather than deepen dependency. As Daniel Gbondo said of Sierra Leone, 'economic growth does not automatically translate into economic development'.
