prompt:
Briefly outline a key difference between positive and negative rights.
(5 marks)
model_answer: A positive right needs someone, usually the state, to act and provide something for you. For example, the right to education means the government must provide schools and teachers. A negative right only needs others to hold back and not interfere with you. For example, freedom of speech means the state must not stop you from speaking. So a positive right demands action, but a negative right demands non-interference.
marking_scheme: 5 marks (3 marks + 2 marks). Responses may make reference to: a negative right is a freedom FROM something, and a positive right is the freedom TO DO something; for example, the rights to free speech and assembly are negative rights, because they restrict others from limiting your freedom; a description of a relevant example. First point: very good description 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Second point: good description 2M, fair 1M. Note: if the first point is awarded 2M or less, the second point is marked out of 3M.

prompt:
Explain the role of the Ceann Comhairle in Dáil Éireann.
(5 marks)
model_answer: The Ceann Comhairle is the chairperson of Dáil Éireann. A new Dáil chooses the Ceann Comhairle first, from among its own TDs, and they must act impartially. They open each day's sitting, chair the debates and call TDs to speak. They are the sole judge of order, so they control the house and can order a TD to leave or suspend them. They also supervise votes (divisions) and declare the results.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may make reference to: chairing Dáil debates; supervising votes and declaring results; takes control of the house. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Key thinker Andre Gunder-Frank proposed Dependency Theory to try and explain why some countries remain underdeveloped. Briefly explain this theory.
[The question shows an image labelled 'Poor nations' and 'Rich nations'.]
(5 marks)
model_answer: Frank's Dependency Theory says underdevelopment is caused by poor countries' economic and political dependence on rich countries, going back to colonisation. Wealthy 'core' states, such as the USA and UK, control technology, finance and multinational companies. Poor 'periphery' states supply cheap labour and raw materials and buy expensive manufactured goods back. Wealth flows from the periphery to the core, so poor nations stay poor. In Frank's words, underdevelopment is created by 'the development of capitalism itself'.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Critique the rise in citizen journalism in the world today.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Citizen journalism is when ordinary people, not trained journalists, record and share news, usually on social media. A strength is that it gives a voice to people silenced by mainstream media and reports news that is censored, as in the Arab Spring and war footage from Syria. However, it is unpaid and untrained, so it can lack credibility. It is published quickly without careful editing, which can spread misinformation and give a platform to far-right views, such as anti-refugee rhetoric.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good critique 4-5M; good critique 2-3M; fair critique 0-1M.

prompt:
Does learning about human rights, in subjects such as Politics and Society, encourage young people to protect and promote the rights of others? Explain your answer.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Yes, I believe it does. Article 29 of the UNCRC says education should develop respect for human rights, and Article 42 gives children the right to know their rights. Once young people know about rights such as the UDHR and UNCRC, they can spot abuses, for example in Direct Provision. Martha Nussbaum argues education should build critical thinking and 'world citizens'. The citizenship project also turns this knowledge into action. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee that every student will act.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. (The marking scheme words the question as: practise, protect and promote the rights of others.) Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Comment on the message in this image in the context of children's rights in the world today.
[The image, posted by UNICEF, shows a poster with the words: 'MY CLASSROOM IS NOT A TARGET'.]
(5 marks)
model_answer: The message is that schools must be safe places and should never be attacked in war. Under Article 28 of the UNCRC every child has a right to education, and Article 19 protects children from violence. Yet in conflicts schools are destroyed, for example Yemeni children studying in a war-damaged school in Taiz in 2020. In 2022 the UN reminded the Taliban that international law prohibits attacks on schools. The poster shows these rights are still not fully respected.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may make reference to: the UNCRC / UDHR; the right to education; a description of a relevant example. Very good commentary 4-5M; good commentary 2-3M; fair commentary 0-1M.

prompt:
Describe the purpose of a manifesto in party politics.
(5 marks)
model_answer: A manifesto is a document that a political party publishes before an election. It sets out the party's vision and what it intends to do if it gets into government. It explains its policies on issues such as housing, health, education and tax. This helps voters compare parties and decide who to vote for. It also lets citizens hold parties to account later. In a coalition, parties use their manifestos when negotiating the Programme for Government.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may make reference to: to set out a vision or intention for government; to explain party policies. Very good description 4-5M; good description 2-3M; fair description 0-1M.

prompt:
Describe two features of a democratic state.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. The right to vote: all adult citizens have a general and equal right to vote in free elections. In Ireland, citizens aged 18 and over on the electoral register vote for TDs, the President and in referendums.
2. Separation of powers (checks and balances): power is split between the government (executive), parliament (legislature) and the courts (judiciary), so no one part becomes too powerful. For example, the Irish President can refer a bill to the Supreme Court.
marking_scheme: 5 marks (3 marks + 2 marks). Responses may make reference to: responsible for basic human rights; free and open media; right to vote; checks and balances; law and order; a description of a relevant example. Accept other relevant features. First feature: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Second feature: good 2M, fair 1M. Note: if the first point is awarded 2M or less, the second point is marked out of 3M.

prompt:
Give two examples of how the education system in Ireland reinforces Irish identity.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. Subject content: Irish is taught as a language in school, and History teaches events that shaped Irish identity, such as the fight for independence and the 1916 Rising. PE often includes Gaelic games, which the GAA sees as 'more a cultural expression than a sporting activity'.
2. Religion: Catholicism has shaped Irish values and education. Just under 95% of primary schools are run by the Catholic Church or the Church of Ireland, and faith schools are said to preserve Ireland's cultural identity.
marking_scheme: 5 marks (3 marks + 2 marks). Responses may make reference to: subject content, e.g. Irish language, History, Music, PE; significance of religion in schools. Example 1: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Example 2: good 2M, fair 1M. Note: if the first point is awarded 2M or less, the second point is marked out of 3M.

prompt:
Describe two ways by which a person can become a Senator in Seanad Éireann.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. Nominated by the Taoiseach: the Taoiseach directly nominates 11 of the 60 senators, which helps the Government have a majority in the Seanad.
2. Elected by university graduates: graduates of the National University of Ireland elect 3 senators and graduates of Trinity College elect 3. (Another 43 senators are elected by TDs, outgoing senators and county councillors.)
marking_scheme: 5 marks (3 marks + 2 marks). Responses may make reference to: 11 nominated by the Taoiseach; 6 selected by NUI and Trinity College graduates; 43 selected by TDs, members of the outgoing Seanad and members of County Councils. Way 1: very good 3M, good 2M, fair 1M. Way 2: good 2M, fair 1M. Note: if the first point is awarded 2M or less, the second point is marked out of 3M.

prompt:
What conclusions can you draw from the statistics below in relation to the media?

Reuters Institute: Digital News Report 2023 - Proportion of respondents that say they saw false or misleading information about each topic in the last week:
Topic | US | UK | Slovakia | Japan
Politics | 42% | 26% | 41% | 18%
COVID-19 | 42% | 31% | 34% | 30%
Climate change | 35% | 22% | 17% | 12%
War in Ukraine | 26% | 19% | 45% | 21%
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. False or misleading information is common in all four countries. In the US, 42% saw false information about politics and 42% about COVID-19 in just one week, which shows how polarised news can be there.
2. Misinformation depends on the topic and the place. Slovakia had the highest figure for the war in Ukraine (45%), probably because it is close to the conflict. Japan had the lowest on most topics, such as 12% on climate change.

prompt:
Briefly outline the relationship between Western imperialism and Edward Said's theory of Orientalism.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Said, in Orientalism (1978) and Culture and Imperialism (1993), argued that the West portrayed the East as exotic, savage and inferior. The West built its own identity ('us') as rational and civilised, by 'othering' the East ('them'). These stereotypes, spread through literature, academia and media, helped to justify Western imperialism and colonial rule, as if the West had a right to govern 'inferior' peoples. Today this continues, for example when media link Islam with terrorism.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good outline 4-5M; good outline 2-3M; fair outline 0-1M.

prompt:
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) issued results in February 2023 from the Survey on Income and Living Conditions (SILC) for 2022. It found that in Ireland, the richest 20% have four times the income of the poorest 20%.
What does this statistic suggest about society in Ireland today?
(5 marks)
model_answer: It suggests that Ireland is an unequal, class-based society. The top fifth has four times the income of the bottom fifth, so economic capital is not shared fairly. This affects housing, health and education. Over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023. Karl Marx would say capitalism creates 'haves' and 'have-nots'. However, without social welfare almost four in ten people would be in poverty (CSO 2022), so taxes and welfare already reduce inequality.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Responses may make reference to: economic inequality in society; lack of social justice; Ireland as a class-based society; description of a relevant example. Very good explanation 4-5M; good explanation 2-3M; fair explanation 0-1M.

prompt:
Briefly describe what it means to have either a left or right-wing political viewpoint.
(5 marks)
model_answer: A left-wing viewpoint supports active government involvement in the economy to create a fairer, more equal society. Left-wing people favour redistributing wealth through taxes and spending on public services, such as free education, universal healthcare and social housing. Socialism and communism are on the left. For example, free education from pre-school to third level is a left-wing policy. By contrast, a right-wing viewpoint favours a free market, lower taxes and limited government, as Margaret Thatcher did.
marking_scheme: 5 marks. Very good description 4-5M; good description 2-3M; fair description 0-1M.

prompt:
Read Documents A and B and answer the question.

Document A: Taking Stock of Women's Representation in Politics Across Europe - A Study by the European Women's Lobby, March 2023.
This research was carried out by the European Women's Lobby (EWL) with the support of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati (WSGR). Its purpose is to map out the current state of women's representation in politics across Europe. The information gathered in this document comes from desk-based research. It also stems from the EWL members' contributions collected through a digital survey in 2022 across 20 European countries.
As of February 2023, Ireland ranked 101st in the world for women's representation in national parliaments, falling behind countries such as China and Iraq. When the Dáil celebrated its centenary in 2019, just 114 women had been elected to it since 1918 compared with 1,190 men. Following the most recent national election (2020), this was 130 women versus 1,211 men (10% versus 90%).
In the twelve general elections in Ireland prior to the 2012 Act (1973-2011) and the introduction of quotas, the proportion of women's representation in the Dáil never rose above 15%.
There are no quotas for local elections in Ireland. Representation of women at local authority level across the country has risen from 12% in 1991 to just 24% in 2019. Only eight women were elected as mayors in June 2022 (25.8%).
A recent report noted that data from the last six local elections suggest that there is no electoral bias against women, but not enough women appear on the ballot papers. It also notes that women are more likely to win a national seat than men if they have served in local government. To drive gender equality in national politics, gender equality at a local level thus needs to be prioritised.
To advance gender equality in politics, in June 2021, members of the Citizens' Assembly recommended that the government introduce measures such as maternity leave for all elected representatives, extend party quotas to local, Seanad, and European elections and increase sanctions for noncompliant parties. These suggestions have not yet been enacted by the current government.
In Ireland, women running for election are more likely to be the victims of personalised, misogynistic violence, with women facing up to eight times the level of online violence compared to their male counterparts. A qualitative study undertaken by NUI Galway's Journalism and Communications unit in 2020 found that 96% of current and former women politicians, at national and local level, have received social media or email messages that used threatening or hateful language, while three quarters report being threatened with physical violence via online or social media.
(womenlobby.org - adapted)

Document B: Web page from Women for Election.
This group organises training programmes, events and mentoring supports, that have helped get hundreds of women elected to local and national government.
This site is a collaboration between Women for Election Ireland and the All-Island Research Observatory (AIRO) at Maynooth University Social Science Institute (MUSSI) and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH). Funding for this project was awarded by the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform (DPER).
The dashboard below from our Data Hub presents women candidates across political parties* (2020). In 2012, the Oireachtas adopted a law obliging political parties to select at least 30% women candidates and 30% men candidates to contest general elections. From 2023 onwards, this gender quota threshold increased to 40%. If the quota is not met, political parties will lose 50% of the State funding they receive on an annual basis to run their operations.
The Data Hub is a comprehensive store of statistical data, organised to provide you with unique insights into the state of gender equality here in Ireland. With this powerful resource at your fingertips, you can make informed decisions, drive meaningful change, and contribute to a more equitable future for all. Engage with the data, share the insights, and ignite conversations about gender equality. Remember, knowledge is power, but only when shared and acted upon.
* Only displays information for the seven political parties that qualified for Exchequer funding under the Electoral Act 1997.
Women candidates across political parties (2020) [shown in the original as a bar chart, with the 2020 quota (30%) and 2023 quota (40%) marked for each party]:
Fianna Fáil 30.9% | Fine Gael 30.5% | Green Party 41% | Labour Party 32.3% | Solidarity-People Before Profit 40.5% | Sinn Féin 33.3% | Social Democrats 55%
Gender Quotas in Politics in Ireland
Since 1992 there has been an increase in both the number of women selected as candidates (from 18.5% in 1992 to 30.7% in 2020) and elected TDs (from 12% in 1992 to 22.5% in 2020).
The quota system challenges political parties to develop a culture and selection process that will encourage women to come forward for election. It is also the responsibility of political parties to select women in winnable seats if the true objective of the quota is to be achieved - that is, improved gender balance in Irish politics. There are currently no quotas in place for Local Elections (where many politicians begin their political journey), or for the Seanad. The issue of quotas in politics is one which causes much discussion - some people do not like quotas, but we like what they do, that is, introduce a short, sharp shock to the political system that makes change happen quickly.
(womenforelection.ie - adapted)

(a) What are the strengths and limitations of the methodology used to gather data in Document A?
(10 marks)
model_answer:
Strengths: Document A uses mixed methods. It combines desk-based research with a digital survey of EWL members, which gives triangulation, since data comes from more than one source. The survey covered 20 European countries, so it allows comparison across Europe. It was carried out by an expert organisation with outside support from WSGR.
Limitations: desk-based research relies on secondary data that may be out of date. The survey only asked EWL members, a lobby group with an agenda to increase women's representation, so there is a risk of bias. This is a self-selecting sample, not a random one, and no sample size is given. A digital survey may also leave out some voices, and only 20 countries took part.
marking_scheme: 10 marks. Very good description 8-10M; good description 4-7M; fair description 0-3M.

'The issue of quotas in politics is one which causes much discussion - some people do not like quotas, but we like what they do, that is introduce a short, sharp shock to the political system that makes change happen quickly.'
(50 marks)
model_answer:
Gender quotas in Ireland have clearly worked to some extent. However, on their own they are not enough to fix the gender imbalance in Irish politics.
The case for quotas: Document A shows that in the twelve general elections before the 2012 Act, women never made up more than 15% of the Dáil. Document B shows that since quotas began, women candidates rose from 18.5% (1992) to 30.7% (2020), and women TDs from 12% to 22.5%. This supports the statement that quotas are a 'short, sharp shock' that 'makes change happen quickly'. The 50% funding penalty gives the law real force, and all seven funded parties met the 30% quota in 2020. More women in the Dáil also gives young women role models. Martha Nussbaum would say political participation is a basic capability everyone needs.
The limits of quotas: Ireland still ranks only 101st in the world (Document A), and over three quarters of TDs are men. The quota only covers candidates, not seats. Document B admits parties must select women 'in winnable seats', or the quota may become a box-ticking exercise. Fianna Fáil (30.9%) and Fine Gael (30.5%) only just passed the minimum. There are also no quotas for local, Seanad or European elections, even though local politics is where most careers start. The Citizens' Assembly asked for these in 2021, but this has not been enacted.
Quotas also do nothing about the deeper barriers. Document A shows 96% of women politicians received threatening or hateful messages. There is still no maternity leave for elected representatives. These problems reflect Sylvia Walby's idea of public patriarchy and Kathleen Lynch's point that women carry most care work.
The statement admits that 'some people do not like quotas'. Critics argue they are a form of 'indirect discrimination', because a stronger male candidate may lose out. They also say women elected this way may be unfairly seen as 'tokenistic'. However, Document A's finding that voters show no bias against women suggests the real block is party selection, which is exactly what quotas target.
In conclusion, quotas have been an effective shock to the system and should be raised to 40% and extended to local, Seanad and European elections. But they are a temporary tool, not a full solution. Real gender balance also needs winnable seats for women, action on online abuse and family-friendly politics.

prompt:
Discuss the impact of globalisation on nationalism and/or cultural identity referring to the theories of key thinker Thomas Hylland Eriksen.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national and/or global context to support your argument.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Globalisation is the growing interdependence of the world's economies, populations and cultures, brought about by technology, trade and the movement of people and information. Many people expected it to create one shared global culture. However, the Norwegian anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen argues the opposite can happen. Because the world is changing 'too fast, unequal and uneven', many people cling more tightly to their nation, religion or ethnic group. In this essay I will argue that globalisation has made identity more fluid. At the same time, it has strengthened nationalism and identity politics among people who feel left behind.

Eriksen's theory
In his book Overheating, Eriksen says rapid global change, such as population growth and new communications technology, creates uncertainty and powerlessness at local level. People find it harder to define who they are in traditional ways. So 'localities in crisis' assert their identity more strongly, and globalisation can actually make localisation stronger. This is the basis of identity politics. Eriksen sets out seven principles, including competition for resources, 'first comers versus invaders', and narrowing complex realities into 'us versus them'. He describes our world as 'an interconnected world, but not a smoothly and seamlessly integrated one'.

Argument 1: Brexit and nationalism
Brexit is a clear example. In 2016 the UK voted by 51.9% to 48.1% to leave the EU. Lord Ashcroft's poll of 12,000 voters found that 49% of Leave voters' main reason was that 'decisions about the UK should be taken in the UK'. A further 33% wanted to regain control over immigration and borders. Eriksen argues this was not just small-minded nationalism. People felt disconnected from distant power holders and voted to 'return to their own community'. His principles fit closely. There was competition for jobs and housing, since about 3.6 million EU nationals lived in the UK. There was nostalgia for British power ('symbolism and rhetoric'), and immigrants and the EU were demonised. Home Office data showed hate crime in England and Wales spiked after the referendum. This shows the darker side of identity politics.

Argument 2: Ireland and the refugee debate
Ireland shows the same pattern. In 2023 Ireland housed about 74,000 asylum applicants, compared with 7,500 in 2021. Against a background of a housing crisis, protests such as those in East Wall used slogans like 'Ireland is Full'. A 2023 poll found 56% believed Ireland had taken too many refugees. Eriksen's principles of competition over scarce resources, such as housing, and 'we were here first' explain this reaction well. Social media also spread false claims about crime, which narrowed a complex issue into 'us versus them'.

Counter-argument: identity is becoming more open
However, globalisation has also made Irish identity more open and diverse. Tens of thousands joined 'Ireland for All' marches in 2023 to welcome refugees. Kwame Anthony Appiah would see this as cosmopolitanism, where people act as global citizens. Irish identity now includes Black-Irish and Muslim-Irish people. The Census shows Catholics fell from 79% in 2016 to 69% in 2022, and same-sex marriage and abortion were legalised. Sean Moncrieff argued that what is changing Ireland is not immigrants but globalisation itself: 'We're not building mosques on every street corner. We're building Starbucks.' This suggests a risk of cultural homogenisation rather than stronger nationalism. Yet Irish culture also travels outward. GAA clubs now exist around the world, which shows how global networks can spread and strengthen national identity. In Northern Ireland, the 2021 Census found 19.8% call themselves 'Northern Irish', a new, more regional identity alongside 'British' (31.9%) and 'Irish' (29.1%).

Evaluation
Benedict Anderson's idea of 'imagined communities' helps here. The nation is a social construct, but it is deeply felt. Global media can strengthen this feeling as easily as they weaken it. Eriksen himself does not say globalisation always causes conflict. He says identity is 'universality plus difference' and can evolve through respectful exchange. I believe the evidence supports him. Where people feel powerless, as many Leave voters and some Irish communities did, globalisation fuels nationalism. Where people feel secure and included, it produces more open, mixed identities.

Conclusion
In conclusion, globalisation has had a double impact on nationalism and cultural identity. It has made identities more fluid and cosmopolitan, as Ireland's changing census shows. But, as Eriksen argues, its speed and unevenness also make people retreat to their 'own', which fuels movements like Brexit and 'Ireland is Full'. To reduce this backlash, governments must tackle the inequalities, such as housing, that make people feel left behind.

prompt:
'You have to understand, no one puts their children in a boat unless the water is safer than the land.'
[This image is a representation of the poem 'Home' by Warsan Shire. The poem explains how some refugees would not leave their home if they were not forced to do so.]
Discuss the refugee crisis in the world today in the context of human rights.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
A refugee is a person who has fled their country and is unwilling or unable to return because of fear of persecution due to their nationality, religion, race, or membership of a social or political group. Warsan Shire's line, 'no one puts their children in a boat unless the water is safer than the land', reminds us that refugees do not choose to leave. They are forced out by war and persecution. Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) gives everyone the right to seek asylum from persecution. In this essay I will argue that, although this right exists on paper, the world's response to the refugee crisis often fails to respect refugees' human rights.

The scale of the crisis
UNHCR data shows the number of people forced to flee worldwide has risen steadily from 2012 to 2022. By the end of 2016, nearly 5.2 million refugees and migrants had reached European shores by sea. They came mainly from Iraq, Syria and Afghanistan, countries with war, persecution or highly repressive governments. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, over 8 million people have fled Ukraine. These are people whose rights to life, liberty and security (UDHR Article 3) were under threat at home.

Europe's response
The EU and its member states have legal obligations to people at their land and sea borders. Some countries met them. Germany took in roughly 1 million people in 2015 and 2016, about 1% of its population. However, many states were reluctant to 'step up to the plate'. Many governments shifted towards deporting people or discouraging them from reaching the EU at all. Far-right groups spread the idea that Europe would be 'replaced', which fed the identitarian movement. There is also a double standard. Europe welcomed Ukrainians quickly, while many fleeing Syria or Afghanistan faced closed doors. Oliver Jeffers' 2023 cartoon made a similar point. The media focused on five wealthy tourists lost on a submarine, while a boat carrying hundreds of refugees had sunk off Greece the week before. It asks whether we have normalised refugee deaths.

Ireland: Direct Provision
Ireland's record is also mixed. Direct Provision, set up in 2000 as a short-term measure, gives asylum seekers food, shelter and a weekly allowance of just €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. The average stay is 24 months, and some people have stayed up to 12 years. Whole families often share a single room with no cooking facilities. Children make up 30% of residents. Many say the system infringes their rights to dignity, family life and an adequate standard of living (UDHR Article 25). The government's 2021 White Paper promised to replace it with own-door accommodation, but asylum numbers rose from 7,500 in 2021 to about 74,000 in 2023 during a housing crisis. This led to protests under slogans like 'Ireland is Full'. President Michael D. Higgins said those 'sowing hate' were 'unforgivable'.

Theorist 1: Edward Said
Edward Said, a key thinker on the course, argued that the West portrays the East as exotic, savage and inferior through 'othering'. This helps explain how refugees from the Middle East and Africa are often described in the media as a threat, such as 'military age' men, rather than as people with rights. Said would see 'Ireland is Full' as an orientalist discourse that wrongly assumes Ireland is a homogeneous nation being overrun by 'foreigners'. This kind of language makes it easier for governments to ignore refugees' rights.

Theorist 2: Kwame Anthony Appiah
Kwame Anthony Appiah offers a hopeful alternative. His idea of cosmopolitanism says 'the boundary of your state is not the boundary of your moral concern'. We have duties to all human beings, not just fellow citizens. The 'Ireland for All' marches in 2023, where tens of thousands welcomed refugees, show this attitude in action.

Evaluation
Some argue that states have the right to control borders, and that housing and services are limited. This is fair. Effective migration controls are legitimate if safe alternatives are given to people seeking protection. However, human rights are universal and inalienable. They do not depend on where a person is born. Martha Nussbaum's 'social minimum' suggests everyone, including refugees, should have the basic capabilities for a dignified life. The problem is less a lack of laws than a lack of political will.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the refugee crisis is fundamentally a human rights crisis. People flee because their rights are destroyed at home, and too often they meet closed borders, dangerous seas or long years in Direct Provision. As Shire's poem says, the water must seem safer than the land. States must match their stated values with action: safe routes, fair and fast asylum processes, and decent housing.

prompt:
Should governments be permitted to take control of social media during periods of social or political unrest?
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Social media are online platforms, such as X (Twitter), Facebook and Instagram, where people create and share information. During unrest, such as riots, protests or a pandemic, they can spread both vital news and dangerous lies. Some argue governments should be allowed to take control of them to keep people safe. In this essay I will argue that governments should NOT be allowed to take control of social media. Instead, platforms should be regulated fairly by independent bodies, with limits only where they are lawful, necessary and proportionate.

The case for government control
Supporters argue that social media can make unrest worse. Misinformation (false information shared by mistake) and disinformation (false information spread on purpose) travel fast online. During the 2023 anti-refugee protests in Ireland, far-right activists spread false claims about crimes through social media, which helped stir up anger against people housed in centres. In health crises, false claims can cost lives. For example, a false claim online that the HPV vaccine causes infertility led some parents to refuse it. Social media also create 'echo chambers', where people only see views that match their own, deepening polarisation. During Covid-19 the Irish government set up a Communications Committee to oversee factual material, and the WHO set up a 'Myth Busters' website. Thomas Hobbes, a key thinker on the course, would support strong control. For Hobbes, the main aim of government is peace and stability, not individual freedom. In a time of unrest, citizens should accept limits in return for protection under the social contract.

The case against government control
However, giving governments control of social media is dangerous, especially during unrest, when governments themselves may be the target of protest. Freedom of expression is a core human right. Article 19 of the UDHR says everyone has the right to 'impart information and ideas through any media regardless of frontiers'. Social media make citizen journalism possible. During the Arab Spring, and in war footage from Syria, ordinary people exposed abuses that mainstream or state media ignored. Citizen journalism is especially vital in countries where news is censored. Where states control the media, as in North Korea or China, it becomes a tool for propaganda. In Iran, the Supreme Leader controls the media and security forces to suppress opposition. Government control during unrest could silence minorities and unpopular opinions, which is exactly when they most need to be heard.

Noam Chomsky's warning
Noam Chomsky, a key thinker on the course, is wary of any authority unless it can be strongly justified. In Manufacturing Consent, he and Edward Herman showed how media 'serve, and propagandize on behalf of, the powerful societal interests that control and finance them'. If governments took over social media, they would become the ultimate 'gatekeepers'. They could use 'flak' to discredit critics and present protesters as a 'common enemy'. Chomsky would say this would manufacture consent, not protect democracy. John Locke would also argue that government rests on the consent of the people. Citizens have a right to resist a government that abuses its power, and they cannot do this if their means of communication are controlled.

A middle way: regulation, not control
Freedom of expression is a qualified right. It can be limited to protect the common good, as other rights were during Covid-19 restrictions. The answer is independent regulation, not government takeover. Ireland's Online Safety and Media Regulation Act set up a Media Commission and an Online Safety Commissioner, with binding codes and financial sanctions for platforms. The EU's Digital Services Act also requires platforms to protect minors. Ireland's hate speech laws are being updated to target incitement to violence or hatred. These tools let harmful content be removed without giving any government control over what citizens may say.

Evaluation
Supporters of control are right that disinformation is a real threat during unrest. Reuters found 61% of Irish people were 'very' or 'extremely worried' about made-up stories. Yet the history of state-controlled media shows the cure can be worse than the disease. A government in crisis has every reason to hide its own failures.

Conclusion
In conclusion, governments should not be permitted to take control of social media, even during unrest. Doing so would threaten freedom of expression, silence citizen journalists and hand propaganda power to the state, as Chomsky warns. Hobbes' concern for order is understandable, but it is better met through independent regulators, clear hate speech laws and media literacy, which tackle harmful content while keeping social media free.

topic_label: Is the UN fit for purpose?
prompt:
Over 50 years ago, former UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld said, 'The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order to save us from hell.'
Is the United Nations still fit for purpose today?
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least one theorist named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The United Nations (UN) was set up after World War II to keep peace and promote human rights and co-operation between states. Dag Hammarskjöld said it was created 'to save us from hell', not to bring us to heaven. To judge whether it is fit for purpose today, we should ask whether it still prevents the worst outcomes, not whether it solves every problem. In this essay I will argue that the UN is still fit for purpose in Hammarskjöld's sense, especially in human rights and development. However, it has serious weaknesses in enforcement and fairness that need reform.

Achievement 1: setting universal human rights standards
The UN's greatest achievement is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted in 1948 and called the 'Magna Carta of all mankind'. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights calls universality 'the cornerstone of international human rights law'. The UDHR led to binding treaties such as the ICESCR (1966), which had 171 states parties by 2020, and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989). These create real accountability. For example, the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child examined Ireland in 2022-2023. It recommended changing school admissions law and expanding multi-denominational schools, which put pressure on the Irish government to act.

Achievement 2: development and poverty
UN development work has saved millions of lives. Under the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015), world hunger was cut in half, extreme poverty fell by nearly half, more children went to school and fewer children died. In 2015 world leaders adopted the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, which apply to all countries. The UNDP works in about 170 countries and is seen as one of the more democratic bodies, as each member of its Executive Board has an equal vote. UNICEF data shows child deaths before age five fell from 1 in 11 in 1990 to 1 in 26 in 2021. In this sense, the UN has helped 'save us from hell'.

Weakness 1: the gap between rhetoric and reality
However, the UN cannot force states to obey. Economic, social and cultural rights depend on 'progressive realisation', so it is hard to hold states to account. Despite the right to education, over 160 million children are still in child labour. South Sudan ratified the UNCRC in 2015, but about 1 in 10 children there die before their fifth birthday. In Afghanistan, the UN reminded the Taliban in 2022 that they are bound by international law. Yet UNESCO reports that 80% of school-aged girls and young women (2.5 million) are now out of school. Statements are not enough when states ignore them.

Weakness 2: inequality and Western dominance
Critics argue that the UN reflects the power of rich, mostly Western states. In 1948 the UN was still dominated by Western interests, as much of Africa was under colonial rule. Saudi Arabia abstained on the UDHR, and 54 Muslim countries later produced the Cairo Declaration. Samuel Huntington, a theorist named on the course, argued that the idea of a universal culture is itself a Western idea. He said the belief in it 'is false; it is immoral; and it is dangerous'. Even UN Secretary-General António Guterres has admitted: 'Inequality starts at the top: in global institutions. Addressing inequality must start by reforming them.' In the Security Council, a small number of permanent members can veto action, which has blocked responses to some conflicts.

Counter-view: Edward Said
Edward Said would agree that Western power shapes how the world is seen. But he would warn against Huntington's 'us versus them' view, which treats civilisations as monolithic blocks. In fact, the UDHR was drafted by representatives from Chile, China, Egypt, India, Lebanon and others, and two-thirds of the 48 votes in favour came from non-Western nations. This suggests the UN's values are genuinely shared, even if its structures are unequal.

Evaluation
Weighing up the evidence, I believe the UN's failures are mainly failures of its member states, not of its purpose. Where states co-operate, as with the MDGs, the UN achieves remarkable results. Where powerful states disagree or ignore it, the UN is weak. Martha Nussbaum's idea of a 'social minimum' for everyone describes what the UN is trying to protect: a floor below which no human should fall.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the United Nations is still fit for purpose if we judge it by Hammarskjöld's standard: it has not brought us to heaven, but it has helped save millions from hell through human rights law, development and humanitarian work. However, to stay relevant it needs reform to make its institutions fairer and its decisions harder for powerful states to block, as Guterres himself argues.

prompt:
[Eurobarometer: '42% of Irish people are not happy with the way democracy works in Ireland.']
Evaluate this finding from the Eurobarometer Poll, carried out on behalf of the European Commission published in December 2023.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Ireland is a representative democracy: citizens elect TDs, who then choose the Taoiseach and Government. The Eurobarometer finding that 42% of Irish people are not happy with how democracy works is significant. It means a large minority is unhappy, although it also suggests that most people are broadly satisfied. In this essay I will evaluate this finding. I will argue that much of the dissatisfaction comes from the system's failure to deliver on issues like housing and fair representation, rather than a rejection of democracy itself.

Context and the source
Eurobarometer is a large, reputable survey carried out for the European Commission, so it is a credible source. However, it is quantitative, closed-question data. It tells us WHAT people think, but not WHY. To evaluate it, we need other evidence.

Reason 1: the housing crisis and the social contract
A major reason for dissatisfaction is the government's failure to deliver basic needs. Over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023, including over 3,000 children. The average Dublin house price was over €430,000. John Locke, a key thinker on the course, argued that government rests on trust and the continuous consent of the people. If it fails to serve the general good, it loses legitimacy. Many young people locked out of housing may feel the state has broken its social contract with them, so they are unhappy with how democracy works.

Reason 2: unequal representation
Many groups are under-represented. Women made up only 22.5% of TDs after 2020, and Ireland ranked 98th in the world for women in parliament. Travellers, people in Direct Provision and the LGBTQ+ community have few or no elected voices. Irish citizens living abroad and under-18s cannot vote. The Seanad is often called undemocratic, since most of its 60 members are chosen by politicians, the Taoiseach or university graduates. This is a 'classist vote'. People who do not see themselves represented are more likely to be dissatisfied.

Reason 3: the electoral system and outcomes
PRSTV gives smaller parties a fair chance, but it often produces coalitions and encourages 'parish-pump politics', where TDs focus on local issues to win votes. In 2020, Sinn Féin won the most first-preference votes (24.53%) but did not enter government, as Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and the Greens formed a coalition. For many voters this felt like their choice was ignored, which may explain some of the 42%.

Counter-argument: Irish democracy works well in many ways
On the other hand, Irish democracy has real strengths. PRSTV produces a diverse Dáil with many parties. Citizens' Assemblies, randomly selected to reflect society, have discussed issues like gender equality, biodiversity and drug use. Referendums have given people a direct say on major social change. These include marriage equality in 2015 and the repeal of the 8th Amendment by 66.4% in 2018, and in 2013 voters chose to keep the Seanad. Trust in news is high, with 74% of Irish consumers trusting 'most news', mainly RTÉ. Compared with non-democratic states such as Iran, where an unelected Supreme Leader controls the courts and media, Irish citizens have real freedoms. As Churchill said, democracy is 'the worst form of government except all those other forms that have been tried'.

Theorist 2: John Rawls
John Rawls offers a useful way to judge this. He argued that a just society arranges inequalities so they benefit the least well off. From behind a 'veil of ignorance', would people choose a system where some children grow up homeless? Rawls would say many of the 42% are reacting to injustice in outcomes, not to the democratic process itself. Robert Nozick, by contrast, would argue the state should stay minimal, and that unhappiness is not proof the system is unfair.

Evaluation
The finding is a serious warning, but it must be read carefully. A majority of people appear to be satisfied, and Irish democracy has delivered peaceful change through referendums and assemblies. However, 42% is too large to ignore. Also, Citizens' Assembly recommendations, such as extending gender quotas, have not always been acted on. This can make people feel their voice does not count, which risks feeding the decline in trust in institutions that helps populists.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the Eurobarometer finding shows that a large minority of Irish people feel democracy is not working for them. This is mainly due to housing, unequal representation and frustration with election outcomes. Using Locke and Rawls, I believe the solution is to make democracy deliver fairer outcomes and include more voices. This could mean acting on Citizens' Assembly proposals, reforming the Seanad and extending votes to young people and emigrants.

prompt:
'An agreement is only as good as its implementation. This historic consensus is only the beginning of the road.' - H.E. Dr. Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, President, COP28 UAE.
A transition away from fossil fuels, the creation of a loss and damage fund and a limit to global warming to 1.5°C were some of the key decisions of COP28.
Critically evaluate the role of international agreements in achieving sustainable development.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least one theorist named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Report (1987), is 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. It requires a balance between economic growth, social progress and environmental protection. Global problems like climate change, poverty and inequality cross borders, so they need global solutions. International agreements, such as the SDGs and the decisions of COP28, are vital in setting shared goals. However, as Al Jaber says, 'an agreement is only as good as its implementation'. In this essay I will argue that international agreements are essential but not sufficient on their own.

Strength 1: shared goals and real results
International agreements give the world a common direction. In 2000, 189 countries agreed the Millennium Development Goals. By 2015, world hunger had been cut in half, extreme poverty had fallen by nearly half, more children were in school and fewer children were dying. In 2015 world leaders adopted the 2030 Agenda, with 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Unlike the MDGs, the SDGs are universal and apply to rich and poor countries alike. They recognise that poverty, inequality and climate change are connected. COP28's agreement to transition away from fossil fuels, create a loss and damage fund and limit warming to 1.5°C builds on this. It shows a global consensus that the climate crisis must be tackled together.

Strength 2: binding regional agreements
Agreements work best when they are legally binding. The European Green Deal (2019) aims to make the EU climate neutral by 2050. Its European Climate Law makes the 55% emissions reduction target legally binding on member states. It also includes concrete plans, such as renovating 220 million buildings by 2050 and cutting plastic litter in the sea by 50%. Its 'just transition' supports workers in traditional industries, which links environmental and social goals as Brundtland intended.

Weakness 1: implementation and national interest
Many agreements are not fully carried out. Governments must balance national interests with global responsibilities, and many choose short-term economic gain. Some still subsidise the fossil fuel industry. Reaching consensus is difficult between nations with very different levels of development. There is also a fairness problem. The Global North grew rich through fossil fuels, but now developing countries are told to limit their growth, while rich countries still produce disproportionately high emissions. Oxfam has warned that climate change 'could undo decades of progress in development and dramatically increase global inequalities'. This is why the COP28 loss and damage fund matters, but only if rich countries actually pay into it.

Weakness 2: greenwashing
Even strong agreements can be criticised as greenwashing. Yanis Varoufakis called the European Green Deal 'a colossal exercise in greenwashing'. He argued that the EU's commitment to austerity limits its ability to change lives, and pointed out that the EU supported a multi-billion-euro gas pipeline at the same time.

Weakness 3: agreements that harm sustainability - Vandana Shiva
Vandana Shiva, a key thinker on the course, shows that some international agreements actually work against sustainable development. The WTO's TRIPS Agreement (1994) allowed the patenting of life forms, such as seeds. Shiva says this lets corporations 'own and control life'. In India, Monsanto's Bt cotton seeds were costly and needed expensive inputs, which pushed many small farmers into debt. Shiva also argues the WTO and IMF pushed Indian farmers towards monocultures, damaging biodiversity. Andre Gunder Frank's Dependency Theory supports this view: agreements shaped by rich 'core' countries can keep poorer 'periphery' countries dependent.

The role of other actors
Agreements also depend on pressure from below. The Fridays for Future movement mobilised over 1.4 million students in 2019 to demand government action. Corporations can contribute through the UN Global Compact and B Corp certification. Father Seán McDonagh argues sustainable development is a moral duty, not just a policy goal, and that 'the cry of the poor for social justice is mirrored in the cry of the earth'.

Evaluation
International agreements are essential because no country can solve climate change or global poverty alone. The MDGs prove that shared goals can achieve real progress. However, their success depends on binding targets, fair sharing of costs and genuine political will. Agreements written to suit powerful states or corporations, like TRIPS, can make inequality and environmental damage worse.

Conclusion
In conclusion, international agreements play a central role in achieving sustainable development. They set shared goals, create frameworks like the SDGs and the Green Deal, and build consensus such as at COP28. But, as Al Jaber admits, they are 'only the beginning of the road'. Without enforcement, fair funding for poorer countries and pressure from citizens, they risk becoming promises on paper, or even greenwashing.

prompt:

Group: Students. Students are the largest group in the school, but they sit at the bottom of the hierarchy and have the least say in making rules.

prompt:
Briefly describe why press freedom should be a key feature of any democratic society.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Press freedom lets citizens discuss, question and challenge the government without censorship. The press acts as a watchdog, checking government power and making sure it acts ethically. It informs citizens so they can take part in decisions and vote with knowledge. The UDHR protects freedom of opinion and expression 'through any media'. Without it, power can become concentrated and abused, as with state propaganda in North Korea.
marking_scheme:
5 marks. Responses may refer to: a free press is a check on government power, giving critical scrutiny and analysis of policies and actions; it helps keep the balance of power between government, the media and the public, preventing concentration of authority; other relevant responses.

topic_label: Hobbes and the state of nature
prompt:
Explain the 'State of Nature' concept through the view of Thomas Hobbes or John Locke.
(5 marks)
model_answer: Thomas Hobbes: The state of nature is life before any government. Hobbes believed humans are selfish, so without a ruling power they would fight over scarce resources like food and property. It would be a 'war of every man against every man', and life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. To escape, rational people make a social contract: they give up freedoms to an absolute sovereign (the Leviathan) in return for protection, peace and security.
marking_scheme:
5 marks. Responses may refer to: an absolute sovereign power allows people to live without fear for their lives (Hobbes); people naturally seek peace and would live in harmony without governments (Locke); other relevant responses.
Very good explanation 4-5 marks; Good 2-3 marks; Fair 0-1 marks.
source: 2025 State Exam - Section A, Short Answer Questions: Q1 (c)

prompt:
Explain the role of the Equal Status Acts 2000-2018 in protecting against discrimination in Ireland.
(5 marks)
model_answer: The Equal Status Acts 2000-2018 make it illegal to discriminate when providing goods and services, education and accommodation, including transport, health services and cultural activities. They protect people on the nine grounds: gender, marital status, family status, age, disability, race, religion, sexual orientation and membership of the Travelling Community. A tenth ground, receiving Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) or rent supplement, was added in 2015. People treated less favourably on these grounds can seek a remedy.
marking_scheme:
5 marks. Responses may refer to: the Equal Status Acts 2000-2018 are a set of Irish laws designed to combat discrimination and promote equality in various areas of society; they prohibit discrimination on ten specific grounds: gender, age, family status, marital status, religious belief, sexual orientation, race, membership of the Travelling Community and receipt of HAP (and disability).
Very good explanation 4-5 marks; Good 2-3 marks; Fair 0-1 marks.
source: 2025 State Exam - Section A, Short Answer Questions: Q1 (d)

prompt:
According to the CSO, 85% of candidates who sat Construction Studies (HL) in the Leaving Certificate in 2023 were male, while 88% of candidates who sat Home Economics (HL) were female.
Comment on these statistics in the context of educational equality/inequality in Ireland.
(5 marks)
model_answer: The figures suggest that equal access to subjects does not lead to equal outcomes. Gender stereotypes still shape choices: Kathleen Lynch notes Ireland traditionally saw women as carers and homemakers and men as breadwinners. Subject availability also matters, as single-sex schools may not offer both subjects. These choices can lead to gender-based careers and help explain the gender pay gap later in life. Lynch would want equality of condition, not just equality of access.
marking_scheme:
5 marks. Responses may refer to: the theories of Kathleen Lynch; subject availability in different schools; gender stereotypes in schools; gender-based career choices.
Very good commentary 4-5 marks; Good 2-3 marks; Fair 0-1 marks.

prompt:
"Being poor controls how you see yourself, how you trust and speak, how you see the world and how you dream." Katriona O'Sullivan.
What is the relevance of this statement in the context of social class in Ireland?
(5 marks)
model_answer: The quote shows that social class shapes more than money. Bourdieu argued that cultural capital (accent, speech, knowing how the system works) and social capital (connections) give middle-class children an advantage, so education reproduces class inequality. Poorer families face insecure housing: over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023. Wealthier students buy grinds to gain CAO points. This limits social mobility and how high poorer young people dare to 'dream'.

prompt:
Describe two functions of the President of Ireland.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
1. The President signs all bills passed by the Dáil and Seanad into law. If unsure whether a bill is constitutional, the President can refer it to the Supreme Court, acting as a check and balance.
2. The President formally appoints the Taoiseach and Government and appoints judges on the Government's advice. The President also dissolves the Dáil on the Taoiseach's advice.

prompt:
In the context of sustainable development, how may technology help us solve our environmental problems?

Neoliberals argue market forces will drive investment in clean energy, making it cheaper. The European Green Deal invests in green technology to make the EU climate neutral by 2050. prompt:
Explain the main difference between direct and indirect discrimination.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Direct discrimination is when a person is openly treated less favourably because of one of the protected grounds, for example losing a job because of their sexual orientation.
Indirect discrimination is when a rule seems neutral and does not intend to discriminate, but still disadvantages a group. For example, a job advert requiring a minimum height may exclude more women. The main difference is intention and openness.
marking_scheme:
5 marks. Responses may refer to: direct discrimination occurs when an individual is treated less favourably than another person in a similar situation specifically because of a protected characteristic; indirect discrimination occurs when a seemingly neutral policy, rule or practice disproportionately disadvantages people with a particular protected characteristic compared to others.
Very good explanation 4-5 marks; Good 2-3 marks; Fair 0-1 marks.
source: 2025 State Exam - Section A, Short Answer Questions: Q1 (k)

prompt:
Name and briefly describe one non-democratic system of government.
(5 marks)

Name: Military dictatorship (junta).

There are no free elections, and a small group makes all decisions. Opposition is suppressed. prompt:
Describe two ways language diversity is protected within the European Union (EU).

prompt:
Name the Key Thinker associated with The Capabilities Approach. Briefly explain this theory.
(5 marks)
model_answer:
Key Thinker: Martha Nussbaum.

prompt:
Document A: Adapted from EU Post-electoral survey 2024

The European Parliament's 2024 post-electoral Eurobarometer looks at citizens' voting behaviour in the recent European elections, at the main issues driving citizens' voting decisions and at their attitudes towards the EU and the European Parliament.

Cost of living is citizens' main concern at the start of the new legislature: Rising prices and the cost of living (42%) and the economic situation (41%) are the main topics that motivated European citizens to vote in the last European elections in June 2024. A third of voters (34%) say that the international situation is a topic that encouraged them to vote, while a similar proportion mentions defending democracy and the rule of law (32%). Those who did not vote also say the cost of living (46%) and the economic situation (36%) could have motivated them to participate in the elections.

Evolution of EU turnout (%): 1979: 62 | 1989: 58 | 1999: 50 | 2009: 43 | 2014: 43 | 2019: 51 | 2024: 51 (no change since 2019)

2024 EU turnout depending on...
Gender: men 53% | women 50%
Age: 15-24: 36% | 25-39: 46% | 40-54: 51% | 55+: 58%
Image of the EU: positive 67% | neutral 42% | negative 36%

European elections - a democratic habit: The study also suggests that voting in European elections has become a democratic habit for many citizens. Asked why they voted, 46% of voters say they always do, while 42% say it is their duty as citizens, and 20% say they want to support the political party they feel close to.

Background: The European Parliament's post-electoral Eurobarometer survey was carried out by Verian research agency between 13 June and 8 July 2024 in all 27 EU Member States. The survey was conducted face-to-face, with video interviews (CAVI) used additionally in Czechia, Denmark, Finland and Malta. 26,349 interviews were conducted in total. EU results were weighted according to the size of the population in each country.

(10 marks)
model_answer: Document A shows that economic worries were the main reasons for voting. Rising prices and the cost of living motivated 42% of voters, and the economic situation motivated 41%. A third (34%) said the international situation encouraged them, and 32% voted to defend democracy and the rule of law. Voting has also become a 'democratic habit': 46% say they always vote, 42% see it as their duty as citizens, and 20% want to support the party they feel close to.

10 marks. Responses may refer to: cost of living; economic situation; international situation; defending democracy and rule of law; democratic habit etc.

(Source: europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/3292 - Adapted)

Question 2 (c): Comment on the European election turnout of 51% in Document A.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
A turnout of 51% means almost half of EU citizens did not vote, which weakens the European Parliament's claim to represent everyone, even though it is the only directly elected EU body.
Over time, turnout was highest in 1979 (62%). It fell steadily to 43% in 2009 and 2014, then recovered to 51% in 2019 and stayed the same in 2024. So the decline has stopped, but turnout has not returned to its early level.
The breakdown shows who is under-represented. Turnout rose with age: only 36% of 15-24 year olds voted compared with 58% of those aged 55+. This means older people's priorities may carry more weight. Men (53%) voted slightly more than women (50%).

Question 2 (g): Using the information in both documents and the statement below, what conclusions can we draw about the importance of citizen participation in the context of the social contract?

'Man's capacity for justice makes democracy possible, but man's inclination to injustice makes democracy necessary.' - Reinhold Niebuhr
(50 marks)
model_answer:
The social contract is an agreement in which citizens give up some freedom in return for protection and order from the state. Niebuhr's quote shows why participation is vital: because people can be just, they can govern themselves, but because people can also act unjustly, citizens must hold power to account.
Conclusion 1: Participation gives government its legitimacy. John Locke argued that a government without the continuous consent of the people is illegitimate. Voting is the main way consent is given. In Document A, 42% of voters said voting is their duty as citizens and 46% always vote, showing many people accept their side of the contract. But an EU turnout of only 51% means almost half did not give that consent.
Conclusion 2: Low participation lets some groups be ignored. Only 36% of 15-24 year olds voted, against 58% of those aged 55+. If young people do not vote, decisions on housing or climate (39% and 22% in Document B's top three) may not reflect their interests. This links to Niebuhr: those with power may act unjustly towards those who are absent.
Conclusion 3: Some citizens have lost trust in the contract. In Document B, 10% of non-voters said 'my vote doesn't matter' and 14% were not interested. Those with a negative image of the EU had a turnout of just 36%. When people feel the state does not protect them, for example from the cost of living, which 49% of Irish voters ranked highly, they may withdraw. Hobbes argued citizens owe obedience only if the state protects them.
Conclusion 4: Barriers must be removed. 25% were away from home and 13% were not registered. The state has a duty to make participation easy, for example for people with disabilities, whom the Electoral Commission specifically studied.
Overall, the documents show participation is the citizens' part of the social contract and the best guard against injustice. Without strong participation, democracy becomes less representative, as Niebuhr warns.

prompt:
Critically assess if increasing inequality poses a threat to the functioning of democracies around the world.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a national and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
A democracy needs more than elections. It needs basic human rights for all, a free press, an equal right to vote and good governance. This essay argues that increasing inequality is a real threat to democracy, because it gives the rich more power over decisions, the media and education, while the poor lose trust and stop taking part. I will use Karl Marx and John Rawls, with Robert Nozick as a counter-argument, and evidence from Ireland and abroad.

Inequality concentrates power
Marx argued that in capitalism the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, hold power over the proletariat, who only have their labour to sell. When wealth is concentrated, political power follows. Noam Chomsky's propaganda model supports this: media are owned by large corporations and 'serve, and propagandize on behalf of, the powerful societal interests that control and finance them'. In Ireland, Reporters Without Borders said in 2019 that highly concentrated media ownership was the 'single largest threat' to press freedom; Denis O'Brien's group once controlled about 40% of media ownership. If a wealthy few shape the news, citizens cannot make fully informed choices, and democracy is weakened.

Inequality excludes people from participation
Inequality also decides who gets heard. Bourdieu showed that cultural and social capital give middle-class families an advantage, so education reproduces class inequality. Kathleen Lynch found that wealthier students use grinds: ESRI data showed about 63% of students in the highest income group took grinds compared with about 33% in the lowest. Those who reach elite courses and jobs then dominate positions of power. Women, too, remain under-represented: only 22.5% of TDs in 2020, leaving Ireland 98th in the world. When parliament does not look like the people, laws may not reflect their needs.

Inequality breeds distrust and unrest
The housing crisis shows the danger. Over 11,000 people were homeless in 2023, over 3,000 of them children, while the average Dublin house cost over €430,000. Protests such as the Winter of Housing Discontent (2021) show anger that the state is failing its side of the social contract. Rising housing and cost-of-living pressures were also linked to anti-refugee protests and the November 2023 riots in Dublin. Globally, Eriksen argues that globalisation is 'too fast, unequal and uneven', leaving people powerless; this helped drive Brexit, where 49% of Leave voters wanted decisions 'taken in the UK'. Populists exploit this anger, which can threaten minorities and democratic values.

Counter-argument: democracies can correct inequality
Not everyone agrees. Nozick argued that inequality is not unjust if wealth was gained legitimately, and that taxing to redistribute is like 'forced labour'. For him, a minimal state protects freedom better than a large welfare state. There is also evidence that democracies can reduce inequality. The ESRI (2020) found that Ireland has the most unequal income in the EU before taxes and benefits, yet no tax system in Europe does more to reduce it. The CSO found that without social welfare almost four in ten people would be in poverty. Rawls would support this: inequalities are only acceptable if they benefit the least well off. This suggests inequality is a threat mainly when democracies stop redistributing.

Evaluation
Weighing these views, I believe Nozick underestimates how wealth turns into political power. Ireland's welfare state shows democracies can respond, but rising homelessness, media concentration and low representation of women and poorer groups show the response is incomplete. Globally, Andre Gunder Frank's dependency theory shows inequality between nations also limits the democratic choices of poorer countries, for example when IMF loans to Sierra Leone required cuts to health and education.

Conclusion
Increasing inequality is a serious threat to democracy. It concentrates power, shapes the media, limits participation and breeds distrust that populists exploit. Democracy is not doomed, as Ireland's tax and welfare system shows, but it must actively reduce inequality, as Rawls argued, if it wants all citizens to keep faith in the social contract.

Evidence (20): identifies and interrogates a broad range of relevant, authoritative and credible sources of evidence (18-20, 14-17, 10-13, 5-9, 0-4).

Evaluation (15): integrates comparative / alternative perspectives; draws insightful, independent conclusions and justifies own position (13-15, 10-12, 7-9, 4-6, 0-3).

prompt:
Critically analyse if the right to protest is essential in a democracy and whether it supports democratic principles.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least two theorists, one of whom must be named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
The right to peaceful protest falls under freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. It is protected by the Irish Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights and Articles 19 and 20 of the UDHR. This essay argues that protest is essential in a democracy because it lets people 'speak truth to power', but that it supports democratic principles only when it respects the rights of others. I will use John Locke and Thomas Hobbes, and refer to Chomsky.

Protest holds power to account
Locke argued that government rests on the trust and continuous consent of the people, and that citizens may resist when power is abused. Protest is a peaceful form of this. In Ireland, the first Pride parade in 1983 highlighted violence against LGBTQ+ people after the killing of Declan Flynn. Campaigning by David Norris and others led to decriminalisation in 1993 and, in 2015, Ireland became the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by public vote (62% yes). Protest helped bring rights to a marginalised group. Globally, Martin Luther King, Gandhi and Mandela used civil disobedience - refusing to obey unjust laws - to win civil rights and independence.

Protest gives a voice to those without one
Protest lets people who cannot vote, such as under-18s, show how they feel. Greta Thunberg's school strike grew into Fridays For Future. On 15 March 2019 over 1.4 million students protested in more than 125 countries, and over 11,000 marched on Dáil Éireann. FFF Ireland also campaigned to lower the voting age to 16. Housing protests, such as the Winter of Housing Discontent in 2021, show government where people want resources focused. This supports democratic principles of participation and equality.

Protest can threaten democratic principles
Hobbes would disagree. He believed citizens give up the right to rebel when they sign the social contract, and that protest threatens stability and leads to chaos. Recent Irish events show this risk. Anti-refugee protests included threats to burn hotels housing refugees, and in November 2023 far-right riots broke out on O'Connell Street, Dublin, fuelled by false information on social media. President Higgins condemned those 'sowing hate and building fear'. Such protests attack the rights of minorities, so they do not support democracy. The law must therefore balance free expression with protecting others, as the new hate offences legislation tries to do, although critics say it may limit free speech.

States that suppress protest
How a state treats protest is a test of democracy. In Catalonia in 2017, Spanish police used force, seized ballots and assaulted voters at an illegal independence referendum. In Iran, unelected bodies control the media and security forces and suppress opposition. Chomsky warns that power is illegitimate unless it can be justified, and that the media often side with elites and give 'flak' to those who challenge them. Without the right to protest, citizens lose a key check on government between elections.

Evaluation
Hobbes is right that protest can become violent, as the 2023 riots show. But his answer - giving all power to the Leviathan - would remove the freedoms democracy exists to protect. Locke's view is more convincing: peaceful protest is part of consent and accountability. The difference lies in aims and methods. Protest that seeks equal rights, like Pride or FFF, strengthens democracy; protest that spreads hate undermines it.

Conclusion
The right to protest is essential in a democracy. It holds power to account, gives a voice to the excluded and has driven major change in Ireland and abroad. It supports democratic principles when it is peaceful and respects the rights of others, which is why the state must protect it while also protecting minorities from hate.

"A lie can travel half way around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." - Mark Twain.
Discuss the impact of misinformation and disinformation through the use of new media in the modern world.
[Your answer should include contemporary examples and evidence from a local and/or global context to support your argument. You should also refer to the ideas of at least one theorist named on your course.]
(100 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction
Mark Twain's quote describes the modern world well. New media, such as social media, podcasts and the internet, let anyone share information instantly with no gatekeepers. Misinformation is false information shared by mistake; disinformation is false information shared deliberately to mislead. This essay argues that both damage trust, public health and social harmony, and can threaten democracy, though new media also brings benefits. I will use Noam Chomsky and Martha Nussbaum.

Impact on public health
False claims spread fast online. A false claim on social media that the HPV vaccine causes infertility led some parents to refuse vaccination, although there was no evidence. During Covid-19 the Irish government set up a Communications Committee to oversee factual material, and the WHO created a 'Myth Busters' website. This shows that the truth often has to chase the lie, exactly as Twain said.

Impact on social harmony
Disinformation can turn communities against each other. In Ireland, social media spread false information and rumours about migrants at a time of housing and cost-of-living pressure. This fed anti-refugee protests and the far-right riots on O'Connell Street in November 2023. Chomsky's propaganda model explains how a 'common enemy', such as immigrants or Travellers, is used to channel public fear. Echo chambers make this worse: people only see views that match their own, so false beliefs are never challenged.

Impact on trust and democracy
The Reuters Digital News Report 2019 found 61% of Irish people were 'very' or 'extremely worried' about stories made up for political or commercial reasons, though only 17% recalled seeing such disinformation. Facebook as a news source in Ireland fell from 67% (2018) to 63% (2022), while 74% still trusted 'most news', mainly RTÉ (2022). This suggests people turn back to trusted traditional media. Nussbaum warns that without critical thinking we get 'a democracy in which people talk to each other but never have a genuine dialogue'; voters who only absorb what they are told cannot make informed choices.

The other side: benefits of new media
New media is not only harmful. Citizen journalism amplified minority voices during the Arab Spring and showed war footage from Syria and human rights abuses that might otherwise be censored. It shifts power away from a few media owners - important in Ireland, where Reporters Without Borders called concentrated ownership the 'single largest threat' to press freedom. Chomsky himself argues traditional mass media 'manufacture consent' for elites, so new media can challenge them. However, citizen journalists are untrained, publish quickly rather than carefully, and can give a platform to far-right views.

Responses: regulation and education
Ireland has acted. The Online Safety and Media Regulation Act created a Media Commission and an Online Safety Commissioner, with binding codes and financial sanctions, and the EU Digital Services Act requires platforms to protect minors. Supporters say this protects democracy; opponents say regulation can silence unpopular opinions and minorities. In my view regulation must be paired with education: media literacy and critical thinking, as Nussbaum and Freire argue, help citizens ask 'what have they left out?'.

Conclusion
Misinformation and disinformation spread through new media harm public health, stir up hatred against minorities and weaken trust in democracy. New media also gives a voice to people silenced by powerful owners, so the answer is not to shut it down. A mix of fair regulation and critical education is the best way to help the truth 'put on its shoes' faster.
